objectives: To investigate the risk perception of professionals regarding prefabricated buildings when adopting the EPC (Engineering-Procurement-Construction) mode in China; to identify major risks, establish a comprehensive risk-assessment system, and construct a grey-fuzzy evaluation method applied to a real case project.
problem_statement: Existing studies on prefabricated buildings in China rarely link risks to the EPC delivery mode, professional understanding of EPC risk perception is insufficient, and there are limited assessment methods for prefabricated buildings using EPC, despite EPC being promoted as the key organizational mode for prefabricated construction.
methodology: A mixed-methods triangulated approach: literature review to generate an initial list of 30 risk indicators; a questionnaire survey (159 distributed, 137 valid responses, Cronbach's alpha 0.774) of AEC practitioners in the Yangtze Delta region to refine indicators to 27 (7 first-level categories); development of a combined AHP-Entropy Weight Method (AHP-EWM) for indicator weighting; construction of a grey-fuzzy comprehensive evaluation model; application of the model via expert scoring (12 managers/engineers) to a real EPC prefabricated concrete school project in Nanjing, China.
key_background_studies: Jiang et al. [1,2] - SWOT analysis and interviews identifying barriers to prefabricated building adoption in China (lack of codes, standards, incomplete policies)
Razkenari et al. [30] - SWOT framework analyzing offsite construction industry strengths/weaknesses/opportunities/threats in the United States
Nadim and Goulding [31] - argued European reluctance to adopt assembly methods due to past unsuccessful experiences
Rahimian et al. [33] - examined offsite construction risks in Nigeria including negative perceptions and insufficient technical capacity
Gan et al. [3,4] - identified stakeholder collaboration as a key risk in prefabricated building development
Xue et al. [6] - explored relationship between stakeholder cooperative management and cost performance of prefabricated buildings
Pal et al. [47] - investigated subcontractor relationships and their effect on EPC project performance
Gao and Wang [48] - determined main risks faced by EPC general contractors across bidding, design, procurement, and construction stages
Yang et al. [43] - path analysis showing interface management and partnering improve EPC project performance and risk management
findings: The risk-assessment system comprised 7 first-level and 27 second-level risk indicators. Applied to the Nanjing case project, the overall risk evaluation value was 3.3203 (medium risk level). Ranking of first-level indicator weights was: construction (0.4814) > design (0.2298) > procurement (0.0885) > management (0.0864) > nature (0.0570) > policy (0.0251) > economic (0.0318, note order differs slightly). Construction risk, particularly temporary support system instability (weight 0.4956) and design risk (particularly insufficiently in-depth design, weight 0.3420) were the dominant risk factors. The general contractor under EPC bears almost all project risks across design, procurement, and construction, making integrated management critical.

ideas.idea: Under EPC, the general contractor assumes nearly total responsibility for design, procurement, and construction, shifting most project risk from owner to contractor.
ideas.quote: The general contractor is responsible for the design, procurement, and construction of the whole project, and finally delivers it to the developer in good condition

ideas.idea: EPC is positioned as a solution to fragmentation and poor integration across the prefabricated construction supply chain (design, production, transportation, hoisting).
ideas.quote: integrated project delivery (e.g., EPC) could be a potential approach to overcome these barriers in fragmented construction

ideas.idea: Design risk in prefabricated EPC projects centers heavily on insufficiently in-depth design and poor coordination between design and other disciplines/stages.
ideas.quote: the design risk mainly lay in the in-depth design, which had a weight of 0.3420, ranking first in the design risk category

ideas.idea: Procurement in EPC can be integrated with design because material and component needs are determined at the design stage, allowing purchasing staff, designers, and engineers to jointly select options.
ideas.quote: the materials required for the whole process of a construction project are also determined in the design stage. The purchasing personnel can share the product model, market price, and supplier information with designers and engineers

ideas.idea: Construction risk, especially temporary support system stability for precast components, is the dominant risk category in EPC prefabricated projects, exceeding design, procurement, and management risks.
ideas.quote: In this project, construction risk occupied the largest weight, which means that it was the biggest obstacle to the smooth implementation of the project.

ideas.idea: Quality defects and transportation damage of precast components are major procurement-stage risks requiring supplier vetting and incentive systems.
ideas.quote: the general contractor should establish a sound material supplier review system to ensure that their qualifications meet the requirements of the project

ideas.idea: Because EPC contracts are typically fixed-price with the contractor bearing most risk, economic risks such as developer payment delays and rising material costs are significant contractual concerns.
ideas.quote: in the EPC mode some developers may deliberately delay payment for completed engineering tasks or force contractors to bring money into the contract and drive the price down excessively

ideas.idea: Insufficient project management experience and poor communication/coordination between units are recurring management risks in EPC prefabricated projects, requiring integrated supply chain management capability beyond simple superposition of design, procurement and construction.
ideas.quote: EPC general contracting management is not simply the superposition of design, production, procurement, and hoisting. It goes beyond the project to the level of business operation and development strategy.

ideas.idea: Policy and regulatory environment significantly affects risk levels, with regions having more mature prefabrication policies experiencing lower policy-related risk.
ideas.quote: policy had the least impact on the final determination of the risk level...Jiangsu has more beneficial policies, in terms of both technology and management, which provide a guarantee for the advancement of prefabricated buildings.

ideas.idea: There is a scarcity of research and standard practice directly addressing the intersection of prefabricated building risks with the EPC delivery model, representing an ongoing knowledge gap relevant to contractual frameworks.
ideas.quote: there are still few assembly-type projects using EPC, which meant that our research lacked a certain amount of data support

objectives: To conduct a systematic literature review identifying the causes of disputes in construction projects and to develop a comprehensive typology and conceptual framework of these causes, including their interrelationships (antecedent and descendant causes), with a particular focus on payment delays.
problem_statement: Despite extensive prior research on construction disputes and dispute avoidance mechanisms, disputes continue to occur and cause severe repercussions throughout project life cycles. Existing classifications of dispute causes are fragmented and limited in scope, and there is no systematic framework mapping the interrelationships (antecedent/descendant) among causes, leaving a gap in understanding the underlying dynamics of disputes needed for proactive management.
methodology: A systematic literature review following the PRISMA flow diagram was conducted using Scopus and Web of Science databases. An initial 2,816 articles were identified via a search string on disputes, causes, avoidance, mitigation and resolution in construction; after removing duplicates and screening titles/abstracts/full texts, 43 articles (published 2013-2023) were selected for detailed review. Causes were extracted, deduplicated, and classified into categories informed by contract theory, systems theory, and behavioral economic theory. Frequency counts of causes across studies were used to identify significant causes, and a conceptual framework was developed using process modeling technique, with payment delays analyzed in depth as a case for antecedent/descendant relationships.
key_background_studies: Wang et al. 2023b - classified dispute causes into delay-related, communication, contractual, site conditions, design problems categories
Titus et al. 2023 - categorized disputes into contract incompleteness and opportunism, studied Nigerian construction industry
Alrasheed et al. 2023 - proposed four dispute classifications (abnormal conditions, financial, delays, project management) based on Kuwaiti court cases, found payment delays as top cause
Arar et al. 2022 - identified multiple dispute categories including owner/contractor/design/contract-related factors in Quebec
El-Sayegh et al. 2020 - classified causes as owner-related, designer-related, contractor-related, contractual, and other; studied UAE bidding and design issues
Cheung and Pang 2012 - classified disputes via risk/uncertainty, collaborative conflict, contract incompleteness; defined opportunism
Francis et al. 2022 - identified payment delay as most frequent dispute cause in Sri Lankan building projects, discussed client administration issues
Mahamid 2016 - classified causes into direct and indirect categories
Rahnamayiezekavat et al. 2022 - found contract incompleteness and payment delays as frequent dispute causes in Australian projects
Hansen and Nindartin 2022 - classified disputes into owner/consultant/contractor-related categories from Indonesian case studies
findings: The review identified 136 causes of disputes across 12 main dispute categories (payment/financial, delay, design/scope, contract, bidding, project management, client administration, quality, risk, claim/dispute management, behavioral/professional, external factors), aligned with contract theory, systems theory, and behavioral economic theory. Payment delays by clients emerged as the most critical and frequently cited cause (28/43 studies), followed by scope of work changes, ambiguities in contract documents, poor quality of work, and progress delays by contractor. Disputes occur in both developed and developing countries, though specific causes vary by context. A conceptual framework was developed showing antecedent causes (e.g., contractor cash flow issues, budget overruns, poor quality work) and descendant causes (e.g., bankruptcy, work suspension, further delays) of payment delays, along with instruments for evaluating payment delay disputes (payment schedules, invoices, correspondence). The study concludes that understanding these causal interrelationships is essential for proactive dispute avoidance strategies.

ideas.idea: Payment delays by clients are the single most significant and pervasive cause of construction disputes across countries and contract types.
ideas.quote: Payment delays by client were quoted by the majority of studies (28 out of 43).

ideas.idea: Contractual ambiguity, incompleteness, and poor drafting are major drivers of disputes because they lead to differing interpretations of obligations.
ideas.quote: a poorly drafted contract causes disputes between the parties, as the project is based on an inadequate agreement, leading to miscommunication between the parties.

ideas.idea: Scope changes and variations, especially those initiated by clients or owners, are a leading contractual/design-related dispute trigger.
ideas.quote: Scope changes often arise from client's requests particularly when the project client lacks familiarity with the building construction.

ideas.idea: Unfair risk allocation, where owners transfer risk to contractors, is identified as a recurring contract-related cause of disputes.
ideas.quote: Unfair risk allocation, owner transfer risk to contractor

ideas.idea: Design errors and incomplete design information (e.g., missing details, ambiguous drawings) are significant contractual/technical triggers for disputes, often linked to time pressures on designers.
ideas.quote: the time limitation in the design phase is seen in several projects. When the designer is limited by time, the quality of the design will be adversely affected, and this ultimately leads to design-related disputes in projects.

ideas.idea: Delay-related disputes often stem from extension-of-time (EOT) claims being rejected or under-compensated by consultants, illustrating a contractual claims-administration weakness.
ideas.quote: In some cases, though the extension of time (EOT) claims are submitted as per the timeframe, the consultant failed to approve it on time. All the EOT claims became disputed at the end (Francis et al. 2022).

ideas.idea: Contract incompleteness (ambiguity, deficiency, inconsistency, defectiveness) is a foundational, frequently neglected cause of disputes that should be addressed early in project life cycles.
ideas.quote: Rahnamayiezekavat et al. (2022) pointed out that contract incompleteness is the most frequent factor contributing to disputes, usually neglected in the early stage of projects.

ideas.idea: Bidding-stage issues such as inaccurate cost estimation, unbalanced bidding, and inadequate tender documentation set the stage for later contractual disputes.
ideas.quote: the major common causes comprise inaccurate cost estimates, inappropriate tender documents, nonproper or untimely notification of errors in a submitted bid, nonproper or untimely notification of errors in tender documents, and noncompliance with request for proposals requirements.

ideas.idea: Differing site conditions and unforeseen risks are recognized contractual claim triggers, often leading to compensation disputes over additional costs and time.
ideas.quote: The contractors encountered several instances of differing site conditions, prompting them to seek extra compensation from project owners. These requests subsequently turn into disputes (Shabana and Gad 2023).

ideas.idea: Poor communication and opportunistic/adversarial behavior among contracting parties exacerbate ambiguity in contract terms and lead to disputes, reflecting behavioral economic dynamics of contracts.
ideas.quote: incomplete contracts allow for opportunism to flourish and define opportunism at work as a circumstance in which a person tries to maximize his interest in any situation in which he stands to benefit in some way.

ideas.idea: Causes of disputes are interrelated as antecedent and descendant factors, meaning contractual provisions addressing one cause (e.g., payment terms) can have cascading effects on other risks (e.g., quality, delay, insolvency).
ideas.quote: progress delay by contractor [B01] and poor quality/standard of work [H01] are found to be antecedent as well as descendant causes.

objectives: To present a fundamental understanding of modular/prefabricated construction systems and to suggest an appropriate construction procurement method, based on project type, that addresses the administrative/managerial shortcomings of modular construction in order to achieve sustainable modular construction.
problem_statement: Modular/prefabricated construction offers benefits (speed, cost, quality, safety) but design professionals often neglect the intensive administrative and coordination work needed between factory and on-site activities; selecting an inappropriate procurement method can undermine design and coordination outcomes, especially in complex applications like precast concrete construction.
methodology: A literature-based conceptual study using a hypothetical 20-story urban office building case to explore modular design options (precast concrete structural framework, precast architectural cladding, and prefabricated MEP service modules). Conclusions from three key prior works (Torre 1994, Gibb 1999, Schoenborn 2012) are synthesized and applied to evaluate procurement and project delivery methods appropriate for modular components.
key_background_studies: de la Torre, M.L. (1994) - Thesis reviewing modular construction practices, advantages/disadvantages, and industry survey; central source for cost, schedule, and coordination implications of modular construction.

Gibb, A.G.F. (1999) - Textbook 'Off-site fabrication' providing case studies (e.g., Modified Roof Erection System, Embankment Place, Scottish Widows HQ, Crown House Engineering) and implications for procurement strategies (strategic partnering, two-stage tendering, nominated suppliers) and design coordination.

Schoenborn, J.M. (2012) - Thesis identifying constraints and barriers to design innovation in modular construction via case studies of five construction companies; modern perspective on benefits/constraints and BIM's role.

Precast/Pre-stressed Concrete Institute (brochure) - Source promoting total precast concrete construction, comparing costs and schedule benefits of total precast vs mixed/steel/site-cast systems for multi-story office buildings.
findings: Total precast concrete construction is identified as the most effective modular structural system for a hypothetical 20-story office building, offering reduced schedule (about five weeks faster) and lower costs compared to mixed steel/precast or site-cast systems. Precast concrete architectural panels are also advantageous for exterior cladding. However, precast concrete construction requires extensive early administrative and design coordination that is often beyond the architect's capacity, favoring the use of a construction management firm to handle procurement, scheduling, and project engineering. Traditional design-bid-build delivery is unsuitable because it prevents early involvement of specialty manufacturers/contractors; design-negotiate-build is an improvement, but integrated project delivery (IPD) is identified as the best method because it allows early determination of designers and contractors, enabling simultaneous design, fabrication, and construction activities. Service modules (MEP) also offer time and cost savings if coordinated closely with the precast structural schedule and if contractors/suppliers are involved early. Overall, success in modular/prefabricated construction depends on early, complete communication and coordination among owners, architects, manufacturers, and contractors, and on procurement/delivery methods that support such early involvement.

ideas.idea: Selecting an appropriate procurement method is essential to address the administrative and coordination burdens of modular/prefabricated construction, which are often neglected by design professionals focused on design perfection.
ideas.quote: Because the design professionals need to concentrate on perfecting the modular design, the intensive administrative work may be neglected.

ideas.idea: Modular construction requires early involvement of contractors and suppliers during the design phase to allow overlap between design and procurement activities, disadvantaging traditional delivery methods where the contractor is excluded from design.
ideas.quote: An important point raised by Torre is that an overlap of design and procurement activities is highly desirable in modular construction. This may put traditionally delivered projects at a disadvantage because the contractor cannot be involved in the design phase.

ideas.idea: Modular/prefabricated construction increases certain construction management responsibilities, including more complex planning, scheduling, and design coordination across fabrication, transportation, and installation.
ideas.quote: Another problem with prefabrication is an increase in some construction management responsibilities. Planning and scheduling will be more complex due to the extensive amount of fabrication, transportation, and intensive erection procedures.

ideas.idea: Trustworthy procurement of modular components is difficult because specialty suppliers and subcontractors must be heavily and early involved in the project, unlike conventional procurement.
ideas.quote: Trustworthy procurement of modular components is much more difficult to achieve because specialty suppliers and subcontractors must be heavily involved early in the project.

ideas.idea: Coordination between multiple trades is increasingly necessary when prefabricated modules combine different building systems, especially where no single contractor can perform all the work.
ideas.quote: Of course, modules that encompass materials from different trades require increased coordination between subcontractors if there is not one contractor capable of performing all the work.

ideas.idea: Certain procurement strategies—strategic partnering, two-stage tendering, and nominated suppliers—can facilitate faster and better-planned project delivery when using off-site fabrication.
ideas.quote: Strategic partnering refers to an owner working repeatedly with reliable suppliers and contractors. Two-stage tendering refers to these suppliers and contractors submitting initial offers early in the project to help the owner and architect make better selections.

ideas.idea: Because of the technical complexity of prefabrication, construction management or design-build delivery methods are recommended over traditional approaches.
ideas.quote: The last suggestion is to choose construction management or design-build as a project delivery method due to the technicalities involved with prefabrication.

ideas.idea: Design-bid-build delivery is unsuitable for total precast concrete construction because it prevents early collaboration between the architect, precast manufacturer, and installation contractor.
ideas.quote: A design-bid-build process is undesirable because early involvement with the precast manufacturer and the installation contractor is necessary.

ideas.idea: Design-negotiate-build offers a slight improvement over design-bid-build by allowing selection of experienced general contractors who likely have prior relationships with precast suppliers.
ideas.quote: The design-negotiate-build method is a slight improvement because only competent and experienced general contractors can be selected, and the chosen general contractor likely will have previous experience with the other parties.

ideas.idea: Owners can mitigate coordination risk by contracting separately with the precast supplier/specialty contractor and then engaging a general contractor for remaining work.
ideas.quote: One way for the owner to eliminate the potential for problems between companies is to form separate contracts with a supplier and specialty contractor to perform the precast concrete work.

ideas.idea: Because architects and building engineers are not well suited to the intensive administrative demands of precast construction, delegating this work to a construction management firm is recommended.
ideas.quote: Because the design firm needs to concentrate on perfecting the modular design, the intensive administrative work should be delegated to a construction management firm.

ideas.idea: Integrated project delivery (IPD) is identified as the best delivery method for total precast concrete construction because it allows designers and contractors to be selected before the final design concept is set, enabling concurrent design and construction activities.
ideas.quote: The best solution for a total precast concrete construction project is to implement integrated project delivery. Under this method, the designers and contractors are determined before the final concept of the project is realized.

ideas.idea: Structural modular building requires all project parties to coordinate from the very beginning since subsequent work depends on the building envelope being completed.
ideas.quote: Structural modular building requires all parties to the project to coordinate their efforts from the beginning, since the remaining work relies on the building being enclosed.

ideas.idea: Service modules should only be used when the owner and agents are confident in the contractor's competence to perform the specialized handling, storage, and installation work required.
ideas.quote: Service modules should only be used if the owner and his agents are satisfied that the contractor is competent to perform the work.

ideas.idea: Successful coordination of multiple modular systems (precast structure and service modules) depends on early and complete communication between all contractors and suppliers.
ideas.quote: The advantages of using multiple modular construction methods is contingent upon early and complete communication between all contractors and suppliers involved.

objectives: To propose a dynamic compensation mechanism and associated genetic algorithm-based optimisation models that enable general contractors and off-site component factories to jointly manage schedule deviations and achieve just-in-time (JIT) component delivery, thereby reducing component delivery waste.
problem_statement: Off-site construction (OSC) supply chains are fragmented and prone to production deviations, causing either excess inventory for general contractors (when assembly is delayed) or factory overtime/waste (when production timing shifts). Existing static compensation mechanisms force factories to absorb demand fluctuations without incentivising general contractors to control schedule deviations, and little research addresses how to jointly optimise component delivery date changes between the two parties.
methodology: Conceptual and mathematical modelling study: a literature review identifies gaps in engineer-to-order production, JIT delivery, and compensation/incentive systems in construction; a dynamic compensation mechanism (an 'inverse Kanban' table of surcharges/incentives released by factories) is proposed; two mathematical optimisation models (Scenario 1: minimising general contractor's total cost when assembly is delayed; Scenario 2: maximising incentive revenue when contractor trades schedule flexibility) are formulated and solved using a genetic algorithm (MATLAB R2020a GA solver) with illustrative numerical examples (20 components) and sensitivity analyses on inventory capacity and surcharge/incentive levels.
key_background_studies: Ohno (1988/foundational TPS work) [22] - defines waste in the Toyota Production System including inventory as most significant secondary-waste-causing waste, foundation for JIT concept
Koskela (1992) [35] - defined lean construction waste as non-value-adding activities, key to framing component delivery waste
Luo et al. [7] - reported poor communication/coordination in OSC supply chains causing inventory, transportation and handling waste, motivating the study's problem framing

Pheng and Chuan (1997/2001) [47,78] - showed complete JIT delivery is impractical in construction due to interdependence, and reported contractors' willingness to pay for flexible delivery, informing the compensation mechanism rationale
Khalfan et al. [79] - described a supplier-Kanban JIT system in UK public procurement, an example of information-sharing based JIT delivery relevant to the inverse Kanban concept proposed

National and AIA California Council (2007) [70] - defined Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) as a collaborative, incentive-based delivery approach, contrasted with the study's proposed operational-level compensation mechanism
Ju et al. [72] - proposed 'incentive pool' reward mechanisms and redistribution of responsibilities to lower-cost parties, informing the dynamic compensation design
Chen et al. [67] - developed JIT ready-mix concrete coordination approach to revise orders for demand variation, an analogous but non-ETO JIT delivery system
Gosling et al. [58]; Gosling and Naim [56] - identified uncertainty factors in engineer-to-order (ETO) production relevant to OSC's ETO nature
Viana et al. [46] - reported that a large proportion of on-site components are stored well before assembly, evidencing the inventory waste problem
findings: The study concludes that static, fixed compensation schemes in existing literature fail to reflect the real-time, dynamic cost of delivery date changes and do not motivate general contractors to control schedule deviations. The proposed dynamic compensation mechanism, implemented via an inverse Kanban information-sharing platform, allows factories to assign surcharges or incentives to delivery date changes, enabling general contractors to make optimal delivery decisions. The GA-based optimisation model for Scenario 1 dramatically reduces total cost (in the example, from over $1 million to about $21,560, a ~98% saving) when assembly schedules are delayed. Sensitivity analysis shows total cost reduction is highly sensitive to on-site inventory capacity and surcharge/incentive levels when inventory capacity is low. The Scenario 2 model shows general contractors can profitably trade schedule flexibility for factory incentives (maximum revenue $1,800 in the example), though solutions are infeasible under very tight schedule constraints. Overall, the framework helps both general contractors and factories reduce component delivery waste when either party has motivation to change the original delivery schedule.

ideas.idea: Fragmentation between off-site prefabrication and on-site assembly creates a complex, hard-to-manage supply chain with poor collaboration and information sharing between contractors and factories.
ideas.quote: The fragmentation of prefabrication and assembly, however, makes the supply chain difficult to manage.

ideas.idea: General contractors and subcontractors/factories often have a mistrustful, conflicting relationship, which undermines coordination in OSC delivery.
ideas.quote: The general contractors and the subcontractors usually have a mistrustful and conflicting relationship [8].

ideas.idea: Existing compensation/incentive systems for JIT delivery are static and place all responsibility for managing demand fluctuation on the factory/supplier, without incentivising the general contractor to control its own schedule changes.
ideas.quote: With the aforementioned inter-organizational just-in-time delivery systems, they pay fixed compensation, regardless of whether or how many general contractors change the component delivery date. The suppliers assume all the responsibility of handling demand fluctuation.

ideas.idea: Because factories and general contractors are separate for-profit entities with different goals, true just-in-time delivery cannot occur naturally without financial incentives or compensation mechanisms.
ideas.quote: Because factories and general contractors are independent for-profit organizations, just-in-time delivery cannot be achieved naturally.

ideas.idea: Component delivery date changes generate quantifiable waste in the form of additional inventory, double handling, and factory overtime costs, distinct from strategic win-win contracting approaches like IPD.
ideas.quote: Component delivery, however, is an operational-level activity. The cost of a component delivery date change is quantifiable, and solutions would not naturally produce tactical win-win outcomes, even if it is not always zero-sum.

ideas.idea: General contractors typically have limited on-site inventory capacity, forcing them to rely on costly third-party warehousing when assembly schedules are delayed relative to delivery.
ideas.quote: Due to the limited capacity of on-site warehouses, general contractors have to lease nearby land [47] or use the logistics providers’ warehouse to store excessive components [48, 49].

ideas.idea: A significant proportion of delivered off-site components sit unused in on-site warehouses for extended periods before assembly, indicating substantial non-value-added inventory waste.
ideas.quote: Viana et al. [46] reported that 60% of the components in on-site warehouses would be assembled more than ten days after they are delivered.

ideas.idea: Information technology and shared information platforms are essential to enable real-time visibility of production status and coordinate delivery date changes between contractors and factories, but this requires contractual/organisational mechanisms since parties are financially independent.
ideas.quote: An information system holds shared information to facilitate coordination between the general contractor and the factory.

ideas.idea: A dynamic, quantitative compensation mechanism (surcharges for unfavourable changes, incentives for favourable ones) can more fairly reflect the real-time cost impact of delivery date changes than fixed compensation, better motivating both parties to coordinate.
ideas.quote: The factory dynamically assigns a positive number as a surcharge for compensation to the date change which increases its cost (e.g., additional inventory). In contrast, the factory allocates a negative number as an incentive to the favourable change.

ideas.idea: General contractors possess schedule float that can be strategically traded for financial incentives offered by factories, turning schedule flexibility into a tradable resource in contractual delivery arrangements.
ideas.quote: A general contractor usually has float time as a production resource [52, 53] for timely project completion [54]... float time can allow for an adjustment to the assembly schedule, thereby enabling the factory to change the component delivery date.

ideas.idea: Precedence relationships between construction activities and contractually specified maximum allowances for schedule changes act as binding constraints on how much delivery dates can be renegotiated.
ideas.quote: The proposed methodology is subject to the following criteria: precedence relationship of activities and the maximum allowance for a date change of specific tasks which the general contractor specifies.

objectives: To develop an adaptive mechanism using smart contracts to encode and manage constraints causing production bottlenecks in prefabricated construction, quantifying constraint impacts via simulation and Shapley value analysis to determine fair reward/penalty payment rules, and to validate the framework through blockchain-based smart contract execution.
problem_statement: While smart contracts show promise in streamlining construction management by encoding predefined consensus, they lack the flexibility to handle unexpected events and complex, dynamic constraint interactions in construction environments. There is a gap in converting intangible process-level constraints into tangible, smart-contract-manageable consensus that quantifies interrelated constraint impacts to enable automated, fair decision-making.
methodology: Case study data was collected from a high-rise residential building project in Singapore using modular construction for Prefabricated Bathroom Unit (PBU) installation, involving 120 PBU installations across three types. Four key constraints (external conditions/weather, material availability, equipment availability, labor availability) were identified with three variability levels each, generating 81 simulation scenarios. A simulation model using historical precipitation and productivity data quantified cost and duration outcomes; the Shapley value algorithm was applied to determine fair reward/penalty allocations among PBU fabricator, crane operator, and installation workers. These scenarios and payment rules were encoded into smart contracts written in Solidity, deployed and tested using Remix-Ethereum IDE and Ganache private blockchain, with validation via test scenario execution.
key_background_studies: Koskela (1999) - identified seven types of constraints (materials, tools/equipment, labor, prerequisite work, design/methods, space, weather) that must be removed during construction planning, forming the basis for constraint classification in this study.
Koskela (2000) - developed the transformation-flow-value (TFV) production theory underpinning the flow perspective on constraint removal and workflow reliability.
Szabo (1994) - coined the term 'smart contract' as a computerized transaction protocol executing contract terms, foundational to the smart contract concept used in this study.
Hunhevicz et al. (2021) - argued that complex construction environments create uncertainties challenging smart contract execution, motivating the need for adaptive/flexible smart contract design.

Hamledari & Fischer (2021a) - noted smart contracts rely heavily on designers to encode consensus and that poorly designed contracts risk irreversible financial loss; also reported smart contracts improve information-sharing accuracy by 200% over digital payment tools.

Lu et al. (2021) - proposed turning construction resources into smart construction objects with awareness/autonomy properties enabling blockchain communication, informing the 'Check' mechanism concept.
Wu et al. (2021) - proposed formal ontology to represent constraints in construction quality regulations to improve blockchain interoperability and auto-generation of smart contracts.
X. Li et al. (2022) - highlighted challenges in developing adaptive smart contracts addressing constraints, risks, and disturbances without redundancy.

Chen, Liu, Zhang, et al. (2023) - conducted a simulation study on prerequisite work readiness as a primary constraint for smart contracts to enforce reliable critical path workflow, directly preceding this study's approach.
Hamzeh et al. (2015, 2016) - identified that constraint removal during make-ready impacts lookahead plans and project duration.
Liu et al. (2011) - demonstrated a positive relationship between workflow reliability and constraint removal via case study.
findings: The simulation showed that weather significantly increases project duration (up to 23.62% longer in wet vs dry weather) and crane idle time while decreasing installation worker wait time, indicating installation workers become the production bottleneck under adverse weather. Without weather considerations, PBU delivery reliability was the dominant contributing factor to project success; with weather considered, installation worker availability became the dominant contributor, especially as conditions worsened. The Shapley value method successfully quantified fair reward/penalty allocations for each constraint-responsible party across 81 scenarios (108 including no-weather baseline). Smart contracts encoded with these scenarios and payment rules were successfully validated in a blockchain testing environment (Remix-Ethereum, Ganache), correctly identifying scenario conditions and disbursing appropriate payments automatically, demonstrating the framework's validity for decentralized, situation-aware constraint management.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automate and enforce fair payment mechanisms tied to constraint removal performance, reducing reliance on centralized project manager intervention.
ideas.quote: Smart contracts can assist construction managers to motivate reliable production and minimize waste caused by bottlenecks in the system.

ideas.idea: A core challenge for smart contracts in construction is their inability to handle unexpected events and complex, dynamic environments, since their 'intelligence' is limited by human-designed consensus.
ideas.quote: the inability of smart contracts to handle unexpected events under complicated environments posited challenges in realizing it automatically.

ideas.idea: Poor smart contract design carries real financial risk, underscoring the need for careful, adaptive consensus design in construction contracting.
ideas.quote: Poorly designed smart contracts may lead to irreversible financial loss (Hamledari & Fischer, 2021a).

ideas.idea: Prefabricated/modular construction introduces unique coordination constraints among fabricator, logistics (crane), and on-site installation that must be contractually managed to avoid bottlenecks.
ideas.quote: The major constraints included uncertain and out-of-sequence PBU arrival due to the fabricator's preference for producing PBUs in a large batch, crane unavailability due to fully scheduled lifting activities, and a minimal number of workers assigned for installation to maximize profitability.

ideas.idea: Fair allocation of risk and reward among project participants (fabricator, equipment provider, labor) can be quantitatively determined using cooperative game theory (Shapley value), suggesting a data-driven approach to contractual payment terms.
ideas.quote: a Shapley value approach was used to determine fair reward/penalty sharing rules.

ideas.idea: External/environmental conditions (e.g., weather) function as a contractually significant constraint that shifts bottleneck responsibility among parties, implying that contracts should account for variable environmental risk allocation in prefabricated projects.
ideas.quote: These results suggest that severe weather (increased precipitation intensity) can increase project duration and crane idle time, while putting more pressure on installation workers.

ideas.idea: Automated smart contracts can shift constraint management from reactive problem-solving to proactive make-ready planning, a concept directly relevant to how MMC/prefabrication projects could restructure contractual administration.
ideas.quote: the smart contract focuses on the make-ready process, proactively avoiding situations where crews wait for conditions to mature instead of reactively resolving them with centralized control intervention.

ideas.idea: Existing standard contract frameworks are not designed to model the multiple interacting constraint types (only 4 of Koskela's 7 were modeled here) relevant to modern prefabricated construction, indicating a gap that contracts (including standard forms) need to address.
ideas.quote: this research only considered the four major constraints that impacted the projects in smart contracts, whereas Koskela (1999) suggested that at least seven types of constraints should be removed during construction planning.

objectives: To provide a comprehensive, holistic, and up-to-date mixed (scientometric and systematic) review of 172 journal articles on construction cash flow, identifying leading authors, keyword clusters, research themes, methods, gaps, and future directions; and to develop a conceptual blockchain-based smart contract payment framework for modular integrated construction (MiC) projects to address identified gaps.
problem_statement: Despite numerous studies on construction cash flow, no comprehensive review focused specifically on cash flow as the main topic exists; prior reviews focus broadly on construction finance, lack quantitative scientometric analysis, and rarely examine methods (e.g., BIM, AI) used to address cash flow issues. There is also a lack of research on cash flow analysis for offsite/modular construction and on automated, technology-enabled payment mechanisms for these fragmented, complex supply chains.
methodology: A mixed review methodology combining scientometric (quantitative, using VOSviewer for co-authorship and keyword co-occurrence analysis) and systematic (qualitative, full-text) reviews. Data were extracted from Scopus using cash-flow and construction-related keywords, yielding 1575 documents; inclusion/exclusion criteria (journal articles, engineering subject area, English) reduced this to 366; PRISMA screening and snowballing techniques resulted in 172 included articles. These were classified into five thematic categories (cash flow factors, cash flow-based schedule, cash flow-based capital structure, cash flow-based project type, cash flow and digitalization) and mapped against research methods used, to identify gaps and propose a conceptual blockchain/smart-contract payment framework for MiC projects.
key_background_studies: Elazouni and Gab-Allah (initiated 'finance-based scheduling', integrating scheduling and cash flow modeling)
Kaka and Price [52,97] (surveyed contractor budgeting practices and developed S-curve profiles for different project types)
Zayed and Liu [42] (identified 43 factors impacting contractor cash flow in USA/China using Monte Carlo simulation)
Ikediashi and Okolie [61] (assessed 31 factors impacting cash flow in Nigerian construction via questionnaire survey)
Elghaish et al. [56,86,93] (developed BIM/blockchain/smart contract-based automated payment and IPD risk/reward systems)
Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez [91] (smart contract for progress payment security and dispute reduction)
Sigalov et al. [94] and Sonmez et al. [87] (combined BIM with smart contracts/blockchain for automated progress payments)
Ali and Elazouni [99] (integrated LOB/CPM techniques for cash flow of repetitive non-serial projects)
Le et al. [62] (grouped multiple factors—financial risk, retention, receivables, cost, macro environment—affecting cash flow)
Al-Joburi et al. [63] (assessed negative cash flow impacts on Dubai construction firms)
findings: Cash flow research has grown substantially over the last two decades, peaking in 2020; Elazouni A. and Kaka A.P. are among the most productive and cited authors; keyword analysis yields five clusters (risk/uncertainty, scheduling/optimization, cost/capital structure, technology/digitalization, contractor-client relationships). Systematic analysis classifies literature into five categories, with cash flow-based scheduling being the most studied topic and optimization the predominant method overall. Significant gaps exist regarding multi-project consideration, procurement approach integration, offsite/modular construction financing, and fully automated payment systems. The study proposes five future research directions and develops a three-stage (preparation, initialization, execution) blockchain-based smart contract framework to automate and secure progress payments among MiC project stakeholders, reducing reliance on third parties and mitigating payment delays and disputes characteristic of MiC's fragmented supply chains.

ideas.idea: Modular/offsite construction (MiC) projects have complex, fragmented supply chains that make conventional cash flow and payment systems incompatible, creating financial risk for stakeholders.
ideas.quote: Conventional cash flow systems are argued to be incompatible with the fragmented and complex nature of modular construction projects [113,114].

ideas.idea: There is a notable research gap in cash flow analysis specifically for offsite construction (OSC) and modular integrated construction (MiC) projects, despite their high industrialization and prefabrication levels.
ideas.quote: there is an absence in addressing cash flow analysis for offsite construction (OSC) projects, especially modular integrated construction (MiC) projects characterized by the highest level of industrialization and prefabrication among OSC types.

ideas.idea: OSC/MiC projects face higher initial capital costs than conventional construction, which can threaten the financial stability of both clients and contractors.
ideas.quote: The OSC projects are argued to be more expensive due to their high initial capital cost requirement, particularly in the earlier phase of the project [110].

ideas.idea: Procurement/project delivery approach selection significantly affects cash flow, but this relationship is understudied, especially for non-conventional projects like OSC.
ideas.quote: There is an absence found in the literature on the association between project procurement approaches and cash flow analysis... future studies can be directed to examine the effect of selecting various procurement approaches in nonconventional construction projects, namely OSC projects, on the cash flow of the project participants.

ideas.idea: Blockchain and smart contracts offer a decentralized, automated alternative to traditional payment administration, reducing the need for third-party administrators/lawyers and mitigating contractual disputes.
ideas.quote: Through the association between blockchain technology and smart contracts, an endorsement policy, compliant with the contract's terms, is enforced for all participants without the need for the involvement of third parties, reducing the chances of potential conflicts and enhancing the project's financial health [86].

ideas.idea: A proposed three-stage blockchain smart-contract framework (preparation, initialization, execution) can automate progress payments in MiC projects, including defining delivery system, digital identities, billing plans, and confirmation/rejection/partial payment logic.
ideas.quote: Figure 12 comprises three stages to adopt smart contracts in MiC: the preparation stage, the initialization stage, and the execution stage.

ideas.idea: Payment delay by clients is consistently identified as the most significant factor negatively affecting contractor cash flow across multiple studies and contexts.
ideas.quote: payment delays by clients was the most frequent and highest-ranked factor that could affect contractors' cash flow [61,62,64,115–117].

ideas.idea: Existing BIM-blockchain payment systems remain only partially automated, requiring manual updates of schedule and cost data, and typically address only a single project delivery system without considering disputes.
ideas.quote: the developed payment systems only considers specific project delivery system; (2) the developed payment systems by the association between BIM and blockchain technologies were partially automated, where the user needs to update the schedule and cost data manually on the system; (3) the developed systems did not consider the possible disputes among participants when developing the smart contracts.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can incorporate defects liability period (DLP) management, extending automated payment logic beyond simple progress payments into post-completion contractual obligations.
ideas.quote: The study also considered the defects liability period (DLP) of the project by using smart contracts to manage the rest of the duties.

ideas.idea: Traditional contractual payment enforcement relies on third parties such as administrators and lawyers, which is costly and inefficient compared to blockchain-enabled smart contract enforcement.
ideas.quote: the agreed terms of a chosen contract are usually hard to be enforced and subjected to third parties, such as administrators and lawyers, which typically require monthly fees [91].

objectives: To investigate the application of just-in-time (JIT) delivery in off-site/prefabricated construction and to propose a conceptual model that dynamically coordinates contractors and manufacturers through an information-sharing platform and compensation mechanism, reducing time and inventory waste caused by delivery deviations.
problem_statement: When delivery of prefabricated components deviates from schedule due to unexpected events, contractors and manufacturers tend to rigidly comply with existing contracts rather than coordinate, resulting in non-optimal outcomes, excess inventory, overproduction, or overburden waste. Existing static incentive/compensation solutions in the literature do not reflect real-time costs of delivery changes, and no dynamic, decentralized coordination mechanism exists for engineer-to-order (ETO) off-site components.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical paper. The authors review literature on lean construction, Toyota Production System, just-in-time, pull systems and Kanban, information technology applications, and incentive mechanisms in off-site construction, then synthesize a conceptual model comprising a data-sharing platform, a manufacturer-side dynamic resource management system, and a contractor-side optimisation system for dynamic delivery compensation.
key_background_studies: Ohno (1988) - foundational Toyota Production System and just-in-time concepts, defining waste and overproduction
Koskela (2000) - Transformation-Flow-Value theory of lean construction and definition of waste as non-value-adding work
Pheng and Chuan (2001) - study on inventory push behavior by manufacturers and survey showing contractors willing to pay for flexible delivery
Wu and Low (2012) - case study showing manufacturers suffering high inventory levels causing production interruptions
Viana et al. (2013) - study on paid-on-delivery and inventory waiting times in construction
Khalfan et al. (2008) - supplier Kanban implementation in UK public project using quality-price selection for just-in-time delivery
Hsu et al. (2018) - supply chain optimisation coordinating manufacturing, transportation and assembly as integrated process
Im et al. (2009) - pull production system in rebar assembly and precast plant using simulation to reduce inventory
Low and Wu (2005) - investigation of RMC suppliers achieving just-in-time delivery via demand-pull system
Dallasega et al. (2016) - information system enabling component supermarket pull between off-site and on-site activities
findings: The paper concludes that current contractual and business models fail to balance the interests of contractors and manufacturers, leading to suboptimal coordination when schedules deviate. It proposes a conceptual model where manufacturers issue dynamic surcharges or incentives via a shared information platform, and contractors make automated, cost-optimised decisions to adjust delivery/assembly schedules. This dynamic compensation mechanism, based on real-time resource cost rather than static contract-based payments, is expected to reduce inventory, overproduction and overburden waste, encourage early notice of changes, and better balance stakeholder benefits, though contracts remain binding if coordination fails. Future work should validate the model with a case study.

ideas.idea: Contracts, intended as pull mechanisms, instead force rigid compliance and act as push mechanisms when schedule variations occur, preventing coordination.
ideas.quote: The contract originally is a method to pull components from factories; however, it turns into a push to force both sides to stick to the contracts when variations occur.

ideas.idea: Under current contractual arrangements, both contractors and manufacturers handle delivery variations unilaterally rather than coordinating, leading to suboptimal outcomes.
ideas.quote: In these scenarios, both sides deal with variations themselves rather than coordinate with their partners (Pheng and Chuan 2001; Zhai et al. 2018).

ideas.idea: Because contractors and manufacturers are separate profit-making entities, just-in-time delivery cannot be achieved naturally without financial/compensation agreements built into contractual relations.
ideas.quote: As manufacturers and contractors usually belong to different profit-making organisations, just-in-time cannot be implemented as naturally as within an organisation.

ideas.idea: Existing incentive or reimbursement provisions for flexible delivery mentioned in some contracts/practices are static and do not reflect the real-time cost impact of delivery changes.
ideas.quote: Some static incentive solutions in the extant literature cannot perfectly reflect the actual cost caused by the change of delivery dates.

ideas.idea: A dynamic compensation mechanism embedded in a shared information platform—rather than fixed contractual payment terms—could better balance risk and incentivize coordination between contracting parties in off-site construction.
ideas.quote: Unlike static compensation such as additional payment according to contracts' prices and non-lowest tender, the surcharges defined in this research is determined by the real-time cost of the resource consumed at that moment, which can significantly eliminate manufacturers' risk.

ideas.idea: Even with an improved coordination model, original contracts remain binding as a fallback when the involved parties fail to reach a mutually beneficial agreement.
ideas.quote: However, contracts are still binding if both sides fail to reach win-win.

ideas.idea: Selecting suppliers based on quality-price mechanisms rather than lowest tender, combined with contractual obligation to deliver on time, has been used to support just-in-time delivery in public projects.
ideas.quote: A supplier Kanban is introduced to achieve just-in-time delivery in a public project in the UK, where a quality-price mechanism, instead of the lowest tender is taken as the standard for selecting suppliers.

ideas.idea: The division of construction into off-site manufacturing and on-site assembly, coordinated through separate contracts, creates interface risks that can erode the benefits of off-site construction if not properly managed.
ideas.quote: The advantage of off-site construction will be eroded, even cancelled out by increased cost and time if the delivery interface between contractors and manufacturers is not properly managed.

objectives: To harmonize the fragmented literature on Modular integrated Construction (MiC) by quantitatively and qualitatively analyzing bibliometric parameters, identifying research themes and trends, uncovering knowledge gaps, and proposing future research directions in MiC.
problem_statement: While MiC has been increasingly adopted worldwide and studied from specific angles (sustainability, success factors, risks, barriers), no study has comprehensively assessed the full range of knowledge areas integrated with MiC or evaluated the state-of-art research across the field, leaving gaps such as lack of cost analysis, lack of quantitative benefit assessment, and lack of analysis of appropriate project delivery methods and contractual relationships.
methodology: A three-stage multi-stage critical literature review: (1) bibliometric search using iterative keyword strings in Scopus (and Web of Science) yielding 237-238 documents from 1969-2020; (2) quantitative/scientometric analysis using VOSviewer and Gephi to examine countries, sources, co-authors, top-cited articles, and keyword co-occurrence; (3) qualitative thematic analysis of 107 screened articles categorized into six main themes and nine sub-themes (sustainability, construction operations, building design, management aspects, information technology management, others), followed by trend analysis and identification of future research directions.
key_background_studies: Gibb and Isack (2003) - top-cited paper on client perceptions of pre-assembly, foundational conceptual work on MiC drivers
Richard (2005) - conceptual paper on levels of construction manufacturing/industrialized building systems
Kamali and Hewage (2016) - critical review of life cycle performance/sustainability of modular buildings, highly influential
Jin et al. (2018) - prior review of off-site construction (OSC) collectively including MiC, prefabrication, panelized and hybrid construction, but not focused specifically on MiC trends
Wuni and Shen (2019) - study on critical success factors of MiC, used for comparison of country rankings
Wuni et al. (2019) - identification of critical risk factors in MiC
Wuni and Shen (2020a) - review of barriers to MiC adoption across countries
Pan et al. (2018) - review of high-rise MiC building applications
Navaratnam et al. (2019) - review of general MiC performance in a specific location (Australia)
Song et al. (2005) - identification of factors affecting adoption of modularization in industrial plants, widely cited reference
O'Connor et al. (2014) - identification of critical success factors and enablers for industrial modularization
Molavi and Barral (2016) - recommendation of construction management/design-build delivery methods for MiC due to project complexity
Dakhli et al. (2015) - cost comparison between design-build and design-bid-build delivery methods for MiC projects
findings: Quantitative analysis showed almost 50% of MiC literature originates from four countries (USA, Canada, Australia, UK), with the USA leading; top journals include Automation in Construction and Journal of Cleaner Production; keyword mapping revealed seven clusters showing MiC's links to simulation, sustainability, scheduling, structural design and BIM, but notably lacking keywords such as risk, supply chain, contractual relationship, and disputes. Qualitative analysis showed building design and management aspects dominate the literature (~50% combined), followed by construction operations, information technology management, and sustainability. Key gaps identified include: lack of quantitative/cost analysis of MiC benefits, absence of studies on optimum project delivery methods for MiC, and a complete absence of literature addressing the contractual relationships among MiC project participants, risk allocation in contracts, and dispute resolution lessons. The study concludes MiC research needs greater integration across design, construction, and operational aspects, and calls for future work on stakeholder analysis, contractual relationships, standards, cost comparisons, and educational integration.

ideas.idea: The project delivery method significantly affects how MiC projects are managed, coordinated, and reimbursed, yet this has been minimally studied.
ideas.quote: This point is highly affected by the project delivery method which has only been discussed two studies (Dakhli et al., 2015; Molavi and Barral, 2016).

ideas.idea: There is a complete absence of literature addressing the contractual relationships between project participants in MiC, including how standard payment and variation mechanisms should adapt.
ideas.quote: a potential knowledge gap is identified as none of the consulted literature has addressed the contractual relationship between various project participants in MiC projects.

ideas.idea: Key contractual questions remain unanswered regarding advance payments, fixed design implications, variation orders, and insurance for module transportation in MiC projects.
ideas.quote: will the advance payment for the contractor be adjusted due to the increased initial amount of money required for materials? How will the employers deal with the issue of early fixed design? How can the variation order procedures be adjusted to suit this new construction method? How the contractor's care for the works will be addressed during the transportation of modules? Will there be an additional insurance policy for modules transportation in the contract?

ideas.idea: The literature has not examined disputes between MiC project stakeholders despite the likelihood that conflicts occur in real projects, and lessons from such disputes could aid smoother MiC adoption.
ideas.quote: the literature has not covered cases of disputes between project stakeholders, even though it is hardly believable that all MiC projects around the world were completed without conflicts.

ideas.idea: Although risks in MiC have been studied, there is no clear discussion of how risks should be allocated contractually, and standard forms of contract have not been assessed for suitability in MiC projects.
ideas.quote: risks in MiC projects have been adequately addressed in the literature (Li et al., 2013; Wuni et al., 2019). Nevertheless, no risk allocation to has been clearly discussed, which is expected to be included in the contract conditions. Standard forms of contract (FIDIC, NEC, etc.) are formed based on risk sharing. However, the literature is yet to assess the suitability of applying these forms in MiC projects.

ideas.idea: Early contractor involvement is essential for successful MiC project delivery but existing literature fails to identify the best project delivery method for MiC.
ideas.quote: Early contractor involvement is key in MiC projects. However, this could be achieved through multiple project delivery methods such as DB, integrated project delivery, EPC, BOT, and so on. However, existing literature failed to present the best project delivery method.

ideas.idea: The design stage in MiC requires special management involving early contractor/supplier engagement and shared design liability, which affects contractual arrangements.
ideas.quote: The contractor or supplier should be involved from the beginning and accordingly, shall share in the design liability.

ideas.idea: Construction management or design-build delivery methods are recommended over traditional methods due to the complexity of MiC projects, enabling better coordination and communication.
ideas.quote: construction management (CM) or design-build (DB) project delivery method was recommended due to complexity of the project (Molavi and Barral, 2016).

ideas.idea: Comparative cost studies show design-build delivery is more effective for MiC because it allows earlier contractor involvement in the design stage compared to design-bid-build.
ideas.quote: Through two case study projects (DB and design bid build- DBB), cost comparison ranked DB as more effective as it allowed the involvement of the contractor in design stage (Dakhli et al., 2015).

ideas.idea: Keyword co-occurrence analysis reveals that important contractual and risk-related terms are largely absent from the MiC literature, indicating an underexplored area.
ideas.quote: the keywords identified lacked important and critical keywords, such as supply chain, risk, contractual relationship, and disputes.

objectives: To critically review published studies applying natural language processing (NLP) to address legal issues in construction, evaluate the achievements and limitations of existing NLP frameworks, and propose a roadmap for future research on NLP applications for legal texts in construction.
problem_statement: Legal issues such as disputes, claims, and litigation are common in construction projects due to ambiguous, biased, or incomplete contractual language and inefficient manual compliance checking against regulations; the body of knowledge lacks a holistic understanding of existing NLP frameworks addressing these issues and the gaps that merit further research.
methodology: A structured literature review following a modified four-step methodology (Arksey and O'Malley 2005): defining research questions and scope; keyword-based search across databases (Google Scholar, ASCE Library, Engineering Village, Web of Science, Scopus, etc.) using terms like 'construction', 'legal issues', 'disputes', 'litigation', 'claims', 'contracts', 'NLP'; screening of 45 initially collected articles down to 28 relevant articles (19 journal, 9 conference) via abstract/conclusion review; and in-depth critical review and synthesis of the screened articles, categorized by legal document type (contracts, regulatory codes/standards, legal cases).
key_background_studies: Lee et al. (2019) - developed rule-based NLP model to detect poisonous FIDIC clauses biased toward owners, central example of contract risk detection
Chakrabarti et al. (2019) - developed 'risk-o-meter' ML-based model outperforming rule-based approaches for risk-prone clause detection
Caldas et al. (2002) and Caldas and Soibelman (2003) - pioneering ML-based classification of contract documents into topical/CSI categories
Hassan et al. (2020) and Hassan and Le (2021) - ML and deep learning models for extracting subcontractor scope from design-build contracts
Zhang and El-Gohary (2016a, 2016b, 2017) - series of studies on automated compliance checking, information extraction from codes, and BIM schema extension using NLP
Curtotti and McCreath (2011) - corpus profiling study distinguishing contract language from general English to reduce ambiguity
Jallan et al. (2019) - used LDA topic modeling on legal case data to identify patterns in construction defect litigation
Fan and Li (2013) and Zou et al. (2017) - developed semantic similarity-based case retrieval systems for legal case libraries
Salama and El-Gohary (2013) - ML-based classification of regulatory provisions into compliance categories, foundational for automated compliance checking research
findings: Existing NLP research in construction legal issues is categorized into three themes: contract review (ambiguity detection, poisonous clause detection, requirement structuring), compliance checking with laws/regulations (classification, rule extraction, BIM compliance), and legal case analysis (defect pattern analysis, similar case retrieval). Machine learning approaches, particularly SVM, generally outperform rule-based approaches but require larger datasets; rule-based approaches remain valuable due to data scarcity in construction. Most existing models are proof-of-concept, tested on limited datasets, and lack real-world validation. Key limitations include lack of domain-specific datasets, insufficient integration of contextual/domain knowledge, and lack of practitioner validation. Future research should address contract drafting assistance, automated contract review (including owner obligations), text simplification for readability, requirement change impact tracing, early-stage compliance checking, construction safety violation assessment, and court outcome prediction.

ideas.idea: Ambiguity and vagueness in contract language is a major cause of disputes and misinterpretation of roles and obligations.
ideas.quote: Examples of well-known linguistic issues of construction contracts include vagueness and ambiguities (Çevikol and Aydemir 2019) or biased clauses that shift risk to one party (Lee et al. 2019).

ideas.idea: Owners sometimes deliberately insert biased or 'poisonous' clauses into contracts to shift risk onto contractors, a recurring contractual risk allocation issue.
ideas.quote: The client often maliciously modifies the contractual terms and specifications to shift risks to the contractors (Lee et al. 2019).

ideas.idea: Incomplete contractual requirements, including in subcontracts, are a recurring source of disputes and rework.
ideas.quote: Mitkus and Mitkus (2014) found that contracts with incomplete requirements often lead to design changes and associated disputes... incomplete project requirements in a subcontract often lead to disagreements among the contracting parties (Sun and Meng 2009).

ideas.idea: NLP-based classification models can automatically extract subcontractor scope from design-build contracts, helping delineate contractual responsibilities among disciplines.
ideas.quote: A few authors also developed NLP models for structuring the requirements of DB contracts to support automated subcontract scope extraction.

ideas.idea: Automated detection of risk-prone or poisonous clauses using NLP can help parties recognize unfavorable contractual terms before signing, relevant to risk allocation practices in standard contracts.
ideas.quote: Another model developed by Lee et al. (2019) used rule-based NLP to detect poisonous FIDIC clauses that are more biasedly favorable to the owner.

ideas.idea: Standard form contracts such as FIDIC and AIA differ in how they define owner obligations (e.g., permits, approvals), which is an important but understudied contractual issue.
ideas.quote: For instance, FIDIC contracts demand that the owner provide assistance in document preparation only in obtaining approvals, whereas ConsensusDOCS contracts require the owner to pay as well to obtain approvals and permits.

ideas.idea: Most existing NLP-based contract research emphasizes contractor obligations while owner obligations remain relatively unexamined, despite their significance for disputes.
ideas.quote: Furthermore, most previous studies on contract administration were orientated towards contractor obligations (Caldas et al. 2002; Hassan and Le 2021). However, owners also have several obligations in a project...

ideas.idea: Changes to contractual requirements during execution can have cascading impacts on other requirements, and tracing these impacts is an unresolved need relevant to contract administration.
ideas.quote: Assessing the impact of the changes made for a specific requirement on other requirements in the contract is essential to maintain the consistency and correctness of requirements.

ideas.idea: Compliance checking against design codes and regulations, if automated, could reduce design errors, rework, and associated legal/financial issues, but existing methods apply late in design when errors are costly to fix.
ideas.quote: Existing NLP models for compliance checking assumed that a set of requirements applicable to the project is given. Thus, they are only applicable to the later design phase when a complete BIM model has been developed. Any errors found at this stage will be costly to fix.

ideas.idea: Legal case data analysis (e.g., defect litigation) can reveal recurring contractual and process failures that inform prevention strategies for future projects.
ideas.quote: This developed automated framework can help project participants to understand better the construction defects that lead to legal cases in the past. Subsequently, this knowledge can reveal the root causes of defects to prevent similar issues and costly litigation in future projects.

objectives: To explore how specialist construction consultancy firms operating in a fragmented construction sector can develop their own product platforms, and to examine how this process addresses industry fragmentation across vertical, horizontal, and longitudinal dimensions.
problem_statement: While product platforms have been studied in manufacturing and in construction contexts where product-based firms (e.g., house builders) develop platforms independently of project delivery, little is known about how specialist, project-based construction consultancy firms (architects, contractors) operating in a fragmented and competitive industry can develop their own product platforms while continuing to deliver projects.
methodology: An explanatory single case study of a UK construction consultancy firm (pseudonym ABC) and its architectural partner (DEF), based on 15 semi-structured interviews with platform leadership and delivery teams (Aug 2019-Dec 2020), plus 3 additional interviews with industry experts and 4 informal conversations, supplemented by review of public reports, site visits, and industrial steering committee discussions. Data were analyzed incident-by-incident using constant comparison, with diagrammatic memo-writing and validation via a feedback session with ABC's Senior Vice President.
key_background_studies: Nam and Tatum (1992) - describe four strategies for overcoming vertical fragmentation between project phases: acquisition, non-contractual alignment, contracts, and information integration
Sheffer and Levitt (2010) - framework for the three dimensions of construction fragmentation (vertical, horizontal, longitudinal) adapted for this paper
Simpson et al. (2001) - distinguish top-down vs bottom-up approaches to product platform development
Lessing (2006) - distinguishes technical platform (product) from process platform (delivery process), central to the paper's platform typology
Jansson et al. (2014) - identify 'platform support methods' ensuring new components are coordinated with existing ones before admission to a platform
Johannesson et al. (2017) - detailed top-down platform development phases (conceptual, system, detailed modelling)
Kudsk et al. (2013) - bottom-up platform development example for balcony/shaft modules
Veenstra et al. (2006) - early bottom-up case study of platform development for an existing house builder
Barlow et al. (2003) and Winch (2003)/Wikner and Rudberg (2005) - distinguish engineering-to-order delivery models and separation of design/engineering from physical product flows
Gosling et al. (2017) - detailed description of ETO design/engineering delivery phase, assuming linear sequential completion
Maxwell and Aitchison (2017) and Lidelöw et al. (2015) - distinguish platform core from service layer/novelty, and open vs closed platform governance
Robertson and Ulrich (1998) and Meyer and Lehnerd (1997) - foundational manufacturing literature on product platform benefits and components
findings: The case shows that ABC and DEF developed a product platform iteratively while delivering client-funded projects, rather than as a standalone top-down or bottom-up exercise. They created two distinct platforms: a digital product development platform ('digital warehouse') containing coordinated, information-rich design components, and a process platform defining assembly. By vertically and horizontally consolidating design, engineering, and manufacturing capabilities within the design/engineering phase, ABC achieved full specification of components and processes before procurement, enabling vertical coordination between engineering and manufacturing to be managed through fully specified contracts rather than acquisition of manufacturing assets. This in-phase consolidation reduced decision deferral, minimized on-site problem-solving and finishing, and allowed construction delivery to more closely resemble the linear, sequential models found in manufacturing. Longitudinal fragmentation was addressed by retaining the same team across projects and reusing the digital warehouse, enabling organizational learning. The study highlights institutional and procurement-related barriers, such as traditional tendering processes and planning authority requirements, that challenge wider adoption of such platforms.

ideas.idea: Traditional construction procurement defers final specification decisions using 'or equal approved' clauses, creating inefficiencies and compromising spatial and design efficiency.
ideas.quote: early specifiers caveat their outline product specification with "or equal approved". This provides the ultimate product specifier with flexibility in procurement.

ideas.idea: Vertical coordination between engineering and manufacturing phases can be achieved through a fully specified contract instead of acquisition of production facilities, avoiding asset redundancy risk.
ideas.quote: vertical coordination between engineering and manufacturing phases can be managed by a fully specified contract, rather than acquisition.

ideas.idea: Contracts struck under incomplete designs, a common vertical coordination mechanism in construction, tend to lead to costly litigation.
ideas.quote: the historical reliance on contracts as vertical coordinating mechanisms between phases, struck almost entirely under incomplete designs, can lead to costly litigation (Li et al. 2012).

ideas.idea: Full specification of building components and assembly processes prior to contracting reduces transaction costs and enables competitive procurement without conflict.
ideas.quote: Transaction costs are minimized in this exchange through the complete specification of the contract.

ideas.idea: Sub-contracting of design and delivery to multiple specialist firms results in 'margins on margins', a loss of value that fully coordinated platform delivery avoids.
ideas.quote: early, complete and concurrent specification of all aspects of the building design avoided the need for design deferral and trade design, reducing designed-in inefficiency and the loss of value associated with the sub-contracting of the design phase, that is, no more "margins on margins" (interview 6).

ideas.idea: Deferred design decisions in traditional procurement protect clients through competitive tendering but create incentives for suppliers to reduce quality to capture value.
ideas.quote: Decision deferral does protect clients, ensuring value at each client procurement stage through competitive tendering, and minimizing losses if a project does not come to fruition.
