ideas.idea: Sensitivity of unit penalty costs (representing contractual or project-specific consequences of early/late delivery) directly shapes contractor decision-making about trade-offs between compliance and cost savings.
ideas.quote: When the unit penalty cost is low, decision makers may be more inclined to choose early or late deliveries to save fuel costs and drivers’ salaries. When the unit penalty cost is high, they are more likely to comply with the time window of modules to avoid paying high penalties.

objectives: To increase understanding of the logistics service value co-creation process in construction, specifically examining how value is manifested in construction logistics setups (CLS) from different actors' perspectives and what drives and maintains the value co-creation process.
problem_statement: There is a lack of awareness among construction actors regarding the importance of logistics and how it creates value; value co-creation processes involving multiple actors (main contractors, subcontractors, TPL providers) in modularised construction logistics setups have been mainly conceptually elaborated but lack empirical implementation studies, particularly regarding how modularisation affects coordination and value creation in loosely coupled construction systems.
methodology: A single in-depth case study of a modularised CLS at a major office building construction project in Gothenburg, Sweden, consisting of three logistics service modules (material management, on-site VMI, and waste management) operated by different TPL providers. Data collection involved four workshops with the main contractor's logistics managers and project supervisor to develop service blueprints, followed by five semi-structured interviews with representatives from the main contractor, subcontractor, and three TPL providers. Additional data (annual reports, news articles, websites) supplemented interviews. Analysis used service blueprinting technique (Bitner et al. 2007) to visualise service design, and interview coding to categorise values into technical, monetary, and perceived value dimensions.
key_background_studies: Dubois and Gadde (2002b) - conceptualise construction logistics as a loosely coupled system, foundational to the study's theoretical framing
Bygballe and Jahre (2009) - project-centric adaptive strategy in construction management, used to explain subcontractor behavior
Bygballe et al. (2010) - argue for broader multi-actor perspective beyond dyadic relationships to improve project outcomes
Crespin-Mazet et al. (2015) - stress mutual trust and resource adaptation streamline processes and reduce risks in construction relationships
Eriksson et al. (2021) - conceptualise CLS as complex service systems and suggest different actors value different services
Fredriksson et al. (2021) - define CLS and describe on-site/off-site logistics service modules
Janne and Fredriksson (2021) - discuss early TPL integration and non-voluntary subcontractor customership reducing commitment
Ekeskär et al. (2022) - propose TPL providers facilitate cooperative competition and coordination among main contractors
Yazdanparast et al. (2010) - three-phase value creation model (learning, innovation/execution, outcome) underpinning conceptual framework
Grönroos and Helle (2010), Kilibarda et al. (2013), Chapman et al. (2003), Xiaodi and Li (2013) - define three value dimensions (technical, monetary, perceived) used in analysis
Bankvall et al. (2010) - identify pooled and reciprocal interdependencies in construction requiring coordination
Huang and Wilkinson (2013) - trust built through experience and outcomes, informing discussion of subcontractor trust development
Håkansson and Ingemansson (2013) - innovation in supplier relationships perspective used to frame contribution
findings: Value co-creation in the loosely coupled construction system is driven by trust and commitment, which require time and patience to develop, especially among non-voluntary subcontractor users. Service blueprinting effectively visualises the connection between service design and value of different service modules, aiding shared understanding. Late involvement of downstream actors (subcontractors) in the co-creation process slows value realization and reduces initial trust/commitment. Modularisation simplifies designing service content but increases the number of actors requiring coordination, meaning modularisation eases service content design but does not simplify service value creation or the co-creation process itself. The main contractor plays a dual role as both customer and supplier (convincing subcontractors to adopt modules). Risks include delayed actor involvement and poor coordination between multiple TPL providers managing different modules.

ideas.idea: Modularisation of logistics services simplifies service content design but does not simplify the overall value co-creation process, since it increases the number of actors that need coordinating.
ideas.quote: Hence, the modularisation simplifies the service content but not the service value creation or the value co-creation process.

ideas.idea: Subcontractors are often non-voluntary users forced by contract to use certain logistics modules, which reduces their commitment and ability to see value from the start.
ideas.quote: Not all actors act as customers of a CLS by choice; instead, the customer relationship can stem from municipal or developer demands on using a CLS to decrease disturbances in the vicinity of construction sites

ideas.idea: Contractual stipulation is the mechanism by which subcontractors are compelled to use logistics service modules, tying use of CLS directly into contract terms between main contractor and subcontractor.
ideas.quote: Its use by subcontractors is stipulated as part of their contract with the main contractor.

ideas.idea: The temporary and project-based nature of construction creates unpredictable resource demands, and contracts leave responsibility for such uncertain events unclear.
ideas.quote: The uncertain nature of construction projects renders resource demands unpredictable, which is a risk, and contracts render the responsibilities for these events uncertain (Loosemore, 1999).

ideas.idea: There is a recurring tension between main contractors and subcontractors where the former view the latter mainly as a source of cost savings, which can lead to unfair practices and erode trust—an issue relevant to how contractual relationships should be structured.
ideas.quote: There is often a tension between main contractors and subcontractors/suppliers, where the former views the latter as key to cost savings, leading to potentially unfair practices and undermining trust (Donato et al. 2015).

ideas.idea: Supply chain and value chain risks tend to be transferred upstream (toward subcontractors/suppliers), damaging trust, reliability, and commitment—an important consideration for contractual risk allocation.
ideas.quote: Deep et al. (2022) identify from the literature review that there is a tendency to transfer the value chain or supply chain risks upstream, which leads to a breach of trust, and lack of reliability and commitment.

ideas.idea: Because construction actors form temporary organisations for each project, trust and coordination mechanisms (including contractual arrangements) must be rebuilt from scratch on every new project, limiting benefits of standardization.
ideas.quote: the construction setting once again introduced hurdles by procuring a new set of modules in the next project, and the co-creation process must start over again.

ideas.idea: The main contractor takes on a dual contractual role, acting simultaneously as a customer of TPL logistics services and as a supplier/enforcer persuading subcontractors to adopt and pay for these mandated services.
ideas.quote: the role of the main contractor as both a customer (user of logistics service modules) and a supplier (convincing the subcontractor to use the logistics service modules) in the co-creation process.

ideas.idea: Lack of coordination among multiple TPL providers servicing different modules is identified as a key risk that can undermine the intended value of a modularised, prefabricated-style service delivery structure.
ideas.quote: potential lack of coordination between service modules, especially with multiple TPL providers.

ideas.idea: Late involvement of downstream contractual parties (subcontractors) in the design/innovation phase of a service delivery system slows down realization of value and mutual understanding, suggesting earlier contractual/practical inclusion could improve outcomes.
ideas.quote: The third contribution is that the late involvement of actors further down the network (e.g. subcontractors) slows down the value co-creation process.

objectives: To systematically review studies on critical success factors (CSFs) for implementing modular integrated construction (MiC) projects published 1993-2019, identifying publication trends, geographical distribution, integrating CSFs into a checklist, and proposing a conceptual model mapping interlinkages among CSFs.
problem_statement: Despite growing academic and industry attention to MiC, a systematic review establishing a common framework of CSFs for MiC implementation is not well-established; existing studies are scattered making it difficult for researchers and practitioners to identify CSFs shared across project types, stages and territories.
methodology: Systematic literature review situated in a realist research paradigm using meta-synthesis and thematic content analysis. Literature search conducted in Scopus using a comprehensive Boolean search string, supplemented by snowballing search strategy, resulting in 55 included publications (1993-2019) spanning journal articles, conference papers, industry reports, books and one PhD thesis. A concept matrix was developed to catalogue CSFs against citing sources, factors ranked by frequency of occurrence, and a stage-gate model and system dynamics-based conceptual causal loop model were developed to map CSFs across project phases and their interdependencies.
key_background_studies: Rockart (1982) - formalized the concept of critical success factors (CSFs) as key areas of activity needed for managers to reach goals.
Martin (1982) - described the CSF methodology as a decision-making tool for prioritizing essential activities.
O'Connor, O'Brien, and Choi (2014) - identified CSFs for industrial MiC projects including timely design freeze and module envelope limitation.
Murtaza, Fisher, and Skibniewski (1993) - identified CSFs for petrochemical MiC projects including early design freeze and standardization.
Kamar, Alshawi, and Hamid (2009) - identified top CSFs for residential MiC projects in Malaysia including training and contractor leadership.
Gibb (2001) - classified pre-assembly degrees of modules in MiC (component manufacture, non-volumetric, volumetric preassembly, modular buildings).
Jonsson and Rudberg (2015) - modified Gibb's classification and highlighted differences between MiC and cast in-situ construction.
Baldwin and Clark (1997, 2000) - provided foundational definitions of modularity and modularization applicable to building construction.
Osei-Kyei and Chan (2015) - reviewed CSFs for public-private partnership projects, providing a comparative CSF review framework.
Antwi-Afari et al. (2018) - reviewed CSFs for BIM implementation, providing a comparative CSF review methodology.
Pan et al. (2007) - discussed improved cooperation between project parties and integration of manufacturers/suppliers in procurement decision-making for MiC.
Tam et al. (2007) - highlighted virtues of design-build delivery method for residential MiC projects and involving contractors at design stage.
Rentschler et al. (2016) - emphasized procurement/contracting strategy for module fabrication and joint design teams.
Choi, O'Connor, and Kim (2016) - noted rising interest in successful planning and execution of MiC projects and CSFs for industrial MiC.
Warszawski (1999) - discussed standardization of design and modules for efficient resource allocation in industrialized building.
findings: The review identified 35 CSFs for implementing MiC projects across 55 studies from 16 countries, with the US, UK, Malaysia, Australia, and Hong Kong as largest contributors. The six most cited CSFs were: good working collaboration/effective communication among participants; effective supply chain management; accurate design and early design freeze; involvement of key participants throughout the project; suitable procurement strategy and contracting; and standardization/benchmarking of best practices. A stage-gate framework mapped CSFs across conception & planning, design & procurement, and construction phases. A conceptual causal loop model using system dynamics revealed mostly reinforcing feedback loops among CSFs, with factors like effective collaboration, systematic economic analysis, and early design freeze being highly interdependent and influential. The findings can inform decision support systems and improve prediction of MiC project success.

ideas.idea: Suitable procurement strategy and contracting, including design-build delivery, is a critical success factor for MiC projects because it integrates design and construction responsibility and encourages early contractor/fabricator involvement.
ideas.quote: Tam et al. (2007) expounded on virtues of using the design-build delivery method for residential MiC projects and highlighted the necessity of involving contractors at the design stage of MiC projects.

ideas.idea: Procurement approaches for MiC should emphasize early integration of manufacturers and suppliers into project decision-making regardless of the specific procurement method chosen.
ideas.quote: Pan et al. (2007) argued that irrespective of the strategy adopted, procurement in MiC projects could be improved through the improved cooperation between project parties and effective integration of manufacturers and suppliers in the project decision-making process as early as a possible.

ideas.idea: Once module fabricators are selected under a contract, there should be minimal interference in their work since the modules are the primary driver in the overall project, implying a contractual allocation of control/responsibility to fabricators.
ideas.quote: Thus, it is prudent to exercise due diligence in the selection of module fabricators... However, once fabricators are selected, there should be less interference in their work since the modules constitute the primary driver in the overall MiC project.

ideas.idea: Early design freeze is essential for MiC success and design changes after freeze are particularly costly and schedule-sensitive, implying contracts should manage change control tightly.
ideas.quote: As design changes are particularly costly, risky and schedule-sensitive in MiC projects, specification, concept and detailed design freezes should be made early to ensure smooth delivery of the projects.

ideas.idea: Fabricators should be given a greater scope of buying production materials and manufacturing when schedule is critical, suggesting contractual scope allocation to fabricators as subcontractors or suppliers.
ideas.quote: Rentschler et al. (2016) recommended that module fabricators should be offered a greater scope of buying all production materials and manufacturing of the modules in a case where the schedule is critical to avoid the emergence of hindrances to performance.

ideas.idea: Risk allocation and management across stakeholders, supply chain, and project execution stages is a critical success factor requiring dedicated contractual and management attention.
ideas.quote: Effective management of stakeholder, supply chain and project execution risks

ideas.idea: The involvement of key participants (owners, designers, fabricators, contractors) throughout all project phases—not just at the outset—is critical, implying contracts should structure ongoing multi-party engagement.
ideas.quote: The services and roles of these project participants are not one-off and do not end immediately after their first involvement in the MiC projects.

ideas.idea: MiC supply chains involve fragmented but interdependent segments (design, manufacturing, transportation, storage, assembly), requiring project planning and control mechanisms to coordinate these stages, which has implications for how contracts allocate responsibility across the supply chain.
ideas.quote: The MiC supply chain involves fragmented but interdependent segments comprising modular design, engineering, manufacturing, transportation, storage, buffer, and on-site assembly, resulting in several uncertainties which could derail the success of MiC projects.

ideas.idea: Owner delay avoidance and timely owner approvals are necessary to enable early design freeze, implying contractual provisions to ensure timely owner decision-making.
ideas.quote: Owner delay avoidance (CSF#24) is required to ensure early design freeze (CSF#8).

ideas.idea: Standardization of modules and best-practice benchmarking reduce costs and improve efficiency but require industry-wide coordination, which may have implications for standard contract terms addressing customization versus standardization.
ideas.quote: Standardization reduces the tendency of producing unique modules to meet the specification of each MiC project.

objectives: To examine the critical success factors (CSFs) for the planning and control of prefabrication housing production (PHP) projects in China, identify underlying relationships among these factors, and provide a useful reference for key stakeholders (designers, manufacturers, contractors) to achieve effective PP&C of PHP.
problem_statement: Although PHP has grown rapidly, especially in China, and is faced with diverse challenges (delays, cost overruns, quality issues), there is no consensus on which factors critically influence its successful implementation. Prior CSF research has focused mainly on management factors or on other project types, overlooking supply chain, technical, and industry-related factors specific to PHP, leaving a gap in systematic understanding.
methodology: A mixed-method approach combining literature review, in-depth interviews and pilot studies with five PHP experts to identify 23 preliminary CSFs; a questionnaire survey (five-point Likert scale) distributed via snowball sampling to 400 designers, manufacturers, and contractors in China, yielding 136 valid responses (34% response rate); data analyzed using mean score (MS) ranking, one-sample t-tests, and exploratory factor analysis (principal component analysis with varimax rotation) using SPSS 19.0.
key_background_studies: Ismail et al. (2012) - identified management factors for PHP, but overlooked supply chain, technical and industry factors, motivating this study's broader scope
Chan et al. (2004) - identified five groups of CSFs for construction projects (project-related, procedures, management actions, human factors, external environment)
Zwikael and Globerson (2006) - explored planning processes and identified most sensitive processes for project success
Ling et al. (2009) - established 24 project practices correlated with project performance, especially risk management
Li et al. (2011) - grouped CSFs for green building projects into five components including project manager competence and designer coordination
Liu et al. (2014) - identified CSFs for PPP infrastructure projects such as feasibility analysis and interface management
O'Connor et al. (2014) - presented 21 CSFs for modularization projects including owner planning resources and fabricator capability
Heravi et al. (2015) - identified four critical stakeholder groups influencing project success
Deng et al. - provided research framework using mean score and factor analysis for inhibiting factors of SI system building
Arif et al. - identified 17 key variables for political risk management using factor analysis and average score methods
Sacks et al. (2004) - proposed automation of design and detailing tasks for precast concrete
Jensen et al. - proposed configuration system supporting design automation via rule sharing between CAD tools
Haller et al. - proposed sequence deviation quotient (SDQ) method to control design iteration risks in PHP
findings: 23 CSFs were identified and validated as significant (mean scores above 3.0). The top five CSFs were: designers' experience of PHP, manufacturers' experience of PHP, project manager's ability to solve problems, maturity of techniques used in the detailed design phase, and persistent policies and incentives. Exploratory factor analysis grouped the 23 factors into five clusters explaining 67.2% of variance: (1) technology and method (dominant cluster, 28.6% variance), (2) information, communication and collaboration, (3) external environment, (4) experience and knowledge, and (5) competence of the project manager. The study concludes that technology/method issues, especially in detailed design and manufacturing, are the most critical determinants of PHP planning and control success in China.

ideas.idea: Design must be substantially finalized before production begins, and design changes are costly due to high rework costs and reduced PHP benefits.
ideas.quote: the design must be largely finished prior to the production. The fast production and assembly of building components need accurate design.

ideas.idea: Architectural design and detailed design of prefabricated components are contractually and organizationally separated in China, with manufacturers acting only as subcontractors for detailed design input.
ideas.quote: The architectural design and the detailed design of prefabricated components in PHP projects are clearly separate in China. This is evidenced by the fact that the manufacturer is only a subcontractor.

ideas.idea: Late delivery by precast component manufacturers is a major issue for main contractors, indicating a key contractual risk in the manufacturer-contractor relationship.
ideas.quote: It has been recognized in PHP projects in Singapore that late delivery by the precast components' manufacturers is the most common issue for the main contractors.

ideas.idea: The project manager plays a central coordinating role between off-site manufacturing and on-site construction activities and is responsible for overall project objectives.
ideas.quote: The project manager is the person in the PHP project who coordinates on-site and off-site activities and is responsible for the project objectives.

ideas.idea: Poor coordination among designers, manufacturers and contractors can cause delays in production, erection schedules, and constructability problems, highlighting the need for early and close collaboration across the supply chain.
ideas.quote: Only when good coordination is achieved among all the key stakeholders involved in a project can problems such as delays in production, erection schedules, and constructability be avoided.

ideas.idea: Early involvement of contractors and manufacturers during the design stage, and of designers during production/construction, is identified as a critical success factor, implying a need for integrated delivery approaches rather than strict sequential contracting.
ideas.quote: involvement of the designer during the production and construction stage, (2) involvement of contractors and manufacturers during the design stage, (3) information sharing among participants, (4) efficient coordination between off-site and on-site, and (5) effective communication among participants.

ideas.idea: Data interoperability limitations between design software (BIM) used by architects and manufacturing software used by fabricators impede integrated detailed design, creating a technical barrier with contractual implications for information exchange.
ideas.quote: numerous limitations related to the information exchange in both geometric shape information and other semantically meaningful information between architects (the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) format) and fabricators (the Standard ACIS Text (SAT) format) have impeded the BIM technology in the detailed design phase.

ideas.idea: Persistent government policies and incentives are necessary to encourage contractor adoption of prefabrication technology when mature systems and market incentives are lacking, suggesting external regulatory/contractual frameworks influence uptake.
ideas.quote: When the PHP is still in its infancy, contractors are more willing to choose a mature method rather than new ones without incentives from local government.

ideas.idea: Lack of manufacturer/contractor expertise and experience can cause conflicts between manufacturers and designers, delays in component delivery, and installation schedule delays—pointing to allocation-of-risk issues in contracts.
ideas.quote: a lack of expertise in components design may cause severe conflicts between manufacturers and designers; a lack of manufacturing experience can cause delays in the flow of deliveries to the construction site; a lack of competence on the part of the contractor can lead to delays in the installation schedule.

ideas.idea: Supplier/manufacturer selection and preordering of materials are important for planning and control, and insufficient competition among qualified precast manufacturers can lead to higher prices, an issue relevant to procurement and contract structuring.
ideas.quote: the supplier selection process is important for the planning and control of appropriate components... If the qualified precast manufacturers are few, a lack of serious competition may lead to higher prices.

objectives: To explore the factors affecting the adoption of Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DfMA) technologies in Singapore's private construction sector, in order to better understand strategies needed to encourage private sector buy-in and operationalize recommendations from the Second Construction Productivity Roadmap.
problem_statement: Despite strong government promotion of prefabrication and DfMA in Singapore, private sector adoption has been slow (only 11.2% of national prefabrication level as of 2001), limiting the industry's ability to achieve productivity targets; the factors driving or hindering adoption are not well understood.
methodology: A questionnaire survey administered via email to developers, contractors, consultants, architects, engineers, and project managers in Singapore, using stratified random sampling from BCA, SIA, Singapore Contractors' Association, and Society of Project Managers directories. 124 surveys sent, 30 valid responses received (24.2% response rate). A pilot interview was conducted first. 17 influencing factors identified from literature review, grouped into six categories (industry, government, stakeholder, design, performance-driven, project-specific factors), rated by respondents and analyzed using one-sample t-tests.
key_background_studies: Boothroyd (2005) - originated the DfMA methodological framework and quantitative evaluation approach for design assemblability
Bogue (2012) - distinguished DfM and DfA approaches and outlined three methods of applying DfMA
Ballard and Howell (1998) - described construction as a design process rooted-in-place requiring site assembly, framing DfMA in construction terms
Gibb and Isack (2003) - classified four levels of off-site production used as a framework for comparing Singapore's DfMA elements
Kamar, Alshawi, and Hamid (2009) - found industry knowledge is critical for successful IBS/prefabrication adoption
Mao, Shen, Pan, and Ye (2015) - identified lack of supporting organizations as an obstacle to prefabrication in China
Park, Yashada, Kim, and Ham (2011) - studied buildability regulations' impact on prefabrication uptake in Singapore

Zakaria, Gajendran, Rose, and Brewer (2018a) and Zakaria, Gajendran, Skitmore, and Brewer (2018b) - reviewed and identified contextual, structural and behavioural factors influencing IBS adoption, informing this study's methodology and factor categorization
Jaillon and Poon (2008, 2010) - identified client support, site constraints, transportation, and design standardization issues as barriers to prefabricated construction in Hong Kong

Blismas and Wakefield (2009), Blismas, Pasquire, and Gibb (2006), Pan, Gibb, and Dainty (2007) - identified reduction in construction time as key driver of off-site construction adoption in Australia and UK
Gerth, Boqvist, Bjelkemyr, and Lindberg (2013) - proposed the 'Design for Construction' (DfC) method as an alternative evaluation framework related to DfMA
findings: All 17 influencing factors were found to have statistically significant positive effects on successful DfMA adoption. 'Reduction in construction time' was the most important factor, followed by 'Site constraints and storage' and 'Integration of project team'. Government-related factors (presence of government legislation and incentives) were rated as least impactful, likely because mandatory requirements already enforce DfMA adoption in Singapore, making incentives less necessary as a driver. Design limitations due to standardization were also rated low in importance, contrary to findings in Hong Kong.

ideas.idea: DfMA is often equated with and treated interchangeably with prefabrication and off-site construction in industry practice and in this study's literature selection.
ideas.quote: In selecting the literature to determine the factors influencing the adoption of DfMA technologies, no distinction was made between DfMA and off-site construction/prefabrication.

ideas.idea: DfMA should be applied early in the design phase rather than after design completion (as with value engineering) to capture maximum cost and productivity savings.
ideas.quote: The former is usually applied in construction after the design stage, when the design has largely been developed, thus missing out on the maximum savings ... DfMA should therefore be applied as part of the design phase.

ideas.idea: Early design freeze is critical for prefabrication projects to specify modular units early, but increases risk for the design team since there is less room for later changes.
ideas.quote: Early design freeze is especially critical in a project involving prefabrication, due to the need for specifications of modular units early on, to ensure timely project completion... This increases the risk taken by the design team, as the room for design changes is reduced.

ideas.idea: Successful DfMA implementation requires integrated, multidisciplinary project teams collaborating from the design phase, contrasting with the construction industry's typically fragmented delivery approach.
ideas.quote: the construction industry has been widely criticized for its fragmented approach to the project delivery process ... for construction projects to carry forward the practice of DfMA, a multidisciplinary team including building design engineers, architects, contractors, and specialists is needed.

ideas.idea: Standardization of components and interfaces creates tension with architectural design flexibility and creativity, a recurring conflict in DfMA/prefabrication adoption.
ideas.quote: the limited number of options available in the market ... and the repetition in design means there is not much room for an architect to be flexible or creative... the conflict between standardization and flexibility has still not been resolved.

ideas.idea: Contractors' willingness to invest capital upfront in prefabrication facilities is a key enabler, and lack of such investment slows adoption, illustrated by a major contractor's substantial capital investment in a prefabrication hub.
ideas.quote: if contractors are unwilling to put the capital upfront to establish specialized prefabrication factories for the adoption of prefabrication technology, the process will be slowed down... Tiong Seng Holdings have invested S$36 million to establish its own multistorey prefabrication hub.

ideas.idea: Government legislation mandating minimum buildable/constructability scores and prefabrication levels on public land sale sites is a direct regulatory lever driving DfMA adoption, though perceived by industry respondents as less influential than performance and project-specific factors.
ideas.quote: the mandatory requirements for prefabrication are enforced in many ways: ... developers will be required to adopt a minimum level of PPVC which shall be at least 65% of the total constructed floor area.

ideas.idea: Government financial incentives (e.g., cost-offset funding) exist to encourage DfMA adoption, but contractual/cost-sharing arrangements among main contractors, prefabricators and MEP subcontractors may discourage SME uptake despite available funding.
ideas.quote: about 40% of the contract sum would be taken by the main building contractors, with the rest going to the prefabricator and MEP (i.e. Mechanical, Electrical and Plumbing) subcontractors. This seems to explain the hesitation of SMEs to consider adopting DfMA technologies.

ideas.idea: Site constraints and lack of on-site storage in dense urban environments are significant barriers to prefabrication adoption, partially mitigated through just-in-time delivery strategies.
ideas.quote: Restricted site layouts pose challenges for the placement of prefabricated modules, which results in the project team being reluctant to adopt prefabrication... adopting just-in-time delivery is a partial solution to a lack of on-site storage areas.

ideas.idea: Transportation logistics (road infrastructure, delivery timing, permits) constitute a critical project-specific consideration affecting the feasibility and cost of off-site production/prefabrication.
ideas.quote: Transportation planning plays an important role in implementing off-site production ... and its cost reduces the profit margin ... the time of delivery, road permits, and protection of works during transportation all need to be taken into account.

ideas.idea: Building Information Modelling (BIM) supports DfMA by enabling digital product data exchange between design and manufacturing/assembly processes, improving standardization and maintainability checking.
ideas.quote: through BIM, digital product data can be exploited in downstream processes and used for the manufacturing and assembly of structural systems.

ideas.idea: Client/developer decision-making is a critical determinant of prefabrication adoption since demand for prefabricated products originates from clients rather than end customers, and misunderstanding of benefits by clients hampers uptake.
ideas.quote: unless client decision-makers understand its benefits and limitations, their misunderstandings and prejudices will continue to hamper further development.

objectives: To design an optimal government-contractor subsidy allocation policy for promoting modular construction (MC) adoption by formulating a bilevel stochastic program that incorporates price and quantity uncertainties, and to develop an exact solution method, validated through a Hong Kong case study.
problem_statement: Existing studies on government subsidy policies for promoting MC adoption rely on deterministic assumptions about future construction volumes, MC prices, and supply quantities, ignoring real-world uncertainties. This can lead to suboptimal subsidy plans that fail to maximize MC adoption within limited government budgets, and existing bilevel models are often solved with heuristic algorithms that sacrifice optimality.
methodology: The study formulates a bilevel two-stage stochastic program where the government (leader) sets a unit subsidy price to maximize MC module usage subject to a budget constraint, and contractors (followers) minimize their total construction costs by choosing between MC modules and cast-in-situ methods under multiple stochastic scenarios of price, supply, and demand. An exact bisection search algorithm is developed exploiting a monotonicity property (Proposition 1) between subsidy price and MC adoption, proven to be polynomially solvable. The model is validated using a real-life Hong Kong case study with 18 districts, 4 Greater Bay Area (GBA) manufacturing factories, 20 stochastic scenarios, and real data on public/private housing construction volumes, MC prices, and transportation costs, solved via CPLEX 12.7.1 in C#.
key_background_studies: Wang et al. (2021) - identified reputational and financial incentives as primary factors influencing contractors' construction method selection among 16 factors, using deterministic parameters.
Yi et al. (2021) - proposed a government-manufacturer subsidy policy using a Stackelberg game framework, showing poorly designed subsidies could increase emissions and reduce adoption.
Yi et al. (2023a) - developed a subsidy scheme analyzing government-manufacturer-contractor relationships, validated with Hong Kong data, but assumed deterministic parameters.
Du et al. (2022) - coordinated precast component supply chains under government subsidies in centralized/decentralized scenarios, deterministic approach.
Jiang et al. (2019) and Gao and Tian (2020) - empirically showed financial subsidies are more effective than technical guidelines or regulations for promoting prefabrication, especially early on.
Du et al. (2023) - used agent-based modeling to compare procurement restriction, carbon credit, and subsidy policies, finding subsidies most motivating for prefabrication adoption.

Shi et al. (2022) and Zhu et al. (2024) - used evolutionary game and Stackelberg game models to study government-contractor interactions but focused on low-carbon policy rather than subsidy design under uncertainty.
Bertram et al. (2019) - provided cost and productivity benchmarks for MC (e.g., 10% higher costs than cast-in-situ, potential 20% savings excluding logistics), used for case study parameterization.
findings: The proposed bilevel stochastic subsidy model, solved via bisection search, increased Hong Kong's MC adoption rate from 10.2% (no subsidy) to 52.3% with an optimal subsidy price of HKD166/ton and average budget use of HKD59.6 million. Considering uncertainty improved MC adoption by 38% compared to a deterministic mean-value approach. Sensitivity analysis showed increasing subsidy budgets yield diminishing returns for adoption rate increases, and cost reductions in MC reduce required subsidy price while increasing adoption. Geographic analysis revealed contractors in northern/central Hong Kong districts are more likely to adopt MC due to lower transportation costs from GBA factories, suggesting phased subsidy rollout strategies. The study concludes that financial subsidies are more effective than other policy types, uncertainty must be incorporated into subsidy design, and diversified procurement strategies should be encouraged to build long-term supply chains between MC manufacturers and contractors.

ideas.idea: High initial and logistics costs are identified as the foremost barrier to MC adoption, motivating the need for subsidy-based cost offset strategies.
ideas.quote: Among these factors, high costs represent the foremost barrier to its widespread adoption (Hong et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2018; The Legislative Council 2022; Li et al. 2024).

ideas.idea: Government financial subsidies are more effective than technical guidelines or compulsory regulations in driving MC adoption, particularly in early development stages.
ideas.quote: The findings of Jiang et al. (2019) were consistent with those of Gao and Tian (2020), emphasizing that financial subsidies are more effective than other types of supportive strategies, especially during the initial encouraging stage of MC development.

ideas.idea: Cross-border transportation and logistics costs for prefabricated modules significantly erode the cost advantages of MC, making contractors reluctant to adopt it without subsidy support.
ideas.quote: However, the cross-border transportation of MCMs incurs extremely high logistics costs, and therefore contractors in Hong Kong have little incentive to adopt this new method (Construction Industry Council 2017).

ideas.idea: Contractors' choice between MC and cast-in-situ construction is fundamentally a cost-minimization decision influenced by subsidy levels, module purchase price, transportation, and assembly costs.
ideas.quote: From the perspective of the contractors, they decide whether to adopt MC, cast-in-situ method, or a mixture of these two methods to perform construction work to minimize their overall costs.

ideas.idea: Subsidy policy design must anticipate contractor responses because government and contractor decisions are interdependent in a leader-follower (bilevel) relationship.
ideas.quote: First, the government, acting as the leader, makes the decision about the unit subsidy price offered to contractors for using MCMs and anticipates the reactions of contractors to its optimal decision.

ideas.idea: Government subsidies can reshape contractor procurement behavior, encouraging diversification of MC supply sources and fostering longer-term supplier relationships.
ideas.quote: government subsidies provide diversified procurement strategies for contractors and facilitate a long-term supply-demand relationship between GBA manufacturers and the Hong Kong contractors.

ideas.idea: Geographic/location-based cost differentials (transportation distance) create uneven MC adoption incentives across regions, suggesting phased subsidy rollout by location.
ideas.quote: This observation highlights the potential for the Hong Kong government to strategically implement phased efforts in promoting the use of MCMs, starting with an emphasis on the northern and central areas and subsequently expanding to the southern area.

ideas.idea: Incorporating real-world uncertainty in construction volume, price, and supply into subsidy policy design meaningfully improves the effectiveness of government incentive schemes compared to deterministic planning.
ideas.quote: the consideration of real-life uncertainties can result in a noteworthy 38% improvement in the adoption of MC compared with the traditional deterministic method.

ideas.idea: There is a practical upper limit on subsidy price to prevent contractors from profiting purely from subsidies rather than genuine cost savings.
ideas.quote: The unit subsidy price α should have a reasonable upper limit, denoted αmax; ... implying that all contractors are not allowed to profit by relying on government subsidies in all scenarios.

ideas.idea: The relationship between subsidy budget size and MC adoption rate exhibits diminishing returns, providing guidance for setting appropriate subsidy budgets.
ideas.quote: The minimum amount of subsidy budget required to increase every 10% of the MC adoption rate progressively increases.

objectives: To identify and categorize the principal challenges to implementing design for manufacture and assembly (DfMA) in construction projects, and to develop a construction-oriented DfMA framework with recommendations for addressing these challenges.
problem_statement: Despite DfMA's long-standing use in manufacturing, its adoption in construction remains limited due to a scattering of unaddressed challenges; no prior study had comprehensively identified these challenges and proposed organizational, contractual, and operational strategies to overcome them.
methodology: A design science research (DSR) approach combining a systematic literature review (232 initial hits, 52 articles retained, analyzed via qualitative content analysis) to extract implementation challenges; two focus group discussions (10 and 14 Canadian construction industry experts) to validate and categorize challenges and develop/validate a conceptual framework; and verification of the framework through observation and stakeholder discussions on two real-world off-site construction case study projects (a multi-residential building in British Columbia and a structural steel facility in Ohio).
key_background_studies: Wuni et al. (cited as [32]) - identified 'limited relevant knowledge and practical experience' as most-cited challenge in design-for-excellence for industrialized construction.
RIBA (2013, 2020) [11] - introduced and revised DfMA overlay to Plan of Work, used as structural basis for the proposed framework.
Gao et al. [15] - categorized DfMA interpretations in construction literature into three groups (philosophy, design process, evaluation system).
[25] - systematic review of 23 DfMA articles identifying three perspectives on DfMA and success factors like multidisciplinary teams and lean principles.
[26] - 2020 review of DfMA development in manufacturing/construction, categorizing research into implementation strategies, frameworks, and on/off-site applications.
[27] - systematic review of DfMA literature to 2021 identifying analogies between prefabrication and manufacturing and future opportunities.
[28] - 2022 review identifying benefits and barriers (including traditional contracting strategies) to DfMA implementation and BIM integration.
[24] - literature review identifying shared practices between DfMA, lean, and digital fabrication (e.g., 'design to target value', 'concurrent engineering').
findings: The study identified 45 challenges to DfMA implementation in construction, categorized into eight groups: contractual, technological, procedural, cultural, commercial, geographical, financial, and technical/cognitive. Contractual and operational challenges were most frequently cited, linked to fragmentation of stakeholder responsibilities under traditional delivery methods. A construction-oriented DfMA framework based on the RIBA Plan of Work 2020 was developed and verified on two off-site construction case studies, showing that projects using integrated/relational delivery methods (e.g., IPD-type hybrid model) and supportive business models achieved better outcomes (fewer change orders, improved schedule, cost, and quality) than those using traditional delivery methods with fragmented subcontracting. Emerging integrated business models (vertical integration, digital systems integration, spinoff factories), relational contracting frameworks (e.g., IPD), and operational tools (BIM, lean, Industry 4.0 technologies) were found to facilitate DfMA adoption by improving organizational, contractual, and operational integration.

ideas.idea: Traditional contract forms like design-bid-build create fragmentation among stakeholders that obstructs DfMA implementation.
ideas.quote: traditional forms of contracts that create vertical, horizontal, and longitudinal fragmentations (i.e., design–bid–build)

ideas.idea: Existing standard contracts lack provisions addressing risk/reward sharing critical for collaborative DfMA delivery.
ideas.quote: Lack of risk/reward sharing consideration in the contract

ideas.idea: Contracts often fail to clearly define guarantees and insurance requirements relevant to prefabricated/off-site work.
ideas.quote: Lack of clarity in terms of guarantees and insurance

ideas.idea: DfMA-related digital platforms are not well aligned with existing standard contracts such as CCDC forms.
ideas.quote: Lack of DfMA platforms which conform with the CCDC contracts

ideas.idea: Contracts often lack clear scope of work leading to duplication and confusion among project participants engaged in prefabrication.
ideas.quote: Lack of clear scope of work, confusions, and duplications

ideas.idea: Standard contracts do not adequately reference multiple manufacturers, limiting flexibility in sourcing prefabricated components.
ideas.quote: Lack of references to several manufacturers in the contract

ideas.idea: Lack of clearly defined stakeholder roles and responsibilities in contracts is a major barrier to DfMA implementation.
ideas.quote: Lack of clear roles and responsibilities of stakeholders

ideas.idea: Disputes and lengthy negotiations between key stakeholders under traditional contracting hinder DfMA adoption.
ideas.quote: Complex litigation and long negotiations between key stakeholders

ideas.idea: Rigid contracts lacking flexibility and agility impede adaptive DfMA-based project execution.
ideas.quote: Lack of agility and flexibility in the contract

ideas.idea: Relational, integrated delivery methods such as IPD better support DfMA by fostering shared risk/reward and joint decision-making, unlike traditional delivery models.
ideas.quote: The IPD-type project delivery method provided incentives for stakeholders to collaborate during all phases of the project. For instance, the shared risks and rewards and joint decision-making principles fostered a collaborative project environment.

ideas.idea: Multi-party IPD contracts (including CCDC30 in Canada) are identified as promising but under-researched tools for enhancing DfMA/off-site construction synergy.
ideas.quote: several standard forms of IPD contracting are available in North America (i.e., CCDC30 in Canada and AIA C-191 and ConsensusDocs 300 in the U.S.)

ideas.idea: Traditional delivery methods keep information siloed by phase, discouraging sharing and undermining DfMA's need for continuous integration.
ideas.quote: In traditional delivery methods, information models are stuck in phase-based silos, project participants are not motivated to share them beyond the phases to which they are related

ideas.idea: DfMA (product/process integration) requires accompanying contractual frameworks like IPD (people integration) to succeed.
ideas.quote: While DfMA focuses on product/process integration, it needs to be accompanied by a contractual framework such as IPD, which focuses on people integration.

ideas.idea: Case study evidence shows that sub-contracting portions of a project under traditional design-bid-build within a broader DB project undermines integrated planning and design essential to DfMA.
ideas.quote: in project A, with several traditionally sub-contracted scopes, the joint planning and design tasks were not feasible.

ideas.idea: Lack of legislative frameworks, codes, standards and guidelines specific to DfMA hampers its systematic contractual and technical adoption.
ideas.quote: the lack of legislative frameworks of specified codes, guidelines, and standards for the implementation of construction-oriented DfMA methods

objectives: To develop an ethnography-based methodological framework for prefabricated construction projects (PCPs) that evaluates, analyzes, and improves dynamic organizational resilience—in terms of efficiency, flexibility, and robustness—from a project life cycle perspective, and to validate this framework using a real EPC-contract PCP case in China.
problem_statement: PCPs are interorganizational and highly vulnerable to disruptions (e.g., COVID-19, supply chain issues, fragmented processes) due to complex stakeholder relationships, yet existing research has focused on risk from a project perspective rather than resilience from an organizational perspective, and there is a lack of a quantitative method to evaluate organizational resilience of PCPs considering dynamic stakeholder roles and relationships across the project life cycle.
methodology: A two-part mixed-method framework combining a qualitative ethnographic method (participant observation and in-depth interviews with eight experienced participants) to identify stakeholder roles and relationships (coordination, power, control) at five life-cycle stages (planning, designing, manufacturing/storage/transportation, assembling onsite, operation), and a quantitative graph theory method using performance criteria and equations to calculate flexibility (F), robustness (R), and efficiency (E) indicators, combined into an overall organizational resilience score. The framework was applied to a real 2-year EPC-contract PCP case by Poly Real Estate Group in Changsha, Hunan, China, including a disfunction analysis of key stakeholders (GC, PC, M) and a comparative analysis of BIM, decentralized collaboration platform (DCP/blockchain), and a stakeholder 'league' scenario.
key_background_studies: McManus et al. (2008) - proposed organizational resilience as a function of situation awareness, keystone vulnerability, and adaptive capacity, foundational engineering resilience perspective used to derive dimensions.
Yahia et al. (2021) - provided the graph theory approach and relationship typology (coordination, power, control) and performance metrics adopted in this study's quantitative framework.
Grossi et al. (2007) and Penserini et al. (2009) - source of graph theory equations and performance criteria used to measure flexibility, robustness, and efficiency.
Li et al. (2016) - identified stakeholder-associated risk factors network in prefabricated housing projects, informing the risk perspective on PCP vulnerability.

Luo et al. (2019) - examined supply chain risks tied to stakeholders across project phases, and identified GC, PC, M as associated with most implementation challenges, used to justify the disfunction analysis.
Sydow and Braun (2018) - conceptualized projects as temporary organizations with interorganizational relations, underpinning the interorganizational perspective on PCPs.

Nguyen et al. (2021) - systematically reviewed stakeholder relationships in off-site construction, categorizing relationship patterns, highlighting the neglect of resilience-focused stakeholder relationship research.
Teng et al. (2017) - noted the complexity of managing cooperation among many stakeholders (GC, designers, manufacturers) in PCPs, supporting findings on GC centrality.
Bhamra et al. (2011) - defined organizational resilience as ability to return to stable condition after disruption, definition adopted and adapted for PCPs in this study.
findings: The organizational resilience of the studied EPC-contract PCP follows a bowl-shaped pattern across the five life-cycle stages, being lowest (most fragile) during planning and highest during manufacturing/storage/transportation, reflecting the dynamic nature of stakeholder roles and relationships. Efficiency dimension performs relatively well, while robustness and flexibility require improvement, particularly through better workflow control and stakeholder communication. Disfunction analysis shows the general contractor (GC) plays the most centralized and important role, with its disfunction most severely undermining resilience, followed by the prefabrication consultant (PC) in design and assembly stages and the manufacturer (M) in the manufacturing stage. Comparative analysis shows that partial relationship changes (a league among GC, DS, M) have little effect on resilience, whereas systematic technology interventions—BIM and especially blockchain-based decentralized collaboration platforms (DCP)—significantly improve organizational resilience by enhancing communication and, in DCP's case, also workflow control (delegation and supervision relationships).

ideas.idea: Prefabricated construction projects are inherently interorganizational, involving multiple stakeholders whose relationships change dynamically across project life cycle stages, affecting resilience and contractual arrangements.
ideas.quote: Because prefabricated construction projects (PCPs) are interorganizational in nature, their successful delivery, especially under uncertain circumstances, relies on organizational resilience performance throughout the life cycle.

ideas.idea: Under an EPC contract, the general contractor takes on combined responsibility for both design and construction, unlike traditional contracts where these are split between owner/developer and contractor.
ideas.quote: For example, in a traditional-contract PCP, general contractor is responsible for construction, and the owner/developer takes charge of early design work. Under an EPC-contract PCP, on the other hand, the general contractor is responsible for both design and construction.

ideas.idea: Stakeholder relationships in PCPs can be legally/contractually categorized into coordination (information flow), power (task delegation and responsibility/obligation), and control (task supervision, including legal right to replace non-performing parties), which are directly relevant to contractual risk allocation.
ideas.quote: A power relationship means task delegation and responsibility; that is, task delegation from stakeholder x to y ends up in the creation of an obligation directed to y. A control relationship points to task supervision, which means that stakeholder x can legally replace y if the latter cannot complete the task as per the agreed requirements.

ideas.idea: The general contractor occupies the most central and critical role in governing project organizational resilience, implying that contractual frameworks should place strong emphasis on GC responsibilities and relationships.
ideas.quote: decision makers should focus on the general contractor and its relevant relationships because the CG plays the most important role in governing the resilience of the PCP organization.

ideas.idea: The project is most vulnerable during the planning stage because key project information and contract documents remain unclear, highlighting the importance of early contractual clarity in prefabricated projects.
ideas.quote: This result shows that this PCP is fragile at planning stage, which makes sense because considerable volumes of project information and contract issues remain unclear and veiled at this stage. When crucial project information is revealed and key contract documents are formalized, the project tends to be stable.

ideas.idea: The manufacturer's role and its supply chain relationships (with suppliers and logistics enterprises) are critical during the manufacturing, storage, and transportation stage, indicating contractual dependencies extending beyond the traditional contractor-owner relationship.
ideas.quote: the M had to find a reliable material supplier (S) and an efficient logistics enterprise (LE).

ideas.idea: Using digital collaboration technologies such as BIM and blockchain-based decentralized collaboration platforms can substantively alter and improve contractual/organizational relationships (communication and workflow control) among PCP stakeholders, suggesting contracts should account for or incentivize such technology use.
ideas.quote: DCP not only improves information communication, but also upgrades delegation and supervision relationship of stakeholders.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication consultants act as intermediaries hired separately by developers and general contractors to ensure design and planning compliance with prefabrication rate requirements, illustrating additional contractual layers unique to PCPs.
ideas.quote: a prefabrication consultant (PC) was hired by the developer (DV)... to plan the documents to demonstrate to G that this project meets the basic prefabricated rate at the planning stage.

ideas.idea: Subcontracting practices in PCPs involve the general contractor delegating specific assembly work to subcontractors while other stakeholders (designer, manufacturer, PC) continue collaborating, reflecting complex multi-party contractual coordination during onsite assembly.
ideas.quote: the GC subcontracted certain assembly works to subcontractors (SCs), as well as to some participating stakeholders, such as the D, M, and PC, who also collaborated with each other to facilitate the onsite modular assembly work.

objectives: To develop a scoring framework that assesses the feasibility of using the design-build (DB) project delivery method for bundled infrastructure projects, based on quantifying and weighting project bundling objectives via expert survey and principal component analysis.
problem_statement: Agencies bundling multiple infrastructure projects into a single contract face difficulty selecting an appropriate project delivery method (PDM), particularly deciding whether DB is feasible; no prior research or tool exists to assess DB feasibility specifically for bundled (as opposed to single) projects, which differ in risk profile, complexity, and mutual dependence issues.
methodology: Mixed-methods framework development: (1) Delphi technique using literature review and 37 bundled project case studies to identify 25 project bundling objectives; (2) a validated 5-point Likert-scale survey distributed to 51 US industry experts (owners, contractors, architect/engineers) to rate importance of each objective for DB feasibility, validated via sample size sufficiency (Cochran's formula), Cronbach's alpha (0.941) for internal reliability, and intraclass correlation coefficient (0.926) for external reliability; (3) Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with data standardization, KMO/Bartlett tests, Kaiser criterion (5 components retained), and Varimax rotation to calculate weights for each objective; (4) statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U) to identify feasibility tiers and cutoff scores; (5) development of a user-friendly Excel/VBA-based scoring tool calculating Project DB Feasibility Score (PDFS) and Industry DB Feasibility Score (IDFS).
key_background_studies: FHWA (2019) - established guidance on bundling contracts, PDM options for bundled projects, and DB advantages, forming basis for gap identification
Gransberg (2020) - discussed challenges of implementing bundling programs including PDM selection difficulty
Tran and Molenaar (2013, 2015) - developed risk-based PDM selection frameworks for single highway projects (DBB, DB, CM/GC), used as comparison baseline showing gap for bundled projects
Al Khalil (2002) - developed AHP-based model for PDM selection among DBB, DB, CM/GC based on owner needs, cited as existing single-project tool
Khwaja et al. (2018) - developed decision-support tool comparing DBB and DB based on user rankings
Zeng et al. (2014) - fuzzy simulation-based optimization approach to identify optimal PDM minimizing cost/duration
Songer and Molenaar (1997) - identified success factors for public-sector DB projects (scope definition, owner sophistication, staffing, budget)
Qiao et al. (2018, 2019a,b,c) - identified project bundling decision factors, benefits (cost, schedule) and case study basis for bundling objectives
Assaf and Assaad (2023) / Assaf et al. (2024) - prior authors' own work identifying bundling decision-making factors, opportunities and challenges, directly motivating this study's gap
Shan et al. (2023) - documented DelDOT case study showing DBB delays due to mutual dependence, motivating use of DB for bundled projects
Xiong et al. (2017) - identified bundle size thresholds and economies of scale benefits
FHWA/Colorado DOT PDSM (Tran et al. 2013; FHWA 2017) - existing risk-based, qualitative PDM selection matrix for single projects, contrasted with proposed quantitative framework
findings: The study identified seven DB feasibility tiers for bundled projects using 25 objectives, weighted via PCA. The three objectives with highest feasibility scores (Tier 1) are: (1) having specific scheduling, sequencing, staging, and phasing; (2) meeting tight milestones or deadlines; and (3) completing the overall project on schedule — all schedule-related, indicating DB is most feasible for bundling programs prioritizing schedule performance due to DB's fast-track, concurrent design-construction nature. A user-friendly Excel/VBA scoring tool was developed allowing project owners to calculate a Project DB Feasibility Score (PDFS) and benchmark it against an Industry DB Feasibility Score (IDFS) to make go/no-go PDM decisions, differing from existing risk-based, qualitative, single-project PDM selection frameworks by being quantitative, goal-based, and tailored specifically to bundled projects.

ideas.idea: In DB delivery, the owner has a single point of responsibility with the design-builder, unlike DBB where design and construction responsibilities are split.
ideas.quote: the owner will have a single point of responsibility, which is that with the design-builder

ideas.idea: DB allows construction to begin before design completion, enabling fast-tracked project delivery.
ideas.quote: Under the DB contract, the construction phase can start before the full completion of the design, which ensures a fast-tracked completion of the project

ideas.idea: DB allows contractor input into design (constructability feedback), reducing change orders and delays later in execution.
ideas.quote: in DB projects, the owner can benefit from constructability feedback and analysis since the contractor provides inputs to the design, which helps in reducing change orders and delays later in the project execution phase

ideas.idea: Different PDMs fundamentally represent different ways of allocating and managing risk among project parties, with DB shifting most design-related risk from owner to contractor.
ideas.quote: the different PDMs at their basic level are mainly different ways to allocate and manage risks among the various project parties... In the case of the DB delivery method, most of the risks... are transferred from the project owner... and allocated to the contactor

ideas.idea: Bundled projects introduce a unique risk of mutual dependence between projects that does not exist in singly delivered projects, since all elements (permits, ROW, utilities) must clear before the whole bundled contract under DBB can be advertised.
ideas.quote: an engineering problem (such as geotechnical or hydrological) or environmental issue at one project location of the bundled projects can prevent the entire package from being advertised under the DBB delivery method since clearance/approval must be obtained for all projects in the bundled contract before the agency's advertises the contract

ideas.idea: Under DB, the design-builder can assume full responsibility for permits, utility coordination, and ROW negotiations across all bundled project sites, mitigating the mutual dependence risk faced under DBB.
ideas.quote: the design-builder (i.e., DB team) was responsible for all aspects of the project, including plan preparation, utility coordination, permit acquisition, and ROW negotiations

ideas.idea: Bundled contracts require the contractor to manage complex construction sequencing across multiple project locations under one aggressive schedule, a challenge not present in single-project delivery.
ideas.quote: the contractor has to schedule, phase, sequence, and finish all the projects according to the generally aggressive schedule for the entire bundled contract

ideas.idea: Bundled projects increase third-party coordination burden (utilities, ROW, permits, railroads) across multiple locations under a single contract, magnifying risk if one location has issues.
ideas.quote: one issue with one project location could impact the delivery of the entire bundled contract

ideas.idea: Larger bundled contract size increases funding/financing considerations for agencies compared to smaller single-project contracts.
ideas.quote: since the bundled contract includes multiple projects, the contract amount or size is bigger and hence the agency's funding availability and financing capacity must be considered and properly addressed for bundled contracts

ideas.idea: Traffic management responsibilities are more complex for bundled projects because the contractor must coordinate detours/lane closures across multiple locations simultaneously.
ideas.quote: the contractor delivering bundled projects has additional responsibilities for traffic management especially in areas where detours and traffic impacts overlap between the various locations of bundled projects

ideas.idea: Existing PDM selection frameworks and tools were developed for single, non-bundled projects and are not directly applicable to bundled contracts due to differences in complexity, scope and execution considerations.
ideas.quote: the existing studies provided guidance on selecting a proper PDM for single (i.e., nonbundled) projects/contracts only. However, bundled projects... greatly differ in their properties, complexities, scope, and execution considerations.

ideas.idea: The PDM selection decision occurs after projects are identified for bundling but before the bundled contract is let/procured, situating the DB feasibility assessment tool at a specific point in the bundling decision process.
ideas.quote: the applicability of the proposed framework in this paper is after the project owner identifies candidate projects to bundle and before the actual letting or execution of the bundled contract

ideas.idea: DB feasibility for bundled projects is most strongly driven by schedule-related objectives (specific sequencing/phasing, meeting milestones, overall schedule completion), reflecting DB's fast-track, concurrent design-construction nature as a contractual/process advantage.
ideas.quote: these results identify that bundling programs that have those three project objectives as their priority will likely be associated with a very high DB feasibility score... this determines that the DB method is highly feasible for bundling programs that have their main goals directed toward enhancing the overall schedule

ideas.idea: DB delivery has notable disadvantages/risks for owners, including reduced control, increased cost of owner-requested changes, potential higher costs due to risk transfer, and need for specific legislation permitting its use.
ideas.quote: These disadvantages include reduced client control, increased cost of client requested changes, client's reduced ability to influence the design, potential higher cost since the contractor assumes most of the risks... and the need to have proper state legislation that allows the public agency to use the DB approach

objectives: To identify and classify the major causes/sources of construction disputes in Kuwait based on a review of actual litigation cases, to rank the severity of these dispute sources, to validate findings through expert interviews, and to develop a regression model predicting disputed claim value.
problem_statement: Construction disputes are widespread and costly, yet most prior research relies on surveys, questionnaires, and literature reviews rather than real litigation cases, and there is a lack of guidelines matching dispute sources to avoidance measures. This study addresses that gap by analyzing actual court cases in Kuwait to identify dispute sources grounded in real legal outcomes rather than perception-based surveys.
methodology: A sample of 177 litigation cases was randomly selected from the Kuwait Ministry of Justice Expert Department records (from over 1,000 cases), covering government and private traditional-delivery construction projects. Case data included contract value, project duration, dispute phase, plaintiff/defendant/offender roles, and main/other dispute sources. Statistical analysis ranked severity of dispute sources by frequency and claim value across four classification groups (abnormal conditions, financial, project delay, project management). Results were validated through structured interviews with 10 construction legal experts using a Likert scale. A linear regression model (SPSS 27) was built using claim value as dependent variable and contract value/project duration as independent variables, run for all cases and separately for building-only cases (89 cases).
key_background_studies: Diekmann and Nelson (1985) - argued incomplete contract documentation and change-related uncertainties are core dispute sources.
Kumaraswamy (1997) - classified disputes into root causes (unfair risk allocation, inappropriate contract types) and proximate causes (design documentation issues, contract administration).
Love et al. (2011) - classified dispute sources into management, organizational, and people systems.
Cakmak and Cakmak (2014) - categorized dispute causes into seven groups including contract-related and owner-related causes.
Daoud and Azzam (1999) - noted Middle East contracts are often one-sided favoring the employer, with poor design of contract documents.
Awwad et al. (2016) - found contractual concerns are the most common dispute source in the Middle East.
Elziny et al. (2016) - identified contract management and contract documentation as top dispute sources in Egypt.
Mahamid (2016) - surveyed Saudi contractors, finding payment delay and unrealistic contract duration as top dispute causes.
Dmaidi et al. (2013) - identified bidding policy and payment delay as main dispute sources in Palestine.
Chan and Suen (2005) - proposed recommendations to mitigate contractual, cultural, and legal disputes.
Mohamed et al. (2014) - proposed measures for minimizing disputes including understanding of contract clauses and risk sharing.
Soliman (2010, 2017) - studied project delay claim values in Kuwait, relevant to design delay findings.
Al-Humaidi (2004) and Alrasheed et al. (2023) - attempted to estimate litigation/arbitration fees based on claimed values.
findings: The most severe and frequent dispute sources were payment delay, contract documentation issues (incomplete information, conflict of interest, noncompliance, lack of knowledge), main contractor time delay, and owner time delay. Financial disputes accounted for 40.68% of cases, with payment delay alone being 25.42% of all cases. Government projects accounted for 63.27% of cases and 94.83% of total claim value, suggesting political and bidding-policy influences. Main contractor time delay produced the highest claim value (51.09% of total claims), and project delay overall accounted for 66.90% of total claim value. In government contracts, contractor time delay caused ~56% of claim value disputes; in private contracts, payment delay caused ~52%. Main contractors were identified as the primary dispute offenders in government contracts, while owners were more often offenders in private contracts. Most disputes emerged after project completion rather than during execution. A moderately fitting linear regression model was developed to predict claim value from contract value and duration (R²≈0.18-0.19). Expert interviews validated four critical dispute sources common with case data: payment delay, main contractor time delay, back-to-back payments, and owner time delay. The study recommends contractual clause revisions, better contractor prequalification, and updated dispute-resolution procedures, and calls for further research across the Gulf region.

ideas.idea: Incomplete or ambiguous contract documentation is a major, recurring source of construction disputes, ranking as the second most frequent dispute cause.
ideas.quote: contractual issues could have stemmed from incomplete information, conflict of interest from both parties, noncompliance, and lack of knowledge from both contractual parties. This ranked second in the number of dispute cases.

ideas.idea: Standard contract documents in use have not been updated for decades, contributing to unfair or outdated contractual terms that fuel disputes.
ideas.quote: the contracts currently being used are still those that have been designed and referred to since 1971; and as of yet, there have been no upgrades or modifications to make them legitimately acceptable and fair to both contracting parties.

ideas.idea: Payment delay is consistently the most severe and frequent dispute source across both government and private contracts, indicating a need for contractual payment mechanisms.
ideas.quote: Ranked first as a source of dispute was delay in payments for both government and private dispute cases.

ideas.idea: Time delay caused by the main contractor generates the highest financial claim value among all dispute sources, reflecting weaknesses in the project delivery and contractor selection process.
ideas.quote: The delay caused by the contractor, and which formed a high percentage, seemed to have a reflection on the unreliable process of the project delivery system in Kuwait.

ideas.idea: Contractual and procedural clauses should be revised to allocate risk and responsibility more fairly between contracting parties to reduce disputes.
ideas.quote: it is timely and urgent that certain agreement clauses should be introduced and perhaps made more impartially stringent and properly screened by legal advisers of both government and private entities.

ideas.idea: The party responsible for causing disputes differs by project type: main contractors are the principal offenders in government contracts, while owners are more often responsible in private contracts, implying that contract terms should address power imbalances between parties.
ideas.quote: main contractors were the offenders for the majority of disputes in government contracts by claim value... Contrariwise, the scenario differed relative to private contracts, with disputes caused by owners being more significant than those caused by main contractors.

ideas.idea: Explicit contractual clauses addressing payment terms, back-to-back payments, and penalties for late payment are recommended to mitigate financial disputes.
ideas.quote: Applying contract payment terms, studying the project's cash flow ahead of project assignment, wise selection of contractors, applying for bank LC payments, and applying penalties for late payments.

ideas.idea: Contractual provisions should require documentation of variation orders and design changes in writing to prevent disputes over scope changes.
ideas.quote: Documenting all changes, applying for proper design review, and having claims in writing.

ideas.idea: Contracts should include clear terms specifying compensation and reasons in the event of work stoppage to reduce ambiguity-driven disputes.
ideas.quote: Contract terms should clearly mention details on the compensation of the affected party and recording the reasons for the work stoppage.

ideas.idea: Pre-tender clarification meetings and specialized contract review can reduce disputes stemming from unclear contract documentation.
ideas.quote: Raising questions during pre-tender meetings to clear any doubts or speculations at the time of bidding and assigning specialized contract specialists.

objectives: To evaluate procurement systems that enable early contractor involvement (ECI) in terms of how well they support off-site manufacturing (OSM), and to develop a two-stage conceptual process model for ECI suited to the New Zealand construction industry.
problem_statement: There is currently no standard form or clearly defined model for two-stage ECI in New Zealand, and OSM/MMC uptake is hindered by design buildability issues and conservative industry culture; existing standard contracts and ECI approaches lack clarity on risk allocation, pricing and design/buildability obligations relevant to OSM.
methodology: Literature review combined with three ethnographic case studies of construction projects in Dunedin, Otago, NZ (2006-2017, NZ$10-20 million each), document analysis, open coding of pre-construction services from ECI literature, and legal doctrine analysis distinguishing design buildability obligations from design code compliance. The resulting conceptual model was presented at a conference and refined based on feedback.
key_background_studies: Jorgensen and Emmitt (2007) - ethnographic case studies identifying factors for effective lean integration in design/construction.
Mosey (2011) - conceptualises two-stage 'conditional' pre-construction contracts and commercial interests of ECI parties.
Shahzad (2011) - classifies barriers to OSM adoption in NZ into seven categories including market culture and skills.
Whitehead (2009) - describes hybrid ECI models in Australia with partnering first stage and DB second stage.
