ideas.idea: Direct and indirect cost considerations are often excluded from the technical evaluation criteria used to approve ATCs, creating a contractual/procurement risk.
ideas.quote: When ATCs are evaluated for equal or better than the standard project requirements, direct and indirect costs are generally not considered as one of the defining criteria for ATC approval.

ideas.idea: Rigorous, well-structured ATC review processes (including one-on-one confidential meetings and staged submittal) reduce errors and legal/contractual disputes during project delivery.
ideas.quote: The positive impact of such a process included a reduction in errors and better coordination, which consequently reduced any legal and contractual issues during project delivery.

objectives: To investigate the significant constraints demotivating the adoption of prefabricated prefinished volumetric construction (PPVC) and to propose feasible mitigation strategies to address these constraints.
problem_statement: Although PPVC's benefits have been widely recognized, PPVC is still in its infancy and the constraints limiting its adoption remain largely unexplored in the literature, with existing off-site construction research not specifically addressing PPVC.
methodology: Mixed methods approach comprising: (1) comprehensive literature review to identify 18 constraints and 9 mitigation strategies for PPVC; (2) pilot interviews with three industry experts to verify and refine the identified constraints/strategies; (3) a structured questionnaire survey administered to 41 Singapore-based construction organizations, rating constraints and mitigation strategies on five-point scales, analyzed using Shapiro-Wilk, Kruskal-Wallis, and Wilcoxon Signed-Ranks tests; (4) an in-depth case study of a real PPVC project (North Hill Residential Hall, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore) to verify empirical findings.
key_background_studies: Arashpour et al. (2016) - summarized constraints of generic off-site construction including coordination lead times, maintenance costs, and quality issues
Kamali and Hewage (2016) - reviewed challenges of modular construction including planning, transportation, cost, and coordination

Mao et al. (2015) - questionnaire survey identifying major barriers to off-site construction in China including governmental incentives, upfront cost, and practitioner dependence on conventional methods
Rahman (2013) - critical review identifying eight categories of barriers to modern construction methods
Chiang et al. (2006) - investigated barriers to off-site construction in Hong Kong public housing including transportation and labor training
Azhar et al. (2013) - identified top constraints of modular construction adoption including designer decisions and site layout restrictions
Jaillon and Poon (2010) - questionnaire survey identifying site storage/access, design time, and flexibility as major limitations to prefabrication
Tam et al. (2007) - investigated hindrances to prefabrication including design inflexibility, lack of research information, and higher initial cost
Goh and Loosemore (2017); Said (2015, 2016) - proposed early collaboration among project stakeholders as mitigation strategy
Khalili and Chua (2013); Mao et al. (2016) - suggested fabricating modules proximal to construction site to reduce transportation issues
findings: The study identified 18 constraints to PPVC adoption, with the top five being: extensive coordination required prior to and during construction, need for additional project planning and design efforts, increased transportation and logistics considerations, requirement for early commitment, and higher initial cost than conventional construction. Nine mitigation strategies were proposed, with the top three most effective being: encouraging close collaborations between project stakeholders during the early phase of the project, use of BIM to improve coordination and facilitate communication among stakeholders, and offering training courses for project teams and workers. The case study of the NTU North Hill Residential Hall project corroborated these findings, showing similar constraints related to cost, planning/design efforts, coordination, and transportation.

ideas.idea: PPVC requires extensive coordination among multiple stakeholders throughout design, manufacturing, transportation, and installation phases, which is the most significant constraint due to the industry's fragmented nature.
ideas.quote: extensive coordination among the different project stakeholders is required, to handle the design, manufacturing, transportation, and installation of the prefabricated modules

ideas.idea: PPVC demands additional upfront project planning and design efforts compared to conventional construction because building layouts must be reinvented for each unique project.
ideas.quote: The planning and design processes of PPVC projects demand early collaboration among different parties such as architects, contractors, and manufacturers, which normally requires additional efforts from different project stakeholders

ideas.idea: Transportation and logistics considerations are a major constraint due to regulatory restrictions on transporting heavy, bulky modules, especially in densely populated areas.
ideas.quote: in most cases there is some special traffic control requirement on transporting heavy and bulky articles in densely populated areas

ideas.idea: PPVC requires early commitment from stakeholders before construction begins, since components must be manufactured in advance, reducing flexibility for later design changes.
ideas.quote: PPVC requires early involvement of project design and planning because the precast components and modules need to be manufactured before construction starts

ideas.idea: The initial cost of PPVC is higher than conventional construction due to expensive prefinished modules and costly shipping, exacerbated by risk of shipping damage to large modules.
ideas.quote: the modules used by PPVC are very expensive because they are typically highly completed (mostly 85e90 of the project work)... the shipping of prefinished modules to site is also costly

ideas.idea: Close collaboration among project stakeholders in the early project phase is identified as the most effective strategy to mitigate PPVC constraints, given the concurrent nature of PPVC work.
ideas.quote: multidisciplinary professionals to work concurrently during the early project phases such as planning and design, which makes close and effective collaborations from different project stakeholders a necessity rather than an option for PPVC projects

ideas.idea: BIM adoption can bridge communication gaps and enhance interdisciplinary coordination among project stakeholders in PPVC projects.
ideas.quote: BIM, which serves as an information platform to bridge the communication gaps between project stakeholders and enhance the interdisciplinary coordination

ideas.idea: Training courses for project teams and workers can address the lack of PPVC experience in design and installation, helping practitioners gain confidence in adopting the method.
ideas.quote: it is imperative to launch a series of training courses for professionals to help improve their knowledge and skills related to the implementation of PPVC

ideas.idea: PPVC changes traditional procurement and contracting complexity due to increased organizational requirements and changing roles of project participants.
ideas.quote: Increased organizational requirements (e.g. changing roles of project participants/increased complexity of procurement and contracting issues)

ideas.idea: In real PPVC projects, inspectors are hired to verify module compliance with binding contract requirements before installation, highlighting the contractual quality assurance dimension of PPVC.
ideas.quote: inspectors were hired to do inspections at the manufacturing factories and Jurong temporary site to ensure the compliance of the completed modules to the requirements stipulated in the binding contract

ideas.idea: PPVC projects often source modules from overseas manufacturing facilities due to limited local industrial capacity, increasing initial cost and adding complexity to project delivery.
ideas.quote: as Singapore is a city-state with limited industrial capacity, the vast majority of the modules required by this project had to be manufactured overseas and then imported to Singapore, which increased the project's initial cost dramatically

objectives: To develop an automatic incentive-penalty enforcement system (smart contract) for modular construction that motivates reliable performance, using discrete event simulation to derive contractual rules and blockchain/IPFS-based image oracles for progress verification, applied to a prefabricated bathroom unit (PBU) case study.
problem_statement: Modular construction success depends on coordination among designers, suppliers, prefabricators, and contractors, but current practices lack timely, transparent enforcement of rewards/penalties for schedule adherence; rewards and penalties are usually only enforced at/near project completion, making it hard to encourage reliability during the project and to retrospectively quantify delay causes. There is a gap in understanding the relationship between individual participants' work plan reliability and project performance, and in developing smart contract rules calibrated to real project scenarios; existing blockchain-in-construction studies have not developed concrete smart contract rules linked to real performance data or addressed how to use images as oracles.
methodology: Case study of a residential high-rise modular construction project in Singapore involving prefabricated bathroom units (PBUs). Two-phase framework: Phase A collected empirical data (74 PBU loading platform assembly durations, 139 PBU hoist-up durations) and built a STROBOSCOPE discrete-event simulation model to test scenarios of PBU delivery variability, crane availability, and worker assignment, generating cost/schedule outputs used to derive smart contract incentive/penalty rules. Phase B developed an Ethereum-based smart contract (built in Remix) with an IPFS-based decentralized image-sharing application (using Web3.js and React) to serve as an oracle for real-time performance verification, feeding into the smart contract to trigger automatic payments/penalties. The simulation was verified (via STROBOSCOPE Trace chronological checks) and validated (confidence interval comparison of actual vs. simulated outputs) per established simulation methodology.
key_background_studies: Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez (2020) - linked cost/schedule data from Microsoft Project to an Ethereum smart contract for secure payments but failed to automate progress payments due to centralized data governance.

Hamledari and Fischer (2021a, 2021b) - proposed using reality capture technologies (e.g., UAVs) to fetch as-built data to trigger smart contract progress payments, but lacked concrete smart contract rules based on real performance scenarios.

Lee et al. (2021) - integrated digital twins and blockchain to make as-built information traceable for stakeholder collaboration but did not develop concrete smart contract rules responding to actual project performance.
Lu et al. (2021) - explored smart construction objects as blockchain oracles to enhance construction supply chain collaboration, informing oracle classification and use.
Hunhevicz et al. (2021) - investigated digital twin-based oracles for performance-based smart contracts to financially incentivize parties meeting performance targets.
Tao et al. (2021) - developed an integrated blockchain-IPFS method to solve BIM design file storage problems, informing the IPFS-based oracle approach used in this study.
Peters and Panayi (2015) - provided foundational definition of smart contracts as self-enforcing mechanisms monitoring external inputs.

Liu et al. (2020), Jung et al. (2018), Bamana et al. (2019), Goh and Goh (2019) - used discrete event simulation to study supply chain and delivery impacts on construction productivity, informing the simulation methodology used here.
findings: The developed smart contract successfully automated incentive/penalty enforcement across all 19 scenarios tested (PBU delivery variability, crane availability, worker assignment) derived from simulation results. Simulation showed PBU delivery sequence variability had a significant impact on schedule and cost: best-case scenario (variability 0-6) completed in 40.93 working days versus 50.79 days in worst case, with proportional differences in crane and worker idle time. If the PBU fabricator performed at the highest reliability level following smart contract rules, the project could save 4.7% of overall cost compared to the benchmark scenario. Crane availability and worker assignment levels similarly affected schedule, cost, and idle times, with optimal points identified for smart contract benchmarks. The blockchain smart contract, deployed on Ethereum via Remix, correctly executed rewards (e.g., 1502 ETH for best performance) and penalties (e.g., up to 18,358 ETH for worst performance), and correctly rejected erroneous/malicious inputs with error signals. The IPFS-based decentralized image-sharing application provided a reliable, transparent, and immutable oracle for verifying subcontractor performance, improving documentation, transparency, and reducing potential disputes over payment conditions. The study concludes that situational-awareness-based smart contracts, informed by simulation-derived rules and image-based oracles, can improve monitoring, motivate reliable performance, and improve productivity and documentation in modular construction, though current systems still require human appraisal of image content and lack flexibility for handling change orders.

ideas.idea: Modular/prefabricated construction requires close coordination and reliable performance among multiple contractual parties (designers, suppliers, prefabricators, contractors), and failures in this coordination create productivity risks.
ideas.quote: the success of modular construction requires additional effort in the form of coordination among multiple participants, such as designers, suppliers, prefabricators, and contractors.

ideas.idea: Traditional contracts enforce rewards and penalties only at or near project completion, which fails to incentivize reliable performance throughout the project and makes delay causation difficult to trace.
ideas.quote: In current construction practices, rewards for on-time performance and penalties for delayed completion are usually not enforced until a project is either completed or near completion, making it difficult to encourage adherence to the schedule and work plan during the project.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automate contractual incentive/penalty clauses tied to real-time performance data, reducing reliance on third-party enforcement and administrative costs, which is directly relevant to how construction contracts might contractually structure MMC delivery incentives.
ideas.quote: Smart contracts work on an "if/when, then" principle... resulting in savings in transaction fees and administrative costs, and expediting the transaction process.

ideas.idea: A key contractual gap exists in linking individual subcontractor/supplier performance reliability to overall project performance and codifying this relationship into enforceable contract rules.
ideas.quote: There is a gap in the body of knowledge in understanding the relationship between an individual participant’s work plan reliability and project performance, and developing smart contract rules to motivate reliable completion based on various possible scenarios.

ideas.idea: Delivery sequencing and variability of prefabricated components (off-site fabrication and shipment) is a major contractual risk factor affecting project schedule and cost, relevant to how contracts should allocate risk for supply variability in MMC projects.
ideas.quote: The simulation results show that the arrival sequence had a significant impact on project success... The accumulated effects of out-of-sequence deliveries disrupted the balance of unloading, hoisting, and installing, and had the potential to endanger the completion of the project itself.

ideas.idea: Contractual benchmarks/performance levels can be quantitatively derived (via simulation) and embedded into automated payment mechanisms, offering a model for objective performance-based payment clauses instead of subjective appraisal.
ideas.quote: The applications developed in this research provide objective and instant feedback on subcontractors' performance. In many current practices, subcontractor performance appraisal tends to be subjective and qualitative, and it is difficult to customize the incentives and penalties to reflect various performance levels.

ideas.idea: Documentation and evidence for contractual compliance in construction is often poorly kept, and blockchain-based image evidence can provide immutable, transparent records that reduce disputes over payment conditions—relevant to standard contract provisions on proof of performance and claims.
ideas.quote: improving the poor conventional documentation processes for construction data, wherein records are often defectively filed and simply lost after project completion... it is difficult for subcontractors to argue about what has been clearly recorded in the images.

ideas.idea: Smart contracts as currently implemented function only as an attachment to conventional contracts and lack flexibility to handle change orders, indicating a limitation relevant to how MMC contractual frameworks must accommodate variations.
ideas.quote: the developed smart contract functions as the attachment to the conventional contract; it lacks the flexibility to deal with multiple change order scenarios.

ideas.idea: Off-site fabrication and shipping introduce contractual risk allocation questions (e.g., who bears cost of fabricator delay/rework), as rework rates and fabrication delays were empirically significant in the case project.
ideas.quote: there was a 30% chance of rework being required for PBU_LP installation and a 10% chance of rework being required for PBU installation.

objectives: To identify and rank liability factors involved in the process from digital design to digital fabrication, and to develop a conceptual framework for contract design that considers these factors across existing project delivery models.
problem_statement: The adoption of digital fabrication in construction introduces new liability uncertainties—such as faulty fabrication due to poorly constructed digital models—that can increase disputes, yet liability factors in the digital design-to-fabrication process have received little scholarly attention, leaving a gap in how to design contracts to manage them.
methodology: A two-stage single case study approach: Stage 1 involved descriptive case study research (document review and 21 semistructured interviews) on Case R within Project Q, a Taiwanese theater project, mapping the digital design-to-fabrication process via a swimlane diagram. Stage 2 involved a three-round Delphi survey of 14 selected project stakeholders to identify and rank 163 liability factors across eight categories (actors, resources, conditions, attributes, processes, artifacts, values, risks), followed by development of a conceptual contractual framework with four provisions (A-D) based on statistical thresholds (quartiles of mean and standard deviation).
key_background_studies: Bock and Linner (2015) - established digital fabrication concepts and robot-oriented design (ROD), foundational to defining digital fabrication.
Ng et al. (2021) - introduced design for digital fabrication (DfDFAB) and studied process/organization/information integration for digital fabrication.
Hamdi and Leite (2014) - identified liability factors for conflicts in BIM implementation, informing the eight-category liability framework.
Alwash et al. (2017) - identified legal uncertainties and liability factors in BIM adoption, contributing categories like negligence and shared information risks.
Celoza et al. (2021a) - identified legal/liability factors for information management in BIM, directly informing the study's liability factor categorization and Delphi methodology.
Celoza et al. (2021b) - found necessary contractual conditions for BIM-related cost success, informing liability factor definitions.
Touran et al. (2011) - described liability and risk allocation differences across DBB, CM, DB project delivery models.
Hall and Bonanomi (2021) - applied Ostrom's common pool resource governance theory to IPD projects, relevant to managing collaborative resources in integrated digital fabrication contexts.
Dalkey (1969) and Okoli and Pawlowski (2004) - established Delphi method procedures used as methodological basis for the study's survey design.
findings: The study identified 163 liability factors across eight categories, with management capability and BIM expertise (both resources) ranked as the two most important. General contractor (actor), BIM modeling coordination platform (resource), and reduce errors (value) were also highly ranked. 85 factors exceeded the second quartile threshold and were organized into four contractual provisions (A-D) based on importance and variability. The study proposes that these provisions be incorporated into contracts via supplementary agreements (e.g., PCSA, BIM protocol), supplementary clauses (e.g., prescriptive tender specifications), or supplementary practices (e.g., concurrent engineering, design-to-target value) depending on the project delivery model (DBB, CM, DB, IPD). IPD was found to require fewer supplementary considerations than other delivery models due to its inherently integrated structure, though it may need enhanced BIM protocols and target-value practices for managing collaborative resources.

ideas.idea: Digital fabrication requires integration of upstream design and downstream fabrication/construction information, and misalignment between these can create liability uncertainty.
ideas.quote: a faulty digital fabrication operated by a downstream contractor could be due to a poorly constructed three-dimensional (3D) design model with inadequate design information passed from upstream design teams

ideas.idea: Clear understanding of liability factors is necessary at the contract design stage to avoid disputes and negligence claims related to digital fabrication.
ideas.quote: To address the liability uncertainties and avoid disputes, a clear understanding of the liability factors in the process is needed for project stakeholders to consider when designing the contracts.

ideas.idea: Management capability and BIM expertise are the most critical resource-related liability factors for successful digital fabrication adoption.
ideas.quote: The resources of management capability and building information modeling (BIM) expertise rank as the two most important liability factors.

ideas.idea: The general contractor bears the most liability responsibility among actor types because they oversee the overall construction process including digital fabrication.
ideas.quote: the general contractor is responsible for the overall construction process including planning and managing digital fabrication.

ideas.idea: On-site constructability is the most important condition-type liability factor, reflecting the need for off-site fabricated systems to integrate properly during on-site assembly.
ideas.quote: a system fabricated digitally off-site should be integrable with other building parts during on-site assembly.

ideas.idea: Early contractor involvement is linked to design for constructability and reduces liability risk in digital fabrication projects.
ideas.quote: The condition of early contractor involvement is relevant to "design for constructability," as stated by one surveyed expert.

ideas.idea: Different project delivery models allocate liability and risk differently, affecting how digital fabrication liability factors should be contractually addressed.
ideas.quote: For each of the four project delivery models, there is little to no research that investigates how they need to change in response to digital fabrication adoption.

ideas.idea: Design-Bid-Build's fragmented, sequential structure can lead to change orders and claims due to lack of early contractor involvement, creating liability challenges for digital fabrication.
ideas.quote: DBB projects could suffer from change orders and claims due to negligence of construction know-how in the early design phase.

ideas.idea: Integrated Project Delivery, through multiparty relational contracting and shared risk/reward, better supports digital fabrication adoption but still poses governance challenges for collaborative resources.
ideas.quote: The early contractor involvement and risk-and-reward sharing mechanism foster systemic innovation across disciplines and adoption of digital fabrication with cost control.

ideas.idea: Liability factors can be incorporated into contracts through supplementary agreements, clauses, or practices tailored to each project delivery model.
ideas.quote: Liability factors can be included in a supplementary agreement such as a preconstruction services agreement (PCSA) or a BIM protocol; Factors can be included in a supplementary clause in a standard agreement... Factors can be included as a supplementary practice, such as concurrent engineering and design-to-target value

ideas.idea: A precise, coordinated 3D BIM model serves as a key contractual artifact for pricing, bill of materials, and construction information in digital fabrication under DBB delivery.
ideas.quote: This artifact is in particular important for DBB projects because it is usually the model that provides "construction information and pricing," including the "bill of materials and quantity takeoff,"

ideas.idea: IPD requires fewer supplementary contractual considerations for digital fabrication than other delivery models due to its integrated structure, though enhanced BIM protocols may still be needed.
ideas.quote: the authors evaluated that, among the other three project delivery models, IPD requires fewer supplementary considerations when designing the contract for design for digital fabrication.

ideas.idea: Preconstruction services agreements can facilitate early contractor involvement in DBB or CM projects to address digital fabrication design needs before construction begins.
ideas.quote: PCSA is recommended for a DBB or CM project to enable the early involvement of the digital fabrication trade contractor to participate in the design process.

objectives: To use a machine learning-driven content analysis approach to examine particular conditions of FIDIC 1999 Silver Book contracts from nine well-performing projects, identifying which aspects (Control, Coordination, Adaptation functions) good particular conditions focus on when modifying general conditions to avert risk.
problem_statement: While general conditions of standard contracts (e.g., FIDIC) are recognized as good practice for managing risk through Control, Coordination, and Adaptation functions, particular conditions—drafted to address project-specific circumstances—can introduce additional risks by unevenly modifying general conditions. Prior research on particular conditions has been practice-oriented, narrowly focused on single issues (e.g., subcontractors, finance), and lacked grounding in contract theory, and human coding of contract functions is costly and potentially subjective.
methodology: Content analysis and machine learning classification of contract texts. Human coders classified 5,785 sentences from FIDIC 2017 Suite of Contracts, FIDIC 1999 Red Book, and five particular conditions based on the FIDIC 1999 Silver Book into 11 subfunctions under 3 functions (Control, Coordination, Adaptation), following Chen et al. (2018b)'s coding scheme. Four classification algorithms (naive Bayes, SVM, logistic regression, random forest) were compared using TF-IDF feature extraction; SVM with linear kernel, C=10, and unigram/bigram/trigram tokens was selected as optimal and used to code four additional particular conditions. Statistics on functional complexity across nine contracts (general + particular conditions) were compiled and compared to the FIDIC 1999 Silver Book general conditions using chi-square tests.
key_background_studies: Mellewigt et al. (2012) and Schepker et al. (2014) - proposed the multifunctional perspective identifying Control, Coordination, and Adaptation as contract functions addressing different risk types.

Chen et al. (2018b) - developed the coding scheme with 11 subfunctions under 3 functions and applied content analysis to FIDIC 1999 general conditions, finding all three functions nontrivially present; this study directly extends their method to particular conditions.
Lawrence (2017) - argued particular conditions can unreasonably transfer risks (e.g., nominated subcontractor risks) to one party, informing the risk concern addressed in this study.
Lee et al. (2020b) - used rule-based NLP to measure how risk allocation is modified by employers in FIDIC particular conditions.
Bodea and Purnus (2016) - analyzed how particular conditions affect contractors' financial issue management.
Lee et al. (2019) - built an automated system to extract 'poisonous clauses' in contracts to help contractors identify risks.
You et al. (2018) - found Control clauses inhibit relational risks and Adaptation clauses promote cooperation under uncertainty.
Yao et al. (2021) - found coordination provisions reduce misunderstandings and disputes after contract violations.
Lee et al. (2020a) - argued contractual control, coordination and adaptation improve BIM delivery quality and project performance.
findings: The SVM model with TF-IDF (unigram+bigram+trigram, linear kernel, C=10) achieved acceptable accuracy (61%-89%) across five test particular conditions. Chi-square tests showed no significant difference in functional distribution (Control, Coordination, Adaptation) between the nine complete contracts (general + particular conditions) and the general conditions alone, indicating particular conditions are coherent extensions of general conditions rather than substantial redistributions of risk-related functions. Within particular conditions, supplement sentences exceeded deletions, with Obligations and Task Descriptions subfunctions showing the largest positive adjusted residuals (most added), Interpretations showing the largest absolute numbers of changes (most explained/clarified), and Adaptation (especially Task Changes) the least adjusted, reflecting the difficulty of foreseeing future contingencies. The study concludes good particular conditions concentrate on explicitly illustrating both parties' obligations and tasks to mitigate risk while making only minor changes to Adaptation clauses.

ideas.idea: Standard/model contracts (like FIDIC) are widely reused with modifications rather than drafted anew, and particular conditions serve to adapt these standard forms to project-specific circumstances.
ideas.quote: Because different construction projects might have certain risks in common, writing a completely new contract for a new project is often unnecessary.

ideas.idea: Modifying general conditions through particular conditions can create additional, potentially uneven risk distribution between contracting parties.
ideas.quote: some particular conditions can set certain contractual and legal pitfalls to bring additional risks to the employer or contractor by deleting some fair clauses or adding some clauses to distribute risks unevenly

ideas.idea: Despite modifications, well-performing contracts show that particular conditions do not significantly alter the overall functional (risk-mitigation) balance established by general conditions.
ideas.quote: no significant differences are found in the functional distributions between a whole contract (containing both general and particular conditions) and its general conditions.

ideas.idea: Good particular conditions primarily add detail to obligations and task descriptions, clarifying responsibilities rather than fundamentally changing risk allocation logic.
ideas.quote: particular conditions should concentrate more on explicitly illustrating both parties’ obligations and tasks prudently to mitigate potential risks.

ideas.idea: Excessive amendment of contingency/adaptation-related clauses is riskier than amending coordination-related clauses, since future events are inherently hard to foresee, so parties should avoid unnecessary changes to adaptation provisions.
ideas.quote: the practitioners should follow the rule of general conditions and do not make unnecessary changes that would just be “gilding the lily.”

ideas.idea: Frequent modification of coordination-type clauses should not be seen as a sign of distrust between parties, but rather as an effort to improve mutual understanding and reduce performance risk.
ideas.quote: These amendments in Task Descriptions contradict the traditional thoughts that too many amendments in particular conditions are the root of a poor relationship (Lawrence 2017).

ideas.idea: Machine learning-based coding can efficiently and objectively analyze large volumes of contract text, supporting knowledge management for firms handling many contracts and particular conditions.
ideas.quote: The machine learning model can help them efficiently analyze the contracts of the projects they have done, which contributes to knowledge management for writing and understanding particular conditions.

ideas.idea: Particular conditions increase overall contract complexity because supplement (additive) sentences outnumber deletions, especially for obligations and task descriptions.
ideas.quote: the number of deletion sentences is less than that of supplement sentences, which indicates that the particular conditions contribute to an increase in contract complexity.

ideas.idea: Clarifying/interpreting terms is the most numerous type of adjustment in particular conditions, reflecting the need to specify project-particular circumstances not covered by general conditions.
ideas.quote: Interpretations take up the largest number and proportion of sentences in particular conditions, and explaining specific situations is the most important task for particular conditions to avert risks.

objectives: To quantify the marginal benefits of prefabrication building system in terms of cost, time and productivity improvements over the traditional building system (TBS), and to examine how building type as a fixed independent factor affects these observed benefits.
problem_statement: Documented benefits of prefabrication compared to traditional construction have largely been anecdotal or fragmented, based on isolated case studies, lacking statistically significant, quantified evidence across building types, which contributes to low industry uptake of prefabrication.
methodology: Mixed method of archival research and case study analysis using historical records of 66 completed prefabricated building projects in Auckland, New Zealand, spanning commercial, house, apartment, educational, and community buildings. Purposive sampling was used to obtain final contract sums, completion dates, gross floor areas, and number of floors from contractors and consulting firms. Equivalent TBS costs and durations were derived from the Rawlinsons Construction Handbook and feedback from designers/contractors. Marginal cost savings, time savings, and productivity improvement were computed using percentage-difference formulas, and univariate ANOVA was used to test the effect of building type on these outcomes.
key_background_studies: Shahzad and Mbachu [1] - argued little differentiation between conventional and prefab building types based on componentization/panelization proportions, and discussed owner preference for bespoke designs limiting prefab flexibility.
Lu [14] - observed that prefab offers more reliable cost estimates and investment outlay beyond just cost savings.
Bell [3] - discussed socio-cultural stigma and misperceptions about prefab quality from post-WWII reconstruction era.
Egan [26] - argued prefab offers speed, lower cost, less skilled labour need, and significant (30%-40%) productivity improvement.

Burgess et al. [27] - New Zealand case study finding prefab did not yield superior economic benefits over onsite construction, contrasting overseas findings; also cited generalized time savings (30-60%) for residential prefab applications.
Mbachu and Shahzad [7] - distinguished construction industry productivity (cost/schedule based) from economist's input-output productivity concept.
findings: Prefabrication delivered average 19% cost savings and 34% time savings over TBS, translating to 7% average productivity improvement. Highest cost saving (24%) was in community buildings; highest time saving (50%) and productivity gain (11%) were in house projects. ANOVA showed building type had no significant effect on cost saving or productivity improvement (p>0.05) but had significant effect on time savings (p=0.0005), indicating time-saving benefits should be reported per building type rather than generalized, while cost and productivity benefits can be generalized across building types.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication is defined by the value proportion of prefabricated components relative to total building value, blurring lines with conventional construction.
ideas.quote: a building is classified as a prefab building where the prefab component is more than 50% of the total building value, or vice versa.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication limits the extent of owner-driven design changes compared to conventional construction, which can affect project outcomes negatively if changes are made late.
ideas.quote: the prefab approach usually limits the extent of the owner’s changes to the standard designs. If significant changes are made, especially at the construction phase, the outcomes for the prefab technology in terms of costs, speed and wastage will be less desirable

ideas.idea: Site condition variability and construction-phase changes make conventional building methods more suitable in certain circumstances than prefab.
ideas.quote: the reality that construction-phase changes are bound to be made due to the variability of site conditions from the initial design assumptions. In these circumstances, the conventional building method proves to be more suitable than the prefab system.

ideas.idea: Logistics and interface issues (haulage, cranage, site connections) represent significant risks/challenges for prefabricated construction delivery.
ideas.quote: Some of the issues relate to the need for expensive haulage and cranage for handling large prefab components [9,13], the long lead time required for ordering and supply of prefab components

ideas.idea: The benefits of prefabrication (cost/productivity) are consistent across building types, but time-saving benefits are not, meaning contractual and planning assumptions about schedule benefits should be building-type specific.
ideas.quote: claims about the superior benefits of prefab can only be generalised in respect of cost and productivity improvements across all building types, whereas claims about time savings should be cautiously applied to specific building types.

ideas.idea: Lack of quantified, evidence-based data on prefabrication's benefits is a barrier to industry uptake, which has implications for how contracts and procurement decisions are justified.
ideas.quote: The low level of industry uptake of prefab hinges in part on the lack of quantifiable evidence to support claims about the numerous benefits credited to the technology.

objectives: To develop, pilot and validate an empirically-based, globally-applicable decision-support tool that helps engineering construction clients and decision-makers determine a project's suitability for modularisation/offsite construction at an early conceptual stage.
problem_statement: Existing decision-support tools for offsite/modular construction are limited, outdated, or not suited to the engineering construction sector, leading decisions about modularisation to be based mainly on capital cost, experience or intuition rather than a holistic, value-based evaluation.
methodology: A mixed-method, two-phase study (2014-2016) involving European Construction Institute (ECI) members (clients, contractors, consultants, suppliers). Phase 1 used a web-based questionnaire (n=18), semi-structured phone interviews (n=12), a Delphi-style plenary questionnaire (n=46) and workshop 1 focus groups (n=28) to identify drivers/constraints. Phase 2 used a further literature review, workshop 2 (n=12), an online questionnaire to the ECI modularisation task force (n=10), and workshop 3 focus groups (n=25) to refine and validate a decision-support tool built in Excel/VBA using a Simple Multi-Attribute Rating Technique (SMART).
key_background_studies: Tatum et al. (1987) - seminal work defining modularisation and modules, foundational to later engineering construction research
Gibb (1999) - established importance of early project-wide offsite strategy and terminology distinctions between offsite and modularisation
Pan et al. (2008) - developed a decision-support matrix for build system selection in housing, highlighting lack of holistic metrics for offsite decisions
Haas and Fagerlund (2002) - developed Modex, the earliest identifiable modularisation decision-support tool, later basis for SMART approach
Blismas et al. (2006) - argued benefits of offsite depend on project specifics and cannot be generalized, informing evaluation approach
Emes (1992) - argued offsite strategy must be evaluated from an 'overall project view' rather than 'element view'
Cigolini and Castellano (2002) - discussed modularisation drivers in remote/constrained sites and offshore sector influence
Farmer (2016) and Egan (1998)/Latham (1994) reports - identified persistent inefficiencies in UK construction motivating offsite uptake
findings: The study identified 46 drivers and 41 constraints for modularisation, categorised into client objectives, site characteristics, project execution/management, and EPC/contractor/industry status. These were used to build the Ecimod tool with three levels (initial selection, applicability, feasibility) using SMART scoring. Validation workshops showed acceptable disagreement levels (20-22%) with the tool's structure, leading to refinements such as allowing user-specified drivers/constraints and adjustable impact weightings. The tool was implemented in Excel/VBA and is presented as the first globally-applicable, empirically validated decision-support tool for modularisation in engineering construction, enabling informed, auditable decisions at the early project stage.

ideas.idea: Early evaluation of modularisation strategy at the project-wide level (rather than element level) is critical to realizing benefits, which has implications for how contracts must accommodate early decision points.
ideas.quote: the offsite strategy must be evaluated from an ‘overall project view’ rather than an ‘element view’

ideas.idea: The benefits of modularisation are not universal but depend heavily on project-specific circumstances, meaning contractual frameworks cannot assume standard benefit realization.
ideas.quote: benefits deriving from offsite depend on the project specifications, circumstances and combination of construction techniques employed. One cannot simply list them and be sure of their realisation in every project

ideas.idea: Modularisation increases upfront engineering and design effort and cost, which has contractual implications for compensation and design responsibility allocation.
ideas.quote: H: Higher engineering and design cost due to higher working hours required

ideas.idea: Modularisation shifts risk, particularly regarding transportation and installation of modules, which raises questions about risk allocation between parties in contracts.
ideas.quote: Risk allocation shift (e.g. from engineering design to engineering construction)

ideas.idea: Increased coordination and communication requirements among project participants when using modularisation implies a need for contractual provisions addressing multi-party coordination.
ideas.quote: More effective communication and coordination required between project operators

ideas.idea: Early freezing of design decisions under a modular approach limits ability to make late changes, which has implications for change-order and variation clauses in contracts.
ideas.quote: H: Limited late changes due to early freeze of design and decisions

ideas.idea: Transportation of modules carries significant risk of damage or loss, a factor relevant to insurance and liability provisions in construction contracts.
ideas.quote: H: High transportation risk (module damaged or lost)

ideas.idea: Lack of industry experience and consolidated management procedures for modular projects among contractors is a barrier, suggesting a need for contractual clarity on responsibilities when parties lack modular expertise.
ideas.quote: Lack of consolidate methods and management procedures in facing modular projects

ideas.idea: Clients' and stakeholders' limited understanding of modularisation's pros and cons can hinder appropriate contractual and procurement decisions.
ideas.quote: Client’s lack of understanding of pros and cons of modularisation

ideas.idea: Existing decision-support tools and standard practices for offsite/modular construction are outdated or absent for large engineering construction projects, reflecting a broader gap in guidance (including contractual guidance) for this delivery method.
ideas.quote: Decision-support tools for determining a project’s suitability for offsite modular construction are currently limited or outdated, leading to decisions being based mainly around capital cost, experience or intuition.

objectives: To develop Shapley value–based smart contracts that automatically quantify subcontractors' marginal contributions in modular construction and assign fair rewards/penalties to motivate reliable, task-level, bottom-up collaboration, and to implement and validate these payment rules on a blockchain network.
problem_statement: Construction projects require highly interrelated collaboration among fragmented subcontractors, yet current centralized contractual and management mechanisms cannot reliably motivate collaborative, reliable behavior or fairly allocate rewards/penalties based on actual marginal contributions. There is no objective, automated mechanism to instantly and fairly distribute benefits/penalties among participants performing at different reliability levels, and existing blockchain/smart contract and game-theory studies on construction incentives remain largely theoretical without validated implementation.
methodology: Empirical delivery and installation data (74 PBU loading platform assemblies and 139 hoisting activities) were collected from a high-rise residential modular construction (MC) project in Singapore involving prefabricated bathroom units (PBUs). A discrete-event simulation model (built in STROBOSCOPE) was developed to permutate three reliability levels (high/middle/low) for three participants (PBU fabricator, crane, workers), generating 27 coalition scenarios run 50 times each, quantifying project duration and cost outcomes. Shapley value calculations were applied to the simulation outputs to derive fair marginal-contribution-based reward/penalty amounts for each subcontractor. These payment rules were then encoded as smart contracts (Solidity, Remix-Ethereum IDE) and deployed on a private Ethereum blockchain (Ganache, MetaMask, Truffle Suite) for validation, including simulated malicious-operation detection.
key_background_studies: Shapley (1953) - introduced the Shapley value concept underlying the fair-allocation mechanism used in this study
Pishdad-Bozorgi and Srivastava (2018) - studied IPD standard contracts and found financial incentives keep parties in the coalition, motivating this study's incentive-based approach
Hunhevicz et al. (2020, 2022a, 2022b) - explored blockchain governance, DAO concepts, and performance-based smart contracts with financial incentives, identified as leaving gaps this study addresses
Elghaish et al. (2020) - developed a smart contract framework for IPD projects coding risk/reward transactions, cited as case-based incentive work needing further validation
Lu et al. (2021a) - recorded reputation scores in blockchain with incentive mechanisms for off-site logistics/assembly, suggested integrating game theory for fairness
Javanmardi et al. (2018) - argued relational contracts can be formed based on cooperative game theory, informing the study's theoretical basis
Assaad et al. (2020) - noted subcontractor interactions are shaped mainly by contractual relationships, framing the collaboration problem
Grigg (2004) - recognized the need to pair smart contracts with legal contracts, informing the study's limitations discussion
findings: The simulation showed that as subcontractors increase reliability levels, project duration shortens and costs decrease, though marginal benefits of higher reliability diminish when other parties remain unreliable. Shapley value-based payments produced three incentive effects: (1) penalties for low reliability, no payment for middle reliability, and rewards for high reliability, motivating collaboration to avoid penalties; (2) individual high performance is the dominant strategy, and high-performing players are incentivized to encourage others' high performance, enabling peer negotiation and production; (3) investing in higher reliability reduces overall costs when Shapley value payments are enforced, even though initial investment is higher. The smart contract, deployed on a blockchain, correctly automated reward/penalty payments matching Shapley value calculations and successfully detected and rejected malicious/incorrect payment attempts, demonstrating feasibility of decentralized, self-enforcing incentive contracts without centralized human judgment.

ideas.idea: Contractual relationships primarily shape how subcontractors interact and coordinate on projects, but contractual/hierarchical coercion alone cannot guarantee reliable collaboration or eliminate opportunistic behavior.
ideas.quote: it has been argued that coercive forces from hierarchical authority or contractual terms cannot guarantee reliable collaboration or reduce opportunistic behaviors (Henisz et al. 2012).

ideas.idea: Relational contracting approaches such as partnering and IPD were introduced to counter fragmentation by embedding shared risk/reward ('pain-share, gain-share') principles into contracts.
ideas.quote: Project teams jointly take responsibility for completing the projects and share the achievements or failures of the projects based on the "pain-share, gain-share" mentality (Yeung et al. 2007).

ideas.idea: Financial incentives embedded in IPD-type contracts help keep parties committed to the coalition and reduce cost overruns, showing the contractual value of incentive-based risk/reward sharing.
ideas.quote: Pishdad-Bozorgi and Srivastava (2018) studied various IPD standard contracts and indicated that parties that were financially incentivized would stay in the coalition and complete the project satisfactorily with a minimized cost overrun.

ideas.idea: Determining fair reward/risk sharing arrangements early in a project, and achieving financial transparency, remains a persistent challenge for collaborative delivery contracts like IPD.
ideas.quote: In addition, determining fair rewards and sharing in the early phases and achieving financial transparency can be challenging (Kahvandi et al. 2019; Rodrigues and Lindhard 2023).

ideas.idea: Smart contracts can automate payment processes, reduce transaction costs, and build trust, but they struggle to handle unexpected or exceptional contractual scenarios, raising concerns for their integration into legally enforceable construction contracts.
ideas.quote: implementing smart contracts in the construction industry is inherently difficult because smart contracts cannot handle unexpected cases (Li et al. 2023).

ideas.idea: A key unresolved contractual challenge is defining coordination mechanisms within smart contracts that fairly align multiple parties' interests without requiring human/centralized judgment.
ideas.quote: defining coordination mechanisms in smart contracts that can align human interests to create collective outcomes represents one of the main challenges of implementing blockchains practically (Hunhevicz et al. 2021).

ideas.idea: Cooperative game theory (and specifically Shapley value) provides a principled way to allocate rewards/penalties among contracting parties based on their marginal contribution to joint outcomes, offering an alternative to purely contractual/administrative allocation.
ideas.quote: The Shapley value... is a mechanism in cooperative game theory that provides a unique and equitable distribution of additional costs when working in a coalition (Sharafi et al. 2021).

ideas.idea: Embedding fair, quantitative incentive rules into smart contracts can shift project governance from centralized command-and-control (typical of standard contract administration) toward decentralized, self-enforcing peer-to-peer coordination.
ideas.quote: Embedding the rules in construction contracts can shape project participants' collaborative behaviors towards desired outcomes, enabling an efficient self-motivated system.

ideas.idea: Because smart contracts execute rigidly, pairing them with traditional legal contracts is necessary to ensure enforceability and to handle unforeseen events such as change orders or extreme disruptions, which current smart contract designs cannot adequately manage.
ideas.quote: it is necessary to pair smart contracts and contracts so that the smart contract can be consistent with legal enforcement.

ideas.idea: Reliance on a single trusted central database for triggering smart contract execution reintroduces a centralization risk (single point of failure), suggesting that contractual/technical frameworks for modular construction must also address data governance, not just payment logic.
ideas.quote: this study assumed the existence of a trustful central database that is responsible for smart contract data input. However, the central database might also suffer from a single point of failure.

ideas.idea: Automated, objective reward/penalty determination based on marginal contribution can replace subjective, delayed manager judgments about performance issues, potentially reshaping how contractual remedies for delay/cost overrun are structured in modular/prefabrication delivery.
ideas.quote: Managers usually have to wait until the end of a project to evaluate how severe the problem is and devote a significant amount of time and effort to determine the amount and collect evidence to prove it.

objectives: To identify and address the obstacles currently preventing further expansion of off-site prefabrication, focusing on timber and MEP services, by examining the coordination and implementation processes between builders and suppliers in Australia.
problem_statement: There is a lack of empirical and qualitative research detailing the specific processes and obstacles in coordinating off-site prefabrication between builders and suppliers, particularly for timber and MEP services, which have not been jointly investigated in prior literature.
methodology: Qualitative field research comprising 40 unstructured, face-to-face interviews with approximately 2 participants each from four builder organizations and four supplier organizations in Melbourne, Australia. Data were coded and analyzed using NVivo software to generate themes via content analysis, followed by comparative analysis between builders' and suppliers' perspectives, with internal (literature) and external (industry expert) validation.
key_background_studies: Bildsten (2014) - established that there is traditionally a lack of collaboration and coordination between builders and suppliers, and that coordination precedes collaboration
Johnsson and Meiling (2009) - studied defects in completed timber modules prefabricated off-site
Tserng et al. (2011) - developed an algorithm for efficient on-site assembly of modular MEP services, highlighting supplier limitations in verifying designs on-site
Salama et al. (2017) - developed a 'Modular Suitability Index' to optimize coordination between off-site prefabricated components and in situ construction
Laurent and Leicht (2019) - defined Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) as multiple stakeholders joining a relational, multiparty contract to better coordinate cross-functional teams
Yunis et al. (2016) - revealed deficiencies between off-site prefabrication and in situ construction, informing interview design
Masood et al. (2021) - studied supply chains of prefabricated houses in New Zealand, identifying key obstacles similar to those found in this study
findings: The study identified builder obstacles (sustainability, QA, mass production, CAD/BIM, technological support, commercial arrangements, system building, buffering in supply, schedule monitoring, productivity, flexibility, engagement, risks, multiple supply arrangements) and supplier obstacles (design, financing and subcontracting, coordination, recognized practices, risks, multiple supply arrangements, constraints). These obstacles can largely be addressed through improved collaboration and coordination, which are traditionally lacking between builders and suppliers. Builders and suppliers have identified ways to harmonize off-site prefabrication practices with in situ construction, offering a framework transferable to other modular construction contexts.

ideas.idea: Commercial contracts between builders and suppliers include specific financial risk-mitigation clauses such as bank guarantees and insurance certificates to manage cash flow risk in prefabrication arrangements.
ideas.quote: Bank guarantees allow the builders to deposit payments, which helps them obtain materials, plant and/or equipment necessary for contending with construction project-specific risks.

ideas.idea: Large Tier 1 builders often impose onerous subcontract terms on prefabrication suppliers that rigidly require delivery regardless of circumstances, creating risk imbalance.
ideas.quote: Tier One (1) builders mightn’t budge . . . There’s no excuse because those contracts blindly say you will deliver.

ideas.idea: Variation orders (VOs) issued by project clients disrupt the prefabrication supplier's production cycle, resources, quality control, and coordination, creating contractual and scheduling risk.
ideas.quote: each variation order (VO) by the project client inevitably changed their cycle of preparation, resources invested, QC, as well as coordination, thereby jeopardizing the functions of logistics, scheduling, meeting deadlines, constructability, and installation efficiency.

ideas.idea: Suppliers are cautious about sharing design intellectual property (shop drawings) with builders/clients due to fear of losing future work to competitors, affecting information flow in contractual relationships.
ideas.quote: Supplier P2 protects their interests in generally preferring to provide verbal information, rather than documents like shop drawings, as they are cautious of the risk of losing future work to a competitor who has managed to get hold of their designs.

ideas.idea: Multiple supply arrangements—engaging duplicate or competing suppliers for the same project—are used by builders as a contractual risk mitigation strategy against delay or non-performance.
ideas.quote: Costs aren’t always the most vital. If you fail in what you deliver, it might be cheaper to let in bulk . . . If you can’t deliver on time, you’ll lose more.

ideas.idea: Insufficient or late design information provided before prefabrication starts creates downstream contractual and cost risks including unforeseen costs, delays, defects, and safety hazards requiring remediation through negotiation.
ideas.quote: without the timely shop drawings with adequate information from off-site prefabrication suppliers, risks of associated unforeseen costs, delays, defects, OH&S hazards, and project client distress would ensue, which normally require remediation measures through potentially hostile negotiations.

ideas.idea: Nominated subcontractor arrangements and joint trading accounts are used to formalize financial relationships between suppliers, builders and clients for prefabricated components.
ideas.quote: Supplier P2 is unique inasmuch that they regularly open a short-term joint trading account with the builders or construction project clients to whom they supply off-site prefabricated timber components. The construction project client would then engage the builder, with Supplier P2 included as a Nominated Subcontractor.

ideas.idea: Integrated Project Delivery (IPD), involving relational multiparty contracts, is identified as better suited than traditional procurement to accommodate off-site prefabrication coordination.
ideas.quote: Integrated project delivery (IPD) better caters for off-site prefabrication than traditionally procured construction projects... 'multiple stakeholders from the design and construction team join a relational, multiparty contract'.

ideas.idea: Lack of collaboration and coordination between builders and suppliers is a traditional, systemic issue in the construction industry that underlies most prefabrication obstacles.
ideas.quote: there is a traditionally a lack of collaboration amongst builders and their suppliers. Furthermore, there is a lack of coordination between them in general.

ideas.idea: Tight tender/quote timeframes lead builders to compress schedules via off-site prefabrication after exhausting design-based cost savings, which strains relationships and contract variation negotiations with clients and suppliers.
ideas.quote: When all avenues to find gains from the design documentation for a project have been exhausted, they are then likely to focus on dynamically compressing their schedule, usually through adopting concurrent construction by way of off-site prefabrication.

ideas.idea: Off-site prefabrication suppliers bear disproportionate risk in the supply chain compared to builders who primarily act as purchasers.
ideas.quote: Hence, it has been the supplier organizations that normally carry most of the risks in the supply chains of construction projects.

objectives: To examine the impact of postpandemic inflation on construction project budgets and costs in Canada, identify high-sensitivity building divisions most affected by inflation, and demonstrate off-site construction (OSC) as a strategic approach to mitigate cost overruns caused by inflation, material waste and project delays.
problem_statement: Persistent, high, and volatile inflation following COVID-19 has driven significant cost overruns in Canadian construction projects, yet there is limited research identifying which specific project divisions are most sensitive to inflation and how off-site/modular construction methods can be strategically applied to protect project budgets against inflationary pressures.
methodology: A four-phase case-study methodology using a real administrative-complex project built with volumetric modular (off-site) construction in Northern Ontario. Historical Building Construction Price Index (BCPI) and material price data for Montréal were collected from Statistics Canada, RSMeans, purchase orders/invoices, and an external cost consultant. Elemental cost analysis (ECA) based on the National Master Specification (NMS) breakdown was performed, followed by data validation with the project owner and financing institutions. Inflation-induced change orders and claim amounts were analyzed, and Spearman's correlation coefficient and a sensitivity coefficient (SC) were calculated to relate inflation rates to claim amounts by division.
key_background_studies: Musarat et al. 2020/2021 - established inflation as a major cause of construction cost overruns and factors influencing it
Alaloul et al. 2021 - defined inflation and its role in cost estimation and overruns
Bertram et al. 2019 (McKinsey) - highlighted efficiency and cost-saving benefits of off-site construction, including faster completion reducing inflation exposure
Goulding and Rahimian 2019 - discussed OSC's role in reducing material waste and project delays
de Laubier et al. 2019 - supported OSC as a holistic solution to cost overrun risks
Smith and Quale 2017 - defined OSC as factory-based prefabrication assembled on site
Jordà and Nechio 2023 - analyzed post-pandemic inflation dynamics and drivers
Ribeirinho et al. 2020 - noted that most construction projects are subject to cost overruns
findings: Inflation caused a 14% (13.73%) increase in the contract sum for the case project, with metals and special construction (prefabricated components) divisions showing the highest inflation and sensitivity coefficients (0.27 and 0.14 respectively). Spearman's correlation between inflation rate and claim amount was strong and positive (r=0.6044), confirming that inflation significantly drives claim amounts across divisions. The study concludes that off-site construction is particularly suited to high-inflation-sensitivity divisions such as metals and special construction, as it allows controlled-environment production, bulk material purchasing with fixed pricing, reduced material waste, and shorter timelines—collectively mitigating inflation-driven cost overruns and improving budget predictability and resilience.

ideas.idea: Off-site construction centralizes production, enabling better control over material usage and quality, reducing risk of cost overruns from waste and delay.
ideas.quote: By centralizing production, OSC allows for better control over material usage and quality, thereby minimizing the risk of cost overruns due to material waste and project delays

ideas.idea: OSC reduces reliance on scarce and expensive on-site labor by shifting work to a controlled factory environment with a stable skilled workforce.
ideas.quote: OSC addresses the critical issue of workforce shortages by reducing the dependency on on-site labor, which has become increasingly scarce and expensive

ideas.idea: Divisions with high sensitivity to inflation (e.g., metals, special construction) are identified as good candidates for off-site construction to mitigate inflation risk.
ideas.quote: the divisions most affected by inflation (i.e., those with a high SC), such as metals and special construction, are good candidates to be studied using the OSC approach.

ideas.idea: OSC enables bulk purchasing of volatile materials like steel with fixed pricing agreements, insulating projects from inflation.
ideas.quote: the use of OSC enables bulk purchasing of materials, such as steel, which is highly susceptible to price fluctuations, further insulating projects from inflationary pressures. (Bulk purchasing agreements often come with fixed pricing, which protects against sudden price hikes.)

ideas.idea: A stipulated-price design-build contract (CCDC-14) does not allow price increases due to inflation, forcing the contractor to build inflation allowances into the bid based on historical benchmarks.
ideas.quote: A Design–Build Stipulated Price Contract (CCDC-14) was applied to the project, meaning that the contract price was not to be increased due to inflation. As such, the design–build company made allowances for inflation in its bid based on the benchmark of the inflation rate from 2018 to 2019.

ideas.idea: Change orders and claims due to inflation require validation and approval from multiple stakeholders including the client, project management consultant, and financing institutions, illustrating the contractual complexity of inflation-driven claims.
ideas.quote: a third-party project management consultant appointed by the client, the client's representative, and the project's financing agencies performed verification of the data analysis.

ideas.idea: Elemental cost analysis combined with inflation tracking supports proactive contractual and budgetary decision-making rather than reliance on after-the-fact contingency adjustments.
ideas.quote: This model should predict price variations over time during the project's initial stages, allowing for proactive budget adjustments, rather than relying on contingency costs for later modifications.

ideas.idea: OSC is framed as requiring collaborative agreement among all project stakeholders to be effectively adopted as an inflation mitigation strategy.
ideas.quote: These results underscore the importance of OSC as a collaborative approach among all stakeholders involved in construction projects.

objectives: To develop a constraint programming based optimization approach that generates an optimal module assembly plan for module yards, minimizing total waiting time of prefabricated small modules by synthesizing information from logistics management systems, contract documents, and resource availability.
problem_statement: Off-shore prefabrication and modular construction have increased supply chain complexity, causing frequent delays to prefabricated modules and creating waiting waste on module yards; existing subjective, experience-based scheduling decisions are inefficient and non-optimal for coping with unreliable module supply and limited assembly resources.
methodology: Development of a mathematical constraint programming model incorporating three constraint sources (logistics database for overseas module supply, construction contract documents for on-site demand/delivery deadlines, and crew/bay resource availability), solved using IBM ILOG CPLEX Optimization Studio; validated through a case study based on a real modular construction project in Alberta, Canada involving 10 large modules assembled from 40 off-shore fabricated small modules under two supply-delay scenarios.
key_background_studies: Ballard and Howell (1998) - advocated the concept of lean construction underpinning the modular/prefabrication approach
Wu and Lu (2013) - noted benefits of modular approach for mega oil sands projects (cost, duration, quality, safety)
Choi and Song (2014) - described modular method for improving labor productivity and off-shore fabrication sourcing
Tommelein et al. (2003) - discussed contractor tendency to deliver early to mitigate late delivery risk, causing waste
Dubois and Gadde (2002) - highlighted difficulty of achieving effective supply chain management in construction vs manufacturing
Liu and Lu (2016) - showed improvised schedule strategies based on common sense increase crew idling time and project delay
Menesi et al. (2013) - demonstrated constraint programming capability for large-scale time-cost trade-off scheduling problems
Liu and Wang (2012) - used constraint programming for scheduling linear construction projects with multi-skilled crews
findings: The proposed constraint programming framework successfully generated optimal module assembly schedules for two supply scenarios, yielding total waiting times of 298 days (Scenario 1) and 311 days (Scenario 2, with delayed container arrivals). The approach effectively integrates contract-derived delivery deadlines, logistics supply data, and crew/bay resource constraints to minimize waiting waste, providing decision support for both crew work planning and materials logistics under uncertain supply conditions.

ideas.idea: Contract documents are a direct data source defining on-site demand and delivery deadlines that constrain module assembly scheduling.
ideas.quote: the pre-set field erection deadlines extracted from construction contract

ideas.idea: Expected delivery times specified in contract documents impose hard constraints on the finish time of module assembly, requiring completion before contractual deadlines with buffer for preparation tasks.
ideas.quote: the module is required to be finished one day before the expected delivery time. For example, module M1 is expected to be delivered on Day 15, so it must be finished by Day 14.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication shifts risk and complexity to supply chain coordination between off-site fabrication, shipping, and on-site assembly, which contract-based deadlines must accommodate.
ideas.quote: The unreliable supply of modules and the temporary nature of the module yard configuration make it difficult for project managers to update plans in a fast and effective manner.

ideas.idea: Off-shore prefabrication for modular projects introduces contractual and logistical uncertainty because fabrication occurs overseas under different jurisdictions and shipping regulations.
ideas.quote: the engineering design and fabrication of modules are usually undertaken by overseas vendors in East Asia, such as South Korea, China

ideas.idea: Traditional contractor practice of early delivery to avoid contractual delay penalties generates waste, suggesting a tension between contractual risk allocation and lean efficiency.
ideas.quote: the contractor tends to deliver the materials or pre-fabricated modules at the earliest time in order to mitigate the risk of late delivery

ideas.idea: Effective coordination of prefabrication supply chains requires integrating contractual deadline information with logistics and resource data, implying that contracts should support such data-sharing to enable optimized scheduling.
ideas.quote: By synthesizing information from the logistics management system, contract documents, and resources availability, a constraint programming based optimization algorithm is proposed.

objectives: To develop and empirically test a theoretical framework for organizing collaboration forms within prefabricated modular high-rise building projects in order to overcome the process-related barriers currently hindering modular construction.
problem_statement: Although modular high-rise construction offers advantages in quality, safety, speed and predictability, process-related barriers (lack of integration, poor cooperation, communication issues) still hinder adoption, and existing research has not focused on which project delivery/collaboration forms best fit modular high-rise projects.
methodology: Qualitative multiple holistic case study of three international modular high-rise projects (The Fizz Spartaan, Amsterdam; CitizenM Bowery, New York; Mapleton Crescent SW18, London). Data were collected via 10 semi-structured interviews with project managers and stakeholders, supplemented by document review and data source triangulation. Data were coded in Atlas.ti using open, axial and selective coding, with within-case and cross-case template analysis. A theoretical framework based on 17 PDM selection criteria (adapted from Hosseini et al. 2015) and a scoring method (Hombergen et al. 2004) was used to compare client profiles against project delivery model (PDM) characteristics using spider charts.
key_background_studies: Blismas et al. (2005) - identified need for intensive collaboration, effective communication, and early design freeze as key process-related barriers in modular construction; also noted client reluctance to commit to a single supplier.
Wuni et al. (2019, 2020) - discussed difficulty of achieving early design freeze and the role of manufacturer input during design.
Hosseini et al. (2015) - provided the basis for the 17 selection criteria used to distinguish PDM characteristics.
Jonsson and Rudberg (2014) - linked modularity to organizational and process design, and high-rise buildings' suitability for modular methods.
Peltokorpi et al. (2018) - framed modularization as explaining architecture of products, organizations and processes.
Hough and Lawson (2019) - discussed suitability of modular buildings for repetitive, cellular-type structures.
De Ridder (2011) - proposed the idea of a new 'Product Delivery Model' with standard product-based contracts for modular suppliers, contrasting with project-based PDMs.
Ferdous et al. (2019); Jabar et al. (2013) - studied barriers to implementing prefab modular housing historically.
findings: The three cases used three different PDMs (Turnkey, Design-Bid-Built, and Design & Build), showing no single PDM universally fits modular high-rise projects. In all cases, clients sought to minimize their own execution responsibility, delegating system architect roles to contractors or suppliers depending on risk appetite and involvement level. Modular knowledge needed to be present early in the design phase in every case, though the mechanism differed (turnkey agreement, consultant involvement, or pre-service contract arrangements). Traditional Design-Bid-Built models were found less suitable due to rigid separation between design and construction phases, which conflicts with the need for early manufacturer input and design freeze. More integrated PDMs (Early Contractor Involvement, Design & Build, Turnkey) better accommodate modular construction needs. None of the cases used serial tendering or framework agreements, reflecting a project-based rather than product-based industry culture. The study concludes that current PDMs are not fully suited to product-based modular concepts, and that fixed, long-term partnerships (à la De Ridder's Product Delivery Model) would better serve modular high-rise development; until such a shift occurs, the best approach is to match client profiles against 17 PDM selection criteria using a spider chart tool.

ideas.idea: Modular construction requires an early 'design freeze' due to the need for extensive pre-engineering before manufacturing begins.
ideas.quote: An extensive preengineering at an early phase of the project is required in order to come to an ‘early design freeze’

ideas.idea: Managing the increased need for multidisciplinary collaboration throughout all phases is the biggest process-related barrier in modular construction.
ideas.quote: Managing this process is seen as the biggest process-related barrier to modular construction.

ideas.idea: Manufacturers should be given a larger, more determining role during the design phase to ensure design and production compatibility.
ideas.quote: One way to achieve this is by assigning a larger and more determining role of the manufacturer during the design phase.

ideas.idea: Clients often resist committing to a single modular supplier because it represents a risk-averse measure, avoiding reliance on one contractor for the modular system.
ideas.quote: a client doesn’t want to commit to a single one supplier as a risk-averse measure.

ideas.idea: The traditional Design-Bid-Built delivery model is poorly suited to modular construction because it separates design and construction, preventing timely optimization for modular methods.
ideas.quote: the traditional DBB model is not particularly well-suited to modular construction methods... the team may be unwilling or unable to make changes to optimize for modular construction.

ideas.idea: More integrated project delivery models—Early Contractor Involvement, Design & Build, and Turnkey—better accommodate the overlapping design-construction needs of modular projects.
ideas.quote: This calls for more integrated PDMs such as Early Contractor Involvement, Turnkey, or Design & Build.
