ideas.idea: The choice of the most suitable PDM depends on client characteristics, determined via 17 selection criteria compared against PDM strengths and weaknesses.
ideas.quote: The most suitable PDM is dependent on the client profile that can be determined by 17 selection criteria.

ideas.idea: Modular construction industry lacks long-term, product-based contractual arrangements (serial tendering/framework contracts), relying instead on project-by-project agreements.
ideas.quote: none of the cases uses a framework contract or serial tendering between a client and a modular supplier, whereby a declaration of intent is signed for several buildings.

ideas.idea: Modular building concepts would benefit from a shift to product-based delivery models with fixed, long-term partnerships rather than traditional project-based PDMs.
ideas.quote: modular buildings will benefit more from a long-term collaboration with fixed partnerships. This requires a complete different approach to the construction industry.

ideas.idea: A new type of 'Product Delivery Model' has been proposed in which the modular supplier provides a standard contract with terms and delivery conditions akin to a consumer product transaction.
ideas.quote: Making a strong argument for new Product Delivery Models such as described in the theory of De Ridder (2011), who argues that the modular supplier not only deliver the product but also has a standard contract that belongs to the product, including terms and delivery conditions

ideas.idea: In practice, the party who develops the modular system typically becomes the 'system architect' responsible for design rules, shifting risk and responsibility away from the client.
ideas.quote: you can really tell that CitizenM acts as the real System Architect deciding upon the design rules related to the product architecture.

ideas.idea: A Pre-Service Contract Arrangement (two-stage tender) can be used to validate technical feasibility of a modular solution before committing to a Design & Build contract.
ideas.quote: Thanks to the Pre Service Contract Arrangement (PSCA), the modular contractor, together with its regular consultant partners, has been able to remove these doubts.

objectives: To explore practical project governance approaches—combining project organizational structure and project governance mechanisms (contract and trust)—that promote inter-organizational collaboration (IOC) between stakeholders in off-site construction (OSC) projects, using a dynamic/adaptive systems perspective.
problem_statement: Prior studies treat project organizational structure and project governance mechanisms as separate, static, and substitutive factors affecting IOC in OSC projects, neglecting their complementary and dynamic interplay; formal contract governance alone struggles to achieve IOC due to contractual incompleteness, fragmented delivery modes, and low trust, leading to disputes, delays, and cost overruns.
methodology: Two-stage mixed-methods design: Study 1 is a cross-sectional survey of 178 valid responses (59.3% response rate) from frontline professionals in 30 OSC projects across 15 Chinese cities, using validated Likert-scale measures for contract, trust, project organizational structure, and IOC, analyzed via Mplus (CFA, reliability/validity, regression, bootstrapping mediation). Study 2 is a system simulation experiment using a Belousov–Zhabotinsky (B-Z) reaction/Oregonator dynamic model implemented in MATLAB to simulate evolutionary paths of the IOC system under different governance-dominated scenarios (contract-dominated, trust-dominated, IOC-dominated, dual-dominated).
key_background_studies: Winch [3] – established that project organizational structure allocates responsibilities and rights among stakeholders (transaction cost theory foundation).
Cicmil, Williams, Thomas and Hodgson [5] – examined horizontal/vertical governance structure functions in project organization.
Müller and Turner [6]; Ning [16]; Yan and Zhang [9] – identified formal contractual and informal relational governance mechanisms as necessary for resource exchange and information sharing.
Zhang, Liu, Gao and Ma [13] – argued contracts provide a legal atmosphere for formal collaboration, and highlighted issues from fragmented contracting in OSC.
Camilo, Andreas, Geert and Jörg [25] – provided validated scales for contract and trust used in the survey; discussed social network formation via contract and trust relations.
Woolthuis, Hillebrand and Nooteboom [51] – showed trust affects project team IOC and lack of trust harms owner-contractor partnerships.
Gokpinar, Hopp and Iravani [39] – found project control affects collaborative relationships through compliance behaviors.
Arya and Zhiang [55] – found organizational structure affects collaboration via contract type and performance.
Kalkman and Waard [59] – found project entities trust partners to comply with informal approvals beyond written contracts.
Prigogine (Brusselator model) – basis for the B-Z reaction dissipative structure model applied to simulate IOC system dynamics.
findings: Project organizational structure, contract, and trust all directly and positively affect IOC; project organizational structure positively affects both contract and trust, which mediate its effect on IOC (partial mediation confirmed via bootstrapping). Contract and trust jointly and dynamically interact with organizational structure rather than substituting for one another—they are complementary. Simulation results show contract-dominated and trust-dominated systems are more sensitive to organizational structure strength, while IOC-dominated systems (driven by willingness to collaborate) reach stability fastest and are less dependent on structure. Trust moderates the relationship between organizational structure and IOC. Overall, effective OSC governance requires dynamically aligning organizational structure (vertical/horizontal) with contract and trust mechanisms depending on project stage and delivery method.

ideas.idea: Conventional fragmented contracting in OSC projects reduces communication and collaboration across design, production and construction stages, raising costs and causing delays.
ideas.quote: The conventional contractual way reduces the communication and collaboration amongst stakeholders in design, production, and construction stages, leading to high production costs of precast components, high construction costs of OSC projects, and schedule delays

ideas.idea: Reliance on formal contract governance alone in OSC projects is prone to disputes, schedule delays and quality issues because of frequent design changes and out-of-contract tasks.
ideas.quote: OSC projects relying solely on formal contract governance are prone to a high level of contract disputes, schedule delays, and quality issues

ideas.idea: Integrated delivery methods such as EPC and IPD flatten the project organizational structure and foster trust-based collaboration among designers, manufacturers and contractors compared to conventional vertical structures.
ideas.quote: Compared to the traditional vertical organizational structure, the organizational structures corresponding to EPC and IPD promote the emergence of relational governance such as trust because clear contract terms are lacking considering cross-operation amongst design, production, and on-site instalment

ideas.idea: Contract governance and organizational structure jointly determine control allocation and reduce disputes by clarifying responsibilities among stakeholders.
ideas.quote: The control of the project is clarified through a project’s organizational structure, reducing the disputes and conflicts between partners caused by unclear power and vague contract terms

ideas.idea: Trust emerges as an informal relational governance mechanism to address contractual incompleteness when out-of-contract work arises during construction.
ideas.quote: In the construction process, uncertain events arise leading to the failure of written contractual terms due to contractual incompleteness, while informal governance mechanisms emerge... project participants who have not signed the contract still collaborate to complete the project tasks in terms of consultation and communication based on trust

ideas.idea: Project organizational structure and governance mechanisms (contract, trust) are complementary rather than substitutive, and should be jointly aligned rather than choosing one over the other.
ideas.quote: Project organizational structure and project governance mechanisms are complementary rather than substitutive for improving inter-organizational collaboration between the OSC project stakeholders.

ideas.idea: A vertical, hierarchical structure paired with strong contract governance suits conventional contracting, while a flat horizontal structure paired with trust suits integrated delivery methods.
ideas.quote: When project participants opt for a project organizational structure with a robust vertical structure, the contract governance approach holds greater significance than trust among OSC project team members. Conversely, when participants choose a flat organizational structure, the trust governance approach proves to be more effective than the contractual governance approach.

ideas.idea: A dual governance mechanism combining contract and trust is more effective than either alone for promoting IOC in OSC, suggesting long-term relational contracts for recurring stakeholder alliances.
ideas.quote: A dual governance mechanism including contract and trust is more effective for promoting the OSC project IOC than a single governance mechanism such as contract and trust... a long-term alliance might be built to collaborate between stakeholders related to OSC projects, such as designers, precast component manufacturers, and general contractors, through a relational contract and mutual trust.

ideas.idea: Bidding practices and one-time project engagements discourage deep trust and increase opportunistic behavior among OSC stakeholders, weakening formal contract governance's effectiveness.
ideas.quote: Considering existing bidding regulations, most project participants view the project as a one-time construction task that lacks deep trust. Participants tend to undertake one-time cooperation, increasing the probability of opportunistic behavior and reducing collaborative performance with their partners

ideas.idea: Project governance approaches and their relative importance evolve dynamically across project stages—contract dominates early on, while trust becomes more influential later as performance feedback accumulates.
ideas.quote: In the early stage, participants establish the content and form of cooperative work by signing formal contracts, which provide legal safeguards for their collaborative endeavors. As the project progresses, trust helps to mitigate conflicts and contradictions among OSC project participants.

objectives: To develop a structured decision-making approach for choosing between in situ and precast concrete in the early design stage of Australian construction projects by identifying influential factors, key decision makers, preferred precast building types, and prioritized concrete construction systems, and examining variations across sectors, contractual parties, and states.
problem_statement: Despite global growth in modular construction, Australia lags in prefabrication adoption; decision-making about construction methods is subjective, experience-based, lacks documented decision-support tools, and early decisions are often made without comprehensive understanding of options or involvement of relevant parties.
methodology: Mixed-methods study combining literature review, a pilot study with four experienced professionals to validate a preliminary list of factors, and an online Likert-scale survey distributed to Australian construction professionals across seven states, yielding 107 valid responses. Data analyzed using reliability analysis (Cronbach's alpha), Relative Importance Index (RII), Severity Index (SI), mean score analysis, factor analysis (PCA with Varimax rotation), t-tests, and ANOVA using SPSS 27.
key_background_studies: Hussein et al. (2014) - identified key decision factors (economic, environmental, technical, organizational, social) and constraints for off-site construction adoption in house building
Chen et al. (2010) - categorized decision attributes into seven dimensions (economic, social, environmental)
Sharafi et al. (2018) - classified decision-making criteria for modularization level into four areas: quality/safety, cost/sustainability, productivity/efficiency, constructability/design ease
Kamali and Hewage (2017) - reviewed sustainability indicators in modular vs conventional buildings, noting shift toward social dimension
Hosseini et al. (2018) - argued cost of off-site production is a substantial obstacle to adoption
Abdul Nabi and El-adaway (2020) - emphasized uncertainty in escalating alternative requirements and need for comprehensive decision criteria understanding
Navaratnam et al. (2022) - noted industry challenges in understanding off-site construction concept, contributing to adoption barriers
Goodier et al. (2019) - highlighted space/storage constraints and evaluative criteria relying on experiential/intuitive judgment for modular feasibility
Wuni and Shen (2022) - linked modularization adoption decisions to site conditions, project requirements, and location factors
Mesaros and Mandicak (2015) - highlighted production/site equipment, construction time, integration, coordination, transportation factors
findings: Schedule control was the most significant factor influencing choice between in situ and precast concrete. Factor analysis revealed six key clusters: HSEQ management, project scheduling and control, project characteristics, quality management, value management, and logistics management. Main contractors, structural engineers, and clients were identified as primary decision makers. Australian professionals preferred precast for industrial, office, educational, parking, and hotel buildings. In situ concrete remained the most preferred overall system, followed by large panel systems and tilt-up production. No significant differences were found between public/private sectors or occupations on most factors, though public sector prioritized regulatory constraints while private sector emphasized project characteristics and market considerations. Regional variations existed across states in building type preferences.

ideas.idea: Decisions about construction method are frequently made early without full stakeholder involvement or consideration of all options, highlighting a gap relevant to contractual timing of method selection.
ideas.quote: It is common for early decisions about a project to be made without involving all relevant parties or thoroughly considering all available options (Jin et al. 2018; Li et al. 2022).

ideas.idea: Cost concerns from both clients and contractors create resistance to prefabrication adoption, indicating a contractual/commercial risk allocation issue.
ideas.quote: Many clients declined to adopt prefabrication primarily due to the additional capital costs associated with it (Xue et al. 2018).

ideas.idea: Effective collaboration among key stakeholders during early project phases is essential for optimizing decisions about modularization, implying a need for contractual mechanisms enabling early collaboration.
ideas.quote: Therefore, a fundamental aspect of optimizing decision-making involves constructive collaboration among key stakeholders during the project's initial phases.

ideas.idea: Early contractor involvement and early design freeze are recognized decision factors affecting flexibility and scheduling, relevant to procurement and contract structuring for MMC.
ideas.quote: F20 Early design freeze or early contractor involvement

ideas.idea: Main contractors, structural engineers and clients are identified as the principal decision-makers for choosing between in situ and precast methods, indicating where contractual responsibility for method selection typically resides.
ideas.quote: the main influencers in the decision-making process between in situ and precast concrete are the main contractor, structural engineer, and client, who hold considerable sway.

ideas.idea: Logistics management—transportation of precast components and crane requirements—is a distinct risk category requiring specific planning and cost allocation in projects using precast methods.
ideas.quote: Transportation of components from factory to construction site is a critical issue in supply chain integration (Kamali and Hewage 2016).

ideas.idea: Volumetric prefabrication faces particular logistical challenges in dense urban areas including site access and storage constraints, which have implications for site management and contractual risk allocation.
ideas.quote: expert opinions underscore potential logistical challenges, particularly with volumetric prefabrication in densely populated urban areas, including issues with site access and on-site storage constraints.

ideas.idea: Regulatory and standard constraints are prioritized differently by public versus private sector practitioners, suggesting contract type/sector influences how MMC-related regulatory compliance is handled.
ideas.quote: Public sector practitioners tend to prioritize regulatory and standard constraints during the design stage.

ideas.idea: Contractor experience and knowledge, and contractor's attitude toward risk are recognized decision factors, pointing to the importance of contractor capability and risk appetite in MMC adoption—an issue relevant to contractual qualification and risk clauses.
ideas.quote: F27 Contractor's experience and knowledge... F28 Contractor's attitude toward risk

ideas.idea: Traditional in situ concrete remains the preferred system overall despite growth in precast, indicating persistent industry reliance on conventional methods and slower contractual/practical shift to MMC.
ideas.quote: Table 7 indicates that in situ concrete remains the preferred construction method among practitioners in the industry.

objectives: To analyze electrical construction prefabrication and identify current best practices and future improvement opportunities, considering the dependency of prefabrication on supply chain collaboration and labor union relations.
problem_statement: While prefabrication is increasingly adopted by electrical contractors for its safety, time, and cost benefits, prior research on electrical construction management has given limited attention to prefabrication itself, and no study had investigated how supply chain collaboration and labor union relations impact the successful implementation of electrical construction prefabrication.
methodology: A three-phase, industry-sponsored mixed-methods study: (1) data collection via semistructured interviews with a 12-member industry taskforce, site visits to prefabrication and vendor distribution facilities, acquisition of descriptive case studies, and an online questionnaire distributed to NECA's ~2,925 member firms (84 responses, 78 usable, response rate 2.9%, from 32 states); (2) development of best practices across operational/design requirements, vendor/distributor role, and manufacturer role by combining literature review, case studies, interview input, and quantitative questionnaire analysis; (3) identification of future improvement opportunities (labor union relations and lean principles) validated through taskforce feedback.
key_background_studies: Bogus et al. 2009 - only prior ELECTRI-sponsored study identifying best practices for operating an electrical contractor prefabrication facility
MHC 2011 - industry report showing electrical contractors as major adopters of prefabrication and relation between project type and prefabrication applicability
Mullens and Kelley 2004; Nahmens and Ikuma 2012 - lean manufacturing principles applied to modular/manufactured housing construction
Lu et al. 2011; Moghadam et al. 2012 - benefits of BIM in design and construction of modular buildings
Neelamkavil 2009 - adoption of automation and robotics in modular building manufacturing
Voordijk et al. 2006; Jeong et al. 2013; Said et al. 2014 - supply chain management as integral to construction prefabrication
Pagh and Cooper 1998 - concept of postponement/mass customization applied to standardized prefabrication components
El Asmar et al. 2013 - integrated project delivery (IPD) combining design and construction expertise to improve project outcomes
Kent and Becerik-Gerber 2010 - contractors aware of IPD benefits but awaiting consistent evidence before full implementation
Warszawski 2003 - long-range capacity planning for industrialized building fabrication, used as basis for suggested phased roadmap
Kumaraswamy and Matthews 2000; Lazar 1997; Eom et al. 2008 - partnership research mainly on owner-contractor/contractor-subcontractor relations, applied here to vendor partnerships
Hanna et al. 2013 - BIM investment requirements and use by electrical contractors
Salem et al. 2006 - lean construction principles successfully applied to onsite construction for over a decade
findings: The study identifies best practices in three categories: (1) operational/design requirements including BIM use, systematic labeling/packaging, assembly modularization/standardization, prefabrication scope identification, and phased capacity planning; (2) vendor/distributor roles including partnership agreements, early involvement, material management agreements, and preassembly kitting/area-based packaging; and (3) manufacturer roles including training workshops, packaging/labeling, and customized cataloged assemblies. IPD was found not to be a prerequisite for successful prefabrication, given the performance-based flexibility of electrical specifications. Two major improvement opportunities are identified: developing win-win relations between IBEW union locals and industrialized contractors (since union resistance, especially to outsourcing, is a significant barrier) and increasing implementation of lean principles, which currently is underused but positively correlated with higher prefabrication volume contribution.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication requires close supply chain collaboration among contractors, vendors/distributors, manufacturers, and even non-traditional participants like electrical fabricators to manage the complexity of splitting work between onsite and offsite.
ideas.quote: Supply chain management is an integral part of construction prefabrication... to mitigate the complexity that arises from splitting the work scope between onsite and offsite processes.

ideas.idea: Labor union relations and agreements can either enable or constrain contractors' ability to adopt prefabrication and outsourcing, representing a key contractual/relational risk.
ideas.quote: resistance of the local electricians' union may constrain contractors to prefabricate building systems outside of the project premises.

ideas.idea: BIM is a critical tool for coordinating prefabrication scope internally and communicating with supply chain partners, and its adoption correlates with greater vendor/manufacturer collaboration.
ideas.quote: there is a clear trend between the existence of BIM capability and (1) increased levels of vendor's early involvement in project planning... and (2) the number of prefabricated assembly types supplied directly from the manufacturer.

ideas.idea: A systematic labeling and packaging system is essential to manage the logistical complexity created when fabrication and installation are performed by different workforces at different locations.
ideas.quote: A clear, informative and consistent labeling/packaging system is therefore needed to distribute the assemblies correctly to their final rooms with the required installation instruction.

ideas.idea: Integrated Project Delivery is helpful but not required for successful prefabrication, partly because performance-based electrical specifications already provide sufficient design flexibility.
ideas.quote: insignificant dependency was found between successful prefabrication implementation and the existence of integrate project teams... IPDs can improve the prefabrication implementation process... but they are not a hard prerequisite.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication capacity should be developed incrementally through a phased roadmap, starting with outsourcing/subcontracting before investing in an in-house facility, partly to respect union labor portability policies.
ideas.quote: very careful attention needs to be paid to respect the imposed prefabrication and labor portability policies of local union locals, if any.

ideas.idea: Vendor partnership agreements, though legally nonbinding, formalize mutual responsibilities covering communication, materials, delivery, payment, technology, and training, effectively functioning as quasi-contractual arrangements supporting prefabrication.
ideas.quote: Vendor partnerships are formed as legally nonbinding agreements that clearly outline the mutual responsibilities of the two parties.

ideas.idea: Early vendor involvement in project planning is strongly associated with prefabrication success, suggesting a need for earlier integration of supply chain partners than traditional delivery methods allow.
ideas.quote: A vendor's early involvement is critical in projects with prefabrication operations to reduce the complexity of integrating onsite and offsite work by coordinating material inventory requirements and JIT deliveries.

ideas.idea: Manufacturers are shifting from simple product suppliers to active partners providing customized prefabricated assemblies, training, and packaging, expanding their contractual role in the supply chain.
ideas.quote: Manufacturers are keen to change their role in the traditional supply chain to act as business partners to electrical contractors.

ideas.idea: Union resistance is significantly higher for outsourcing prefabrication work to third parties than for in-house prefabrication, indicating a differentiated risk depending on where fabrication work is performed.
ideas.quote: Contractors with prefabrication facilities experience, on average, less resistance from the local union locals to prefabrication (−0.33 acceptance) and supply chain outsourcing (−1.02 acceptance), compared to contractors with no prefabrication experience.

ideas.idea: Cataloging prefabricated assemblies as standardized products (rather than custom assemblies) is a strategy manufacturers use to navigate union constraints on outsourced fabrication work.
ideas.quote: transforming the item description from an assembly to a catalog product may help in complying with current electrician union constraints.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication increases rework risk because errors and changes discovered onsite require costly redoing and resupply of offsite-fabricated components, a risk best mitigated through BIM coordination.
ideas.quote: prefabrication increases the magnitude of the rework risk as the major bulk of the work is performed offsite away from the final installation onsite location.

ideas.idea: There is a recognized need for future research into new labor union policies and contractual strategies, such as prefabrication outsourcing agreements and labor portability between union locals, to resolve union-contractor tensions.
ideas.quote: New policies and contractual strategies (such as prefabrication outsourcing and labor portability between locals) can be proposed to reach a win-win business conditions for both union locals and electrical contractors.

objectives: To evaluate prefabrication levels of buildings through the assembly rate and to develop a Stackelberg game model of the prefabricated construction supply chain (PCSC), consisting of a developer and general contractor, to determine optimal assembly rate and revenue-sharing decisions under government subsidies, and to design coordination contracts that achieve Pareto-optimal outcomes for both parties.
problem_statement: Although governments have introduced various subsidy policies (unit price subsidies and incremental cost subsidies) to promote prefabricated construction, the effectiveness of these subsidies in raising prefabrication levels remains ambiguous, and no analytical framework exists to model how developers and general contractors interact and decide on assembly rates given asymmetric bargaining power and information, nor how to design contracts that coordinate the supply chain and distribute the resulting surplus fairly.
methodology: Analytical/game-theoretic modeling study. The authors build a two-echelon Stackelberg game (developer as leader, general contractor as follower) representing the PCSC under two government financial subsidy schemes (unit price subsidy and incremental cost subsidy). They derive profit functions for decentralized and centralized decision scenarios, solve for optimal assembly rate and subsidy revenue-sharing coefficient using first-order optimality conditions and inverse induction, compare the two scenarios, propose a subsidy revenue-sharing contract and an improved transfer payment contract for supply chain coordination, and validate results with numerical simulation (MATLAB) using parameter values drawn from prior literature (e.g., Hong et al., 2018; Meng et al., 2021) representative of Chinese construction cost/subsidy data.
key_background_studies: Gao & Tian (2020) - compared directive vs supportive prefabrication policies in China, finding only strong incentive policies encourage widespread adoption
Liu et al. (2020) - used evolutionary game theory to show government subsidy alone cannot sustain adoption of prefabricated construction by construction units
Li et al. (2018) - surveyed construction enterprises to show subsidy policy significantly affects willingness to accept prefabrication
Pan et al. (2007) - identified capital cost, complex interfacing, and lead-time as barriers to precast construction uptake in UK housebuilders
Hong et al. (2018) - established cost-benefit analysis framework examining effect of prefabrication adoption on total project cost, used for parameter calibration
Jaillon & Poon (2008) - assessed economic, environmental and social benefits of prefabrication versus conventional construction
Chen & Hong (2015) - built a government subsidy model under asymmetric and complete information showing subsidy benefits depend on construction cost and developer preference
Jin et al. (2020) - developed tripartite evolutionary game (government-contractor-consumer) recommending tax and financial incentives to promote adoption
Wang & Liu (2020) - designed cooperative game profit incentive and collaborative pricing mechanism among PCSC stakeholders
Dou et al. (2021) - found contractors generally willing to adopt prefabrication but developers' negative investment behavior is the main barrier in Changchun
findings: The optimal assembly rate under the centralized scenario exceeds that under the decentralized scenario, indicating efficiency loss due to double marginalization in decentralized decision-making. A subsidy revenue-sharing contract with a revenue-sharing coefficient of 100% can coordinate the PCSC and achieve the centralized-scenario assembly rate, but this benefits the general contractor while reducing the developer's profit relative to the decentralized case, so it does not achieve a genuine Pareto improvement for both parties. An improved transfer payment contract, combining a fixed transfer fee with the subsidy revenue-sharing mechanism, can achieve full Pareto improvement for both developer and general contractor when the transfer payment falls within a specific favorable range ('Pareto zone'). Numerical analysis shows that increasing the incremental cost subsidy percentage raises both the optimal assembly rate and the revenue-sharing coefficient, and increases total PCSC profit, though the developer's profit may decline within certain subsidy ranges. A higher assembly rate benchmark set by government can discourage enterprises from participating if it becomes too costly to meet. Overall, appropriately designed subsidies and coordination contracts (especially transfer payment contracts) can promote prefabrication uptake and align incentives between developers and general contractors.

ideas.idea: Developers and general contractors have differing, sometimes conflicting, interests and bargaining power that shape prefabrication decisions, mirroring contractual allocation of risk and responsibility.
ideas.quote: The developers have the advantage of information resources, and their business decisions can guide and coordinate the general contractors to make corresponding decisions.

ideas.idea: General contractors bear the primary economic and quality/engineering risk of implementing prefabrication under contract terms set by developers.
ideas.quote: The general contractors respond to the needs of the emerging industrialized construction market and assume more responsibility and risk in terms of economic and engineering quality.

ideas.idea: Contracts can be structured to pass through government subsidies from developer to contractor via a revenue-sharing mechanism, illustrating how financial incentive flow-through can be embedded contractually between project parties.
ideas.quote: Developers could transfer the subsidies to incentivize the general contractors to improve prefabrication levels via a revenue-sharing contract.

ideas.idea: A simple revenue-sharing contract, even at its optimal coordinating value, fails to achieve a genuine win-win outcome because it favors one party (contractor) over the other (developer), highlighting the limits of single-mechanism contracts in construction supply chains.
ideas.quote: The developer cannot profit from the coordination, and the general contractor gains the excess profit from the coordination because of information asymmetry.

ideas.idea: A more sophisticated contract combining a fixed transfer payment with variable revenue-sharing can achieve genuine Pareto-improving coordination between contracting parties, suggesting contractual design complexity is needed to fairly allocate risk/benefit in prefabrication delivery.
ideas.quote: When the transfer payment amount is within the [86, 130] range, the improved transfer payment contract can increase the profits of the developer and general contractor and realize the overall coordination of the PCSC.

ideas.idea: Setting an assembly rate benchmark as a contractual/regulatory threshold affects willingness of enterprises to adopt higher levels of prefabrication, since exceeding the benchmark imposes additional cost burdens.
ideas.quote: As the assembly rate benchmark increases, it is common to see an assembly rate that is the same as the benchmark... a business may have been unwilling to construct prefabricated buildings in order to maximize its own profit.

ideas.idea: Information asymmetry between developer and contractor regarding cost data is a structural driver of inefficiency (double marginalization) in delivery of prefabricated projects, relevant to how contracts allocate information and risk.
ideas.quote: the developer cannot accurately observe the general contractor’s cost information, which leads to a double marginalization effect.

ideas.idea: Government subsidy design (level and type) interacts directly with contractual incentive structures between supply chain parties, suggesting subsidy policy and contract terms must be co-designed to promote prefabrication uptake.
ideas.quote: the government sector should appropriately increase government subsidies... and set a comparatively high subsidies factor and assembly rate benchmark to motivate prefabrication technology innovation.

objectives: To identify key principles for implementing strategic organizational and process changes in US design and construction companies (particularly SMEs) so they can successfully adopt offsite construction (OSC) in multifamily housing projects, contributing to more affordable and sustainable housing.
problem_statement: Despite the potential of OSC to improve efficiency, cost, quality and sustainability in the tight, affordability-challenged US multifamily housing market, adoption remains incipient in many regions due to risks (cost, logistics, insufficient standards, lack of experience) and a lack of holistic, expert-validated strategies—especially for SMEs—to guide companies through the transition, a gap not addressed by prior literature focused mainly on factors rather than implementation strategies.
methodology: A multi-phase mixed-methods design: (1) a Delphi survey with three panels of experts (contractors, designers, consultants/manufacturers/academics) over four rounds to validate and rank factors and changes needed for OSC adoption; (2) an online survey of 25 AEC professionals to obtain a reliable ranking of the most significant changes identified in the Delphi phase; (3) deductive qualitative analysis using the WEF (2016) company-level framework to draft principles, followed by semi-structured validation interviews with 12 mid-level AEC professionals (6 design, 6 construction) with OSC experience in US multifamily projects, coded and analyzed to refine a final set of eight principles.
key_background_studies: Gibb (2001) – provides the widely accepted categorization of OSC levels (component manufacture, non-volumetric, volumetric, modular buildings) used to define OSC scope in the study.
Gusmao Brissi et al. (2021a) – prior systematic literature review identifying 27 factors affecting OSC adoption in US multifamily projects, forming the basis for the Delphi survey content.

World Economic Forum (2016) – supplied the company-level framework (technology/materials/tools; processes/operations; strategy/business model; people/organization/culture) used to structure and organize the draft principles.
Sexton and Barrett (2003) – highlights SMEs' lack of organizational slack limiting their ability to test and commit to strategic changes, informing the leadership/mindset principle.
Bertram et al. (2019) – McKinsey report on OSC market conditions, risks, and drivers (demand, labor shortage) that frames the US context and logistics principle.
Akintoye and Main (2007) – on partnerships and risk-sharing in construction, underpinning the partnerships/contractual models principle.
Lessing and Brege (2015, 2018) – on industrialized/product-oriented business models and logistics integration in offsite housing.
Colton and Ahluwalia (2019) and Dodge Data and Analytics (2020) – industry surveys quantifying current OSC/modular use among multifamily builders, establishing market context.
findings: The study produced eight validated principles for adopting OSC in multifamily design and construction firms: (1) develop product-oriented business models, (2) promote leadership and mindset engagement with OSC, (3) engage in partnerships and more innovative contractual models, (4) shift toward digital transformation and automation, (5) develop training and knowledge management strategies, (6) adopt lean construction practices, (7) improve monitoring and quality control, and (8) integrate logistics and supply chain management with AEC processes. Sustainability was not perceived by practitioners as a driving principle but rather a consequence of OSC adoption; early stakeholder involvement was deemed important but outside the control of design/construction firms, so it was excluded from the final principles. The principles are interrelated (e.g., digital transformation depends on business model and training changes) and are especially relevant for SMEs, with implications for evolving company roles (e.g., becoming assemblers or vertically integrated firms) as OSC adoption deepens.

ideas.idea: Adopting more innovative contracting models that share responsibilities, risks, profits and expenses is identified as a key change needed to support OSC adoption.
ideas.quote: Adopt more innovative contracting models sharing responsibilities, risks, profits, and expenses

ideas.idea: Collaborative delivery methods such as Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) are recommended to support early engagement between parties and reduce adversarial relationships in OSC projects.
ideas.quote: Adopt collaborative delivery methods (such as IPD) that support early engagement between parties, reduce adverse relationships and encourage true inter-and multidisciplinary collaboration and transparency throughout the process.

ideas.idea: Designers and construction professionals often lack authority over the choice of delivery/contract model, which typically rests with owners or developers, limiting their ability to implement innovative contracts unilaterally.
ideas.quote: designers and construction professionals often do not have the power to decide on the type of contract that defines the delivery method.

ideas.idea: Partnerships between general contractors and subcontractors/manufacturers improve project delivery effectiveness, relationships, and procurement, which is particularly important given OSC's reliance on external manufacturing partners.
ideas.quote: Partnerships between GC and subcontractors increase the effectiveness of the project delivery process, improving relationships between parties and facilitating procurement (Dainty et al., 2001).

ideas.idea: Early involvement of all project stakeholders (including owners/developers) is widely seen as important for OSC success, but this responsibility often falls outside the control of design/construction firms, so it was not adopted as a firm-level principle.
ideas.quote: this strategy is more applicable to owners and developers; therefore, they did not include it in the final set of principles.

ideas.idea: Vertically integrated companies handling design, manufacturing, logistics and assembly under one contractual/organizational structure may emerge as OSC adoption deepens, changing traditional contractual boundaries between design and construction roles.
ideas.quote: the processes of design, engineering, manufacturing of construction parts, as well as the control of logistics and assembly on-site will all be performed by a single company (Lessing and Brege, 2018; Pullen et al., 2019).

ideas.idea: Contractual relationships with suppliers may need to be substantially revised when a company shifts its business model to focus on OSC.
ideas.quote: the company\u2019s contractual relationships with suppliers had to be completely revised to adapt to the new business model completely focused on the use of OSC.

ideas.idea: Insufficient laws, policies, and standards for OSC, along with new permitting/inspection models, are recognized risks, though design/construction firms have little direct control over regulatory frameworks.
ideas.quote: because of the little direct control design and construction companies have over new models of permitting and inspections, the authors removed this principle from the final set of principles.

ideas.idea: Logistical and supply chain issues must be treated as integral to the project process from project onset, requiring collaborative definition of module dimensions and handling requirements between design and construction teams, since these affect cost and schedule risk allocation.
ideas.quote: logistical issues must be an integral part of the project process since the project onset (Bertram et al., 2019; Lessing and Brege, 2015), with design and construction teams collaborating to define the dimensions of modules and components, temporary reinforcements, lifting points, etc.

ideas.idea: Allocating more time for design coordination, submittals analysis, planning and scheduling was the only change ranked as significant by all three expert panels, reflecting the heightened need for upfront coordination in OSC projects compared to traditional construction.
ideas.quote: Only one of the 17 changes was in the list of changes ranked by the three panels of experts: allocate more time for improved design coordination, submittals analysis, planning and scheduling.

objectives: To investigate how BIM contract practices impact stakeholder BIM implementation on AEC projects, specifically to evaluate the association between BIM implementation and contractual BIM requirements, and to examine stakeholder perceptions of the impact of contract requirements on BIM implementation at the project level.
problem_statement: While numerous BIM contract documents and guidelines exist (e.g., AIA, ConsensusDocs), there is little understanding of how these contracts are actually implemented on projects and their impact on BIM implementation by key stakeholders, nor of stakeholder perceptions and experiences of BIM-related contract requirements at the project level.
methodology: Mixed-methods approach: (1) a survey via Qualtrics of AEC professionals capturing project attributes (delivery method, project type, location, stakeholder BIM use, BIM contractual requirements, BEP use and requirement) for projects completed 2015-2021, with 36 usable responses analyzed using Fisher's exact test; (2) 21 semistructured interviews (23 interviewees) with AEC professionals (owners, contractors, designers/engineers, legal/claims consultants) conducted virtually August 2021-April 2022, analyzed using grounded theory qualitative coding (open, axial, selective coding) in NVivo, with peer review validation.
key_background_studies: Arshad et al. 2019 - developed a contractual framework for BIM-enabled design/bid/build projects and recommendations on model ownership, deliverables, and BIM execution planning
Ashcraft 2008 - discussed BIM contractual challenges including responsible control, admissibility of digital data, copyright, and standard of care
ConsensusDocs 2016/2015 - developed the 301-BIM addendum template addressing model vs. drawing precedence and BIM manager designation
AIA 2013a (E203) - defined authorized uses of models and consequences of undefined authorized uses, and LOD definitions
Messner et al. 2019 (BIM Project Execution Planning Guide) - provided structure/template for BIM execution plans and process maps
Celoza et al. 2021b/2023 - evaluated relationship between BIM contract requirements and project performance, and recommendations for requiring subcontractor BIM use
Assaad et al. 2020 - recommendations on data use limited to scope of work and contractually requiring BEPs
Chong et al. 2017 - recommended the party providing model data is responsible and liable for it
Francom and El Asmar 2015 - found BIM use leads to greater owner involvement due to visualization capability
Lee et al. 2020 - found contracts providing coordination procedures like model review impact stakeholder relationships and project success in EPC
findings: Fisher's exact test revealed significant associations between each stakeholder's (A/E, contractor, subcontractor) BIM use and their respective BIM contractual requirement, and a significant association between BEP use and its contractual requirement. Qualitative analysis of interviews identified four main categories of contract requirements impacting BIM implementation (deliverables, BIM-related meetings, BIM workflow documents, software requirements) and four main categories of contract-related BIM challenges (model-related challenges, reliance on 2D contract documents, lack of BIM standard practice, and BIM regulatory challenges). Findings suggest BIM contract requirements meaningfully influence BIM implementation, but significant challenges remain, particularly around the primacy of 2D documents over models, inconsistent standards, and regulatory limitations on model use for stamping/permitting.

ideas.idea: Standard contracts must decide whether the 2D drawings or the BIM model governs in case of conflict, since BIM is often not treated as a formal contract document.
ideas.quote: The two options are (1) the model takes precedence over 2D drawings or (2) the 2D drawings take precedence over the model when discrepancies arise.

ideas.idea: Even where contracts allow model use, absence of defined authorized uses places the risk of reliance on the model onto the receiving party.
ideas.quote: any use of, transmission of, or reliance on the Model is at the receiving Party's sole risk

ideas.idea: Model ownership and licensing terms are needed so authors retain ownership while other parties obtain licenses to use the model within their scope of work.
ideas.quote: It is recommended that whoever authors a model should retain ownership of it (Arshad et al. 2019).

ideas.idea: Defining BIM manager/information manager roles and formal collaboration meetings (kickoff, coordination, clash detection) in contracts supports BIM implementation.
ideas.quote: Arshad et al. (2019) recommends that a client define an "information manager" who will chair the BIM execution planning meetings.

ideas.idea: Common software requirements and defined information exchanges are recommended to prevent interoperability problems and data loss between project parties.
ideas.quote: there are recommendations for a common software (Arshad et al. 2019; Messner et al. 2019) to address potential interoperability challenges or data loss when transferring models and other data from one software to another

ideas.idea: Lack of direct contractual relationship between designer and contractor in traditional delivery methods (e.g., DBB, CMAR) can create information exchange gaps with no contractual remedy for insufficient model information.
ideas.quote: if the A/E produces a model that does not include sufficient information for construction or the correct type of information for construction, there are no contractual repercussions for the A/E, as there is a lack of formal contractual relationship between the A/E and contractor.

ideas.idea: Contractually requiring BIM execution plans (BEPs) is a recognized strategy to mitigate BIM-related risks and is associated with successful implementation.
ideas.quote: Numerous academic studies have recommended contractually requiring BEPs to mitigate potential BIM risks on projects (Arshad et al. 2019; Assaad et al. 2020), and BEPs have been identified as a critical success factor on BIM projects (Badrinath and Hsieh 2019).

ideas.idea: Inconsistent BIM maturity among project participants can cause contract requirements to be revised downward (e.g., dropping a specific software mandate) to accommodate contractors using less advanced tools, including prefabrication/CNC equipment.
ideas.quote: their CNC [Computer Numerical Control] equipment, their [ : : : ] prefabrication [machines don't] utilize Revit. They would have had to upgrade all of their machines. So, we actually ended up dropping the Revit requirement

ideas.idea: Reliance on 2D contract documents rather than the BIM persists in practice even when models are actively used, undermining full realization of BIM benefits.
ideas.quote: it's still written contractually that [ : : : ] it's a printed set of plans that you have to build from.

ideas.idea: Repeated translation of project information between 2D and 3D formats throughout a project's lifecycle introduces inefficiency and risk of data loss/conflict.
ideas.quote: The exchange of project information from 2D to 3D and back to 2D can result in a number of interoperability problems, including data loss or corruption, which can result in conflicts between project stakeholders

ideas.idea: Regulatory and professional liability constraints (e.g., stamping/sealing only 2D drawings, permitting only accepting 2D) limit the ability of BIM to replace 2D documents as authoritative contract/legal instruments.
ideas.quote: I don't know if I'd be comfortable stamping or certifying a model, because it seems like it would just be vulnerable to changes

ideas.idea: Lack of industry-wide standardization of BIM practices leads to bespoke, organization-specific processes that can conflict and create additional rework across project teams.
ideas.quote: Each organization develops and adopts its own BIM processes to achieve their specific objectives, which may or may not support other project organizations' processes or objectives.

ideas.idea: Model access restrictions and shared/live models raise unresolved liability questions about who is responsible for particular modeled elements.
ideas.quote: you need them to be able to access that BIM model. And now the question is, who's liable for what gets thrown in there?

ideas.idea: Inconsistent level of development (LOD) requirements among stakeholders can cause errors and limit the model's usefulness for downstream parties such as contractors.
ideas.quote: developing those standards and [ : : : ] communicating that with the design team would definitely allow [us to avoid] some of the errors that tend to happen when we get different levels of models.

objectives: To investigate the impact of Prefabricated Bathroom Unit (PBU) delivery reliability on on-site installation productivity, and to establish a situation-awareness-based Smart Contract using Blockchain technology to motivate reliable prefabricated construction material delivery.
problem_statement: Construction site managers face challenges tracking progress, coordinating task handoffs under interruptions, and motivating reliable work plan commitment from specialty trades and suppliers, especially under supply chain disruption (e.g., COVID). Current practices rely on subjective, delayed, and manual monitoring/penalty mechanisms, and there is a gap in using simulation-informed Smart Contracts to generate objective, real-time incentive/penalty rules for modular construction delivery reliability.
methodology: A case study of a high-rise residential project in Singapore using Prefabricated Bathroom Units (PBUs) was used. PBU loading platform and hoisting data (74 and 139 activities respectively) were collected on-site and fitted to statistical distributions (PERT, Gamma). A STROBOSCOPE discrete-event simulation model was built to represent PBU delivery, storage, and installation processes across an 11-floor building, tested under five delivery variability scenarios (via k-means clustering) run 100 times each. Cost and schedule outputs from the simulation were used to derive incentive/penalty amounts, which were then encoded into a Smart Contract deployed on the Ethereum blockchain (via Remix-Ethereum) and tested for automated incentive/penalty execution.
key_background_studies: Bamana et al. [4] and Goh and Goh [6] - simulation models comparing JIT vs non-JIT delivery, showing cycle time and productivity improvements with JIT
Liu et al. [13] - discrete event simulation of supply chain configurations showing importance of multi-supplier setups for manufacturing efficiency
Jung et al. [10] - showed construction and material supply should be viewed as one system, recommending on-site storage under supplier uncertainty
Mason [14,15] - introduced Smart Contract as a logical extension of BIM, noting full automation is limited by social/legal system constraints
Li et al. [12] - reviewed Blockchain applications in AEC industry with case studies demonstrating feasibility
Wang et al. [16] - developed a Blockchain platform to verify modular component delivery against planning in a precast project
Elghaish et al. [5] - proposed using real-time BIM 4D/5D data to assign incentives/penalties to crews
Ahmadisheykhsarmast and Sonmez [3] - built a construction contract platform linking MS Project data to Ethereum Smart Contracts for secure payments
Hamledari and Fischer [8] - proposed using reality capture technologies to trigger Smart Contract progress payments, but only at conceptual stage
findings: The simulation showed that PBU delivery variability significantly affects project schedule and cost: low variability (scenario 1) shortened duration to 40.9 days and saved $2,080 versus the benchmark (scenario 2, 41.5 days), while higher variability scenarios (3–5) increased duration to 45.7–50.8 days and cost overruns up to $29,600. These quantified impacts were converted into Ether-based incentives (e.g., 1.74 Ether) and penalties (e.g., 9.92–19.98 Ether) within a Smart Contract deployed on Ethereum. The Smart Contract successfully automated incentive payment and penalty enforcement based on detected delivery variability levels, and rejected attempts to underpay penalties, demonstrating rigorous, transparent, and tamper-proof contract execution. The study concludes that combining simulation-derived cost impacts with Blockchain-based Smart Contracts can objectively and instantly motivate reliable supplier delivery performance, reduce management burden, and be adapted to other modular construction projects.

ideas.idea: Delivery variability of prefabricated modules has a direct, quantifiable impact on installation productivity, project schedule, and cost, which can be modeled via simulation.
ideas.quote: A STROBOCOPE-based computer simulation model was established to study the productivity performance under different delivery scenarios.

ideas.idea: Current contractual practice penalizes delayed completion only at or near project completion, lacking mechanisms for prompt, transparent enforcement of reliability.
ideas.quote: In the current construction practice, the penalty of delayed completion is usually not enforced until project completion or near completion.

ideas.idea: Smart Contracts can encode simulation-derived incentive and penalty rules to automatically reward or penalize suppliers based on real-time delivery performance, reducing manual administration.
ideas.quote: Smart Contract alleviated the time-consuming work of tracking and paying by automating the consensus algorithms.

ideas.idea: Blockchain-based systems can provide objective, transparent, and tamper-proof records of supplier performance and payment transactions, replacing subjective performance appraisal methods.
ideas.quote: In many current practices, subcontractor performance appraisal tends to be subjective and qualitative. It is also difficult to customize the incentives and penalties that can reflect various levels of contributions.

ideas.idea: Smart Contract enforceability prevents parties from manipulating agreed terms once conditions are met, strengthening contractual reliability in construction supply chains.
ideas.quote: Therefore, no one can manipulate the contract once the detected condition is identified. Such rigorous execution of the Smart Contract enforces the commitment to be performed reliably to enhance the project’s overall performance.

ideas.idea: Uncertainty in manufacturing and shipping of prefabricated components, exacerbated by disruptions like COVID-19, increases the need for contractual tools that manage delivery risk in modular construction.
ideas.quote: Such a need is especially critical for modular construction project under the impact of COVID pandemic because of delay caused by the uncertainty and disruption of manuracturing and shipping time in supply chain.

ideas.idea: Current Blockchain/Smart Contract implementations for construction remain only semi-decentralized, as data inputs still require manual verification by a general contractor, limiting full automation of contractual administration.
ideas.quote: the inputs for Blockchain platform need to be verified and entered by the GC. So at the current stage, the Blockchain platform is not a fully decentralized system.

ideas.idea: The study builds on prior recognition that automated progress payment mechanisms are needed in construction contracts, extending this by linking cost/schedule impacts directly to smart contract incentive design.
ideas.quote: As recognized of the importance of necessity of the design of smart contracts for progress payments by previous researches [3, 8], this project provided an incentive-penalize Smart Contract prototype to promote reliable delivery of suppliers based on the customized needs.

objectives: To develop and validate a framework for identifying and classifying sources of ambiguity in construction contract documents, using both a comprehensive literature review and analysis of Supreme Court of Canada litigation cases, in order to support early detection of potential root causes of construction claims and disputes.
problem_statement: Despite the use of standard contract forms, construction contracts are frequently modified for individual projects, introducing ambiguities that lead to costly and lengthy disputes and litigation. Existing research on causes of disputes is fragmented, taking niche perspectives or discussing sources of ambiguity qualitatively, without a comprehensive, quantifiable framework linking common causal factors to actual litigation outcomes.
methodology: A two-phase mixed qualitative-quantitative approach: Phase 1 involved a comprehensive literature review (105 articles from 1985-2019) to extract 104 unique sources of ambiguity, which were clustered into a four-level hierarchical fishbone model (5 categories, 15 subcategories, 62 classes, 104 subclasses) building on Azghandi-Roshnavand et al.'s (2019) five-category framework, with frequency-based quantification of each category's support in the literature. Phase 2 involved screening 30,500 Supreme Court of Canada cases down to 285 construction-related cases, narrowing by topical/temporal/geographic criteria to 50 cases for first-level analysis and 13 cases for detailed analysis, cross-examining case motives against the fishbone model.
key_background_studies: Azghandi-Roshnavand et al. (2019) - proposed the original five-category conceptual framework (language, contract, design, stakeholders, external factors) that this study modified and expanded into the fishbone model
Cakmak and Cakmak (2013) - identified 28 common causes of disputes classified by contractor, contract, design, owner, project, human behavior, and external factors
Mahamid (2016) - studied dispute causes in residential building projects, ranking top reasons including payment delays and unrealistic contract duration

Odeh and Battaineh (2002) - identified 28 reasons for delay in traditional contracts through interviews, grouped into client, contractor, consultant, material, labor, contract documents, contractual relationships, and external factors
Broome and Hayes (1997) - studied clarity of NEC Engineering and Construction Contract, identifying word order, rationale clauses, and layout as key factors in contract clarity
Chehayeb et al. (2007) - analyzed motives of court cases related to CCDC-2 general conditions
Chan and Ann (2005) - studied clarity in expression of design liability and contractual provisions in design-build contracts, finding roles/responsibilities not clearly defined
Wright and Fergusson (2009) - reported that contract wording changes can impact project cost by as much as 5% of total budget
Fateh et al. (2017) - emphasized need for proper procurement route selection, particularly for industrialized/modular construction projects
findings: Incomplete and/or redundant information in contract documents were found to be the core reasons for conflict between contracted parties in Canadian construction litigation. The top five motives for SCC case filing were ambiguity in contract terms, poor contract draftsmanship, incompatible interpretation of terms among contract entities, missing information, and modification issues—all originating from the contract and stakeholder categories of the proposed model. Comparison between literature-based (top-down) and case-based (bottom-up) analyses showed four of the top five subcategories were common to both, though ranked differently; notably, lack of local industry readiness was prominent in literature but absent from court cases, while external factors related to modular/off-site construction had literature support but no corresponding SCC cases were found.

ideas.idea: Standard contract forms are frequently modified to meet project-specific needs, which introduces additional risks and ambiguities rather than eliminating them.
ideas.quote: In practice, however, these standard contract forms are often modified to satisfy the project requirements given by owners (and other parties involved).

ideas.idea: The literature places specific emphasis on the need for contractual arrangement guidelines for modern construction methods such as industrial and modular projects, indicating a recognized gap in matching contract forms to these delivery methods.
ideas.quote: The need for contractual arrangement guidelines, particularly in modern construction (such as industrial and modular) projects, is highlighted in the literature (Fateh et al. 2017).

ideas.idea: Modular/off-site construction (MOC) contracts suffer from a lack of separate, adequate specifications compared to conventional construction, contributing to ambiguity and dispute risk.
ideas.quote: Insufficient specifications in conventional construction and the lack of separate specifications for modular and off-site construction (MOC) are pointed out in this regard by the literature.

ideas.idea: Design decisions in modular construction are constrained by transportation/shipment method choices, creating a distinct category of design-related ambiguity not present in conventional construction.
ideas.quote: In modular construction, volumetric modules are transported from a production factory to the construction site. Therefore, depending on the choice of shipment method, there would be limitations and constraints to the module design.

ideas.idea: Systematic, fault-tolerant design approaches are necessary in modular construction to reduce on-site rework during module assembly, highlighting a design-stage risk unique to prefabrication.
ideas.quote: Shahtaheri et al. (2015) identified that the systematic design of fault-tolerant systems is required to minimize rework during the assembly of modules on-site.

ideas.idea: External factors specific to modular construction—such as transportation restrictions, contradictory transportation regulations between jurisdictions, and lack of a modular building code—are significant sources of ambiguity and dispute risk not present in traditional construction.
ideas.quote: Volumetric transportation difficulties in modular construction can negatively affect the overall control of the project's cost, schedule, and productivity... transportation restrictions and/or contradictory transportation regulations among different territories can become the source of claims and disputes.

ideas.idea: The maturity level and readiness of the local construction industry to adopt modern/efficient practices like industrialization and automation is a contractually relevant risk factor that must be considered in contract drafting.
ideas.quote: the level of local industry maturity and the adoption level of modern/efficient construction practices (e.g., digitalization, industrialization, and automation) in the workplace can strongly affect the progress of construction and must be overseen and taken into consideration in the contract.

ideas.idea: Despite literature emphasis on modular/off-site construction risks as a significant category of external-factor ambiguity, no Supreme Court of Canada cases were found relating to this delivery method, revealing a gap between anticipated risk and observed litigation.
ideas.quote: Some of the categories, such as external factors, which have considerable support in our literature analysis, particularly correspond with modular and off-site construction methods. However, the relevant court cases at the SCC did not include any projects of this type.

ideas.idea: Sources of contractual ambiguity and dispute can be strongly linked to the chosen project procurement strategy and contract type, an area not captured in the SCC case data and flagged for future research.
ideas.quote: it must be noticed that the common sources of confusion or ambiguity in construction contracts can be strongly correlated with the project procurement strategy adapted (e.g., delivery method, contract type).

ideas.idea: Recycling or reusing contract templates from previous projects without adequate modification is identified as a major barrier and source of ambiguity in the industry, relevant to standardized contracts like CCDC being reused without customization for new methods.
ideas.quote: Nasrollahzadeh et al. (2016) described recycling contracts from previous projects without proper modifications as one of the top barriers frequently occurring in the industry.

objectives: To identify and prioritize stakeholder-associated supply chain risks (SCRs) in prefabricated building projects (PBPs) in Hong Kong and to examine the dynamic interactions between these risks using social network analysis (SNA).
problem_statement: Prior SCR research has mainly adopted a static perspective, neglecting the dynamic interactions between risks and their associated stakeholders in prefabrication supply chains, despite the high interdependency of SCRs across multiple stakeholders in cross-border PBP supply chains in Hong Kong.
methodology: A mixed-methods case study approach: (1) literature review and expert interviews (3 experts) to identify 30 stakeholder-associated SCRs across 7 stakeholder groups; (2) a case study of a public housing project in Tuen Mun, Hong Kong (5,000 units, 5 buildings, 34-38 stories, June 2015-September 2017); (3) a focus group with project stakeholders to quantify risk interrelationships (likelihood and level of influence) using a five-point Likert scale, producing a risk structure matrix; (4) SNA using Netminer 4 software to compute network and node/link measures (density, cohesion, nodal degree, betweenness centrality, status centrality, brokerage, ego size) and identify critical risks and links.
key_background_studies: Koskela (2003) - explained the complexity of SCM-PBP from four perspectives (longer chain, more design work, longer error correction, higher dimensional accuracy requirements)
Christopher and Peck (2004) - categorization of SCRs into process, control, demand, supply, and environment risk types, adopted as the classification framework for this study
Pfohl et al. (2011) - discussed high interconnectedness and manifold nature of SCRs and their negative impacts on supply chain performance
Chiang et al. (2006) - argued that control over the supply chain, not prefabrication itself, provides sustainable competitive advantage
Yu et al. (2017) - methodology for assessing risk interrelationships via stakeholder questions on likelihood and level of impact, adopted in this study's focus group method
Yang et al. (2016) - prior application of SNA to stakeholder-related risks in complex green building projects, informing this study's approach
Li et al. (2016) - identified schedule delay issues in Hong Kong PBP supply chains related to tower crane breakdown and site management
Luo et al. (2015) - identified economic, market, on-site management, and technical risks in Chinese prefabrication supply chains
Choi et al. (2017) - identified site access, on-site storage, site operations, and labor productivity as barriers to PBP implementation in Hong Kong
findings: A total of 30 stakeholder-associated SCRs across 7 stakeholder groups were identified. SNA of the case project's risk network (43 nodes, 195 links) revealed nine critical risks and 11 critical links, which were grouped into three major challenges: (1) poor supply chain planning (e.g., inaccurate initial time/resource estimation by the main contractor, leading to labor shortages and quality problems); (2) poor control of working flows (e.g., delayed delivery of precast elements and delayed assembly schedules causing propagated schedule and quality issues); and (3) poor information sharing between stakeholders (e.g., design changes not communicated promptly between client, designer, main contractor, and manufacturer, leading to outdated production and delays). Removing the critical nodes/links substantially reduced network density (by 62%) and cohesion (by 79%), confirming their central role in driving overall supply chain risk complexity. The main contractor, manufacturer, and assembly subcontractor were found to play pivotal roles in the risk network.

ideas.idea: Prefabrication supply chains require close, frequent, integrated information exchange among many stakeholders (client, designer, contractor, manufacturer, transporter, assembly subcontractor) beginning at the design stage.
ideas.quote: Prefabrication should be integrated at the outset of the design stage, which requires a high degree of integration among stakeholders to ensure close coordination in maintaining labor, materials, and equipment

ideas.idea: Cross-border transportation between manufacturing facilities and site adds significant uncertainty and complexity to the contractual/logistical relationship in PBPs.
ideas.quote: most precast factories are in the Pearl River Delta area of Mainland China from which the components are transported by trucks through customs to Hong Kong, resulting in substantial uncertainty and task complexity during the transportation process.

ideas.idea: The design-bid-build delivery model used for public housing PBPs in Hong Kong places the client at the top of a chain that separately contracts consultants for design and a main contractor for supply chain management, who then subcontracts manufacturing, transport, and assembly.
ideas.quote: The housing authority is the client of public housing projects who directly recruits a consultant for design work and a main contractor for management of the project supply chain. The main contractor employs a manufacturer, a transporter, and an assembly subcontractor and reports the project status to the client on a weekly basis.

ideas.idea: Poor planning of resources and schedule by the main contractor, evidenced by frequent revisions of the master program, propagates disruption throughout the supply chain including labor shortages and quality issues.
ideas.quote: The master program has been revised seven times, indicating the poor estimation of resources and schedule (S3R14). As a result, resources deployment in the factory and on the site is largely disorganized

ideas.idea: Design changes initiated by the client that are not promptly communicated to downstream parties (main contractor, manufacturer) cause cost overruns and delays, highlighting a contractual/communication risk around variations.
ideas.quote: design changes (S1R1) as a common problem in building projects often occur in the case supply chain without prior consultation (S2R5) with the manufacturer and the main contractor.

ideas.idea: Delayed delivery of precast elements and delayed assembly schedules are critical, highly interconnected risk nodes reflecting poor control over working flows between manufacturing and site assembly, a key contractual coordination issue in prefabrication.
ideas.quote: Delayed delivery of precast elements to the site (S4R6) and delayed assembly schedule (S6R23) are two important nodes that reflect the poor control of working processes in both the upstream and the downstream chains and cause significant schedule and quality problems.

ideas.idea: Manufacturers often serve multiple clients/projects simultaneously, leading to competition for factory resources that can cause delays affecting a single project's contractual obligations.
ideas.quote: the manufacturer does not work for only one project but has signed contracts with multiple clients. The factory, therefore, has to plan resources for several projects at the same time but suffers from poor coordination of resources among different projects.

ideas.idea: Obsolete communication methods (email, WhatsApp, hard copies) among stakeholders are identified as a root cause of many supply chain and contractual coordination problems in PBPs.
ideas.quote: the stakeholders interact with each other mainly by email, WhatsApp, and hard copies of project documents. Such obsolete ways of communication and the unawareness of frequent information exchanges between stakeholders are the root cause of many problems in the supply chain.

objectives: To evaluate and compare the effects of a subsidy mechanism versus a reward-penalty mechanism on environmental responsibility (ER) decisions of contractors and suppliers within the prefabricated construction supply chain (PCSC), determine optimal ER levels and profits under both mechanisms, assess which mechanism yields greater environmental benefits, and identify applicable scenarios for each policy type.
problem_statement: Prefabricated construction shifts environmental burdens from on-site construction to off-site manufacturing, requiring coordinated environmental responsibility across upstream suppliers and downstream contractors. While government subsidy and reward-penalty mechanisms are used to incentivize ER behavior, existing studies treat government policy as exogenous, ignore strategic interdependence between upstream and downstream agents, and rely on single-dimensional indicators (e.g., emissions) without considering government financial expenditure, leaving a gap in understanding how these mechanisms should be designed and compared for the decoupled PCSC structure.
methodology: The study develops a three-level Stackelberg game model involving the government (leader), contractor, and supplier (followers) in a PCSC, with a sequential decision structure (government sets policy; contractor sets overall ER level; supplier sets its ER-undertaking rate). Backward induction is used to derive optimal decisions and profit functions under a subsidy mechanism (Model A) and a reward-penalty mechanism (Model B), compared against a no-policy baseline. Two indicators—Optimal Environmental Benefit (OEB) and Net Environmental Benefit (NEB)—are used to assess policy effectiveness. A real-world case study of a prefabricated construction project in Beijing (2018, ~188,996.08 m3 construction area, 60-80% prefabrication rate) is used with numerical simulation to validate theoretical findings.
key_background_studies: Wang and Wang (2023) - showed unit cost subsidies reduce emission intensity but may increase total emissions under volumetric schemes
Wang et al. (2024) - found green subsidies and unit subsidies yield equivalent carbon allocation outcomes in PCSCs, used for comparison with this study's finding of equal ER allocation
Yi et al. (2024) - designed a government-manufacturer-contractor three-tier subsidy model to enhance sustainability
Weng et al. (2023) - demonstrated reward-penalty intensity drives decarbonization but has an incentive-intensity paradox
Zhao et al. (2020) - showed reward-penalty schemes in remanufacturing supply chains optimize buyback pricing and recycling performance
Chen and Ulya (2019) - found reward-penalty mechanisms incentivize green production and product return rates
Jia et al. (2017) - proposed combining penalties, waste disposal fees, and subsidies for construction waste management effectiveness
Rathore and Sarmah (2021) and Wang et al. (2022) - found reward-penalty mechanisms improve waste collection rates more than subsidies, contrasted with this study's profitability findings
Liu et al. (2021) - noted role of subsidies in promoting environmental participation
findings: Under both mechanisms, contractor and supplier adopt equal ER levels (50% each), achieving balanced allocation of environmental effort. The subsidy mechanism increases both agents' profits relative to baseline but yields lower environmental benefits (lower OEB and NEB) than the reward-penalty mechanism, especially once the subsidy cap is reached.
